question_stem:
Your company recently created an Azure subscription.
You have been tasked with making sure that a specified user is able to implement Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM).
Which of the following is the role you should assign to the user?
explanation:
To start using PIM in your directory, you must first enable PIM.
1. Sign in to the Azure portal as a Global Administrator of your directory.
You must be a Global Administrator with an organizational account (for example, @yourdomain.com), not a Microsoft account (for example, @outlook.com), to enable PIM for a directory.
Scenario: Technical requirements include: Enable Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM) for contoso.com
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/bs-latn-ba/azure/active-directory/privileged-identity-management/pim-getting-started
answer_summary: Enabling and administering PIM for the tenant requires Global Administrator; that role is also the only one here that can consent to onboard PIM and then delegate PIM management.

option_rationales.A: A Global Administrator (with an organizational account, not an MSA) is required to enable PIM for the directory and to grant the first PIM role assignments. Note: in today's Microsoft Entra ID, day-to-day PIM administration can then be delegated to Privileged Role Administrator.
option_rationales.B: Security administrator can read Identity Protection and security settings but cannot enable PIM or manage privileged role assignments.
option_rationales.C: Password administrator can only reset passwords for non-administrative users — no directory or role-management rights.
option_rationales.D: Compliance administrator manages Purview/compliance features and has no rights over directory roles or PIM.

verification.note: Still current: Global Administrator is required for initial PIM onboarding; PIM itself is now licensed under Microsoft Entra ID P2 / Entra ID Governance.

question_stem:
Note: The question is included in a number of questions that depicts the identical set-up. However, every question has a distinctive result. Establish if the solution satisfies the requirements.
Your company has an Active Directory forest with a single domain, named weylandindustries.com. They also have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant with the same name.
You have been tasked with integrating Active Directory and the Azure AD tenant. You intend to deploy Azure AD Connect.
Your strategy for the integration must make sure that password policies and user logon limitations affect user accounts that are synced to the Azure AD tenant, and that the amount of necessary servers are reduced.
Solution: You recommend the use of pass-through authentication and seamless SSO with password hash synchronization.
Does the solution meet the goal?
explanation:
For pass-through authentication, you need one or more (we recommend three) lightweight agents installed on existing servers. These agents must have access to your on-premises Active Directory Domain Services, including your on-premises AD domain controllers. They need outbound access to the Internet and access to your domain controllers. For this reason, it's not supported to deploy the agents in a perimeter network.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/hybrid/how-to-connect-pta
answer_summary: Pass-through authentication validates every sign-in against an on-premises domain controller in real time, so on-prem password policy and logon-hour restrictions are enforced, and its lightweight agents can run on existing servers. Enabling password hash sync alongside PTA is only a backup and does not change the active sign-in method.

option_rationales.A: With PTA as the sign-in method, authentication is evaluated by an on-premises DC, so password policies and logon restrictions apply; the PTA agent installs on existing servers (including the Entra Connect server), so no extra servers are needed. PHS here is only a failover option that an admin must manually switch to.
option_rationales.B: The presence of password hash synchronization does not disable PTA. Hashes are synced but not used for authentication unless the tenant's sign-in method is deliberately changed.

verification.note: Answer changed from B to A. Microsoft's hybrid identity comparison lists PTA as enforcing on-premises account policy at sign-in, and PHS is documented as an optional backup for PTA. Community votes are split (64% Yes / 32% No); the exam bank's stored key was No.

question_stem:
Note: The question is included in a number of questions that depicts the identical set-up. However, every question has a distinctive result. Establish if the solution satisfies the requirements.
Your company has an Active Directory forest with a single domain, named weylandindustries.com. They also have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant with the same name.
You have been tasked with integrating Active Directory and the Azure AD tenant. You intend to deploy Azure AD Connect.
Your strategy for the integration must make sure that password policies and user logon limitations affect user accounts that are synced to the Azure AD tenant, and that the amount of necessary servers are reduced.
Solution: You recommend the use of federation with Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS).
Does the solution meet the goal?
explanation:
A federated authentication system relies on an external trusted system to authenticate users. Some companies want to reuse their existing federated system investment with their Azure AD hybrid identity solution. The maintenance and management of the federated system falls outside the control of Azure AD. It's up to the organization by using the federated system to make sure it's deployed securely and can handle the authentication load.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/hybrid/how-to-connect-pta
answer_summary: AD FS does enforce on-premises password policies and logon restrictions, but it fails the second requirement: federation needs additional federation and Web Application Proxy servers, so the server count goes up, not down.

option_rationales.A: Federation meets the policy-enforcement half of the requirement but requires a dedicated AD FS farm plus WAP/proxy servers, which conflicts with reducing the number of servers.
option_rationales.B: AD FS is the most infrastructure-heavy option. Pass-through authentication achieves the same on-premises policy enforcement with lightweight agents on existing servers.

verification.note: Community 100% B.

question_stem:
Note: The question is included in a number of questions that depicts the identical set-up. However, every question has a distinctive result. Establish if the solution satisfies the requirements.
Your company has an Active Directory forest with a single domain, named weylandindustries.com. They also have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant with the same name.
You have been tasked with integrating Active Directory and the Azure AD tenant. You intend to deploy Azure AD Connect.
Your strategy for the integration must make sure that password policies and user logon limitations affect user accounts that are synced to the Azure AD tenant, and that the amount of necessary servers are reduced.
Solution: You recommend the use of password hash synchronization and seamless SSO.
Does the solution meet the goal?
explanation:
Password hash synchronization requires the least effort regarding deployment, maintenance, and infrastructure. This level of effort typically applies to organizations that only need their users to sign in to Office 365, SaaS apps, and other Azure AD-based resources. When turned on, password hash synchronization is part of the Azure AD Connect sync process and runs every two minutes.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/hybrid/how-to-connect-pta
answer_summary: With password hash synchronization, sign-ins are validated by Microsoft Entra ID in the cloud against synced hashes, so on-premises password policies and logon-hour limitations are not enforced. The requirement is only met by pass-through authentication.

option_rationales.A: PHS is the lightest deployment, but authentication happens in the cloud. On-prem complexity/expiry rules and logon hours are not evaluated, so the stated requirement fails.
option_rationales.B: PHS cannot enforce on-premises account policy at sign-in (only account-disabled/deleted state flows through on the next sync). Pass-through authentication is the option that satisfies the requirement.

verification.note: Answer changed from A to B. Microsoft's hybrid identity comparison table: 'Enforces on-premises account policy at sign-in' = No for PHS, Yes for PTA. Community 95% B.

question_stem:
Your company has an Active Directory forest with a single domain, named weylandindustries.com. They also have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant with the same name.
After syncing all on-premises identities to Azure AD, you are informed that users with a givenName attribute starting with LAB should not be allowed to sync to Azure AD.
Which of the following actions should you take?

options.A: You should make use of the Synchronization Rules Editor to create an attribute-based filtering rule.
options.B: You should configure a DNAT rule on the Firewall.
options.C: You should configure a network traffic filtering rule on the Firewall.
options.D: You should make use of Active Directory Users and Computers to create an attribute-based filtering rule.

explanation:
Use the Synchronization Rules Editor and write attribute-based filtering rule.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/hybrid/how-to-connect-sync-change-the-configuration
answer_summary: Attribute-based filtering — excluding objects by an attribute value such as givenName starting with LAB — is configured in the Synchronization Rules Editor that ships with Entra Connect Sync.

option_rationales.A: You add an inbound sync rule with a scoping filter on givenName so matching objects are not projected into the metaverse, and therefore never sync to the tenant.
option_rationales.B: A DNAT rule translates inbound network addresses on a firewall; it has no relationship to directory synchronization scope.
option_rationales.C: Network traffic filtering blocks or allows packets. It could break sync entirely but cannot exclude specific user objects.
option_rationales.D: Active Directory Users and Computers manages on-premises objects; it has no sync-filtering capability. Filtering is a function of the sync engine, not AD DS.

verification.note: Still valid for Entra Connect Sync. If you use Entra Cloud Sync instead, the equivalent is an attribute-based scoping filter in the cloud sync configuration.

question_stem:
You have been tasked with applying conditional access policies for your company's current Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
The process involves assessing the risk events and risk levels.
Which of the following is the risk level that should be configured for users that have leaked credentials?
explanation:
These six types of events are categorized in to 3 levels of risks – High, Medium & Low:

| Sign-in Activity | Risk Level |
|------------------|------------|
| Users with leaked credentials | High |
| Sign-ins from anonymous IP addresses | Medium |
| Impossible travel to atypical locations | Medium |
| Sign-ins from infected devices | Medium |
| Sign-ins from IP addresses with suspicious activity | Low |
| Sign-ins from unfamiliar locations | Medium |

Reference:
http://www.rebeladmin.com/2018/09/step-step-guide-configure-risk-based-azure-conditional-access-policies/

diagrams.diagram_description: Table showing six types of sign-in activity events categorized into three risk levels: High (users with leaked credentials), Medium (sign-ins from anonymous IP addresses, impossible travel to atypical locations, sign-ins from infected devices, sign-ins from unfamiliar locations), and Low (sign-ins from IP addresses with suspicious activity).

answer_summary: Leaked credentials is the one detection Microsoft classifies as High risk, because a matching username/password pair has been found in a public or dark-web dump — evidence of compromise rather than a suspicious signal.

option_rationales.A: None is not a level you configure for a detection; it would mean the event is ignored entirely.
option_rationales.B: Low is used for the weakest signal — sign-ins from infected devices.
option_rationales.C: Medium covers the behavioural signals: anonymous IP address, impossible travel, unfamiliar location and IP addresses with suspicious activity.
option_rationales.D: Leaked credentials is rated High risk; it is the trigger typically wired to a Conditional Access policy that forces a secure password change.

verification.note: Leaked credentials is still a High-risk detection in Microsoft Entra ID Protection. Caution on the table printed in this question's explanation: it shows infected devices as Medium and suspicious-activity IPs as Low, which is the reverse of Microsoft's own risk-event reference (infected devices = Low, suspicious-activity IPs = Medium).

question_stem:
You have been tasked with applying conditional access policies for your company's current Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
The process involves assessing the risk events and risk levels.
Which of the following is the risk level that should be configured for sign ins that originate from IP addresses with dubious activity?
explanation:
Reference:
http://www.rebeladmin.com/2018/09/step-step-guide-configure-risk-based-azure-conditional-access-policies/
answer_summary: Microsoft's risk-event reference rates 'Sign-ins from IP addresses with suspicious activity' as Medium: many failed sign-ins across multiple accounts were seen from that IP, but several devices can share one address, so it is not treated as High.

option_rationales.A: None would mean the detection is not risk-rated at all, which is not the case.
option_rationales.B: Low is the level for sign-ins from infected devices — the detection whose evidence is weakest because it is inferred from an IP talking to bot servers.
option_rationales.C: Medium is correct: suspicious-activity IPs sit alongside anonymous IP, impossible travel and unfamiliar location at Medium.
option_rationales.D: High is reserved for leaked credentials, where a valid username/password pair is known to be exposed.

verification.note: Verified against Microsoft's risk-event-types reference, which lists this detection as Medium and 'sign-ins from infected devices' as Low. Beware: a widely-copied blog table (cited by this bank in Topic 1 Q6 and Topic 2 Q6) swaps those two levels. Community 62% C. In current Entra ID Protection these fixed legacy levels are gone — each detection now carries a Low/Medium/High rating Microsoft tunes over time.

question_stem:
You have been tasked with configuring an access review, which you plan to assigned to a new collection of reviews. You also have to make sure that the reviews can be reviewed by resource owners.
You start by creating an access review program and an access review control.
You now need to configure the Reviewers.
Which of the following should you set Reviewers to?
explanation: In the Reviewers section, select either one or more people to review all the users in scope. Or you can select to have the members review their own access. If the resource is a group, you can ask the group owners to review.

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure Portal screenshot showing Reviewers dropdown menu with options: Group owners (selected and highlighted), Group owners, Selected users, and Members (self), alongside a Programs section with Link to program option.

answer_summary: Setting Reviewers to Group owners is what makes an access review be performed by the resource owners, which is exactly the stated requirement.

option_rationales.A: Selected users hands the review to named individuals you pick, not to whoever owns the resource.
option_rationales.B: Members (self) makes each user attest to their own access — self-review, not owner review.
option_rationales.C: When the resource is a group, choosing Group owners delegates the review to the resource owners, who can change over time without the review needing to be edited.
option_rationales.D: Anyone is not an available Reviewers option in an access review.

verification.note: Current Entra ID Governance access reviews still offer Group owners / Selected user(s) or group(s) / Members (self); the wording is now 'Group owners'.

question_stem:
Your company recently created an Azure subscription. You have, subsequently, been tasked with making sure that you are able to secure Azure AD roles by making use of Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Privileged Identity Management (PIM).
Which of the following actions should you take FIRST?

options.A: You should sign up Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Privileged Identity Management (PIM) for Azure AD roles.
options.B: You should consent to Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Privileged Identity Management (PIM).

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/privileged-identity-management/pim-getting-started
answer_summary: Nothing in PIM can be configured until the tenant has consented to (onboarded) PIM — that consent is the first step, and only then can you sign up roles, discover privileged roles or discover resources.

option_rationales.A: Signing up PIM for Azure AD roles comes after consent; the option is not available until PIM has been onboarded for the directory.
option_rationales.B: Consent is the first action — a Global Administrator gives consent, which registers PIM in the tenant and unlocks every other PIM task.
option_rationales.C: Discovering privileged roles is a review activity you perform once PIM is running, not a prerequisite.
option_rationales.D: Discovering resources applies to PIM for Azure resource roles, and again only after onboarding.

verification.note: Matches the legacy 'Start using PIM' sequence (consent → sign up roles → discover). In current Microsoft Entra ID, PIM needs no separate consent step: with Entra ID P2 it is available immediately, so this question is historical.

question_stem:
You need to consider the underlined segment to establish whether it is accurate.
You have been tasked with creating a different subscription for each of your company's divisions. However, the subscriptions will be linked to a single Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant.
You want to make sure that each subscription has identical role assignments.
You make use of Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM).
Select 'No adjustment required' if the underlined segment is accurate. If the underlined segment is inaccurate, select the accurate option.
explanation:
The Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM) service also allows Privileged Role Administrators to make permanent admin role assignments.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/privileged-identity-management/pim-how-to-add-role-to-user
answer_summary: PIM only governs how existing role assignments are activated for individuals — it cannot replicate a role-assignment set into many subscriptions. Azure Blueprints packages RBAC assignments (plus policies and templates) as artifacts and applies them identically to each subscription.

option_rationales.A: PIM is a just-in-time activation and review tool for privileged roles. It does not deploy or standardize assignments across subscriptions, so the underlined segment is wrong.
option_rationales.B: Azure Blueprints deploys role assignments, policy assignments, resource groups and ARM templates as a repeatable package, which is what makes several subscriptions identical.
option_rationales.C: Conditional Access controls the conditions under which users authenticate — nothing to do with subscription-level RBAC assignments.
option_rationales.D: Azure DevOps is a CI/CD and work-tracking service; it could run scripts, but it is not the governance feature this question targets.

verification.note: Answer changed from A to B (community 100% B). Currency caveat: Azure Blueprints is on a deprecation path — Microsoft now recommends Template Specs plus deployment stacks for the same repeatable-governance goal, so expect newer exam items to name those instead.

question_stem:
Your company has an Azure Container Registry.
You have been tasked with assigning a user a role that allows for the uploading of images to the Azure Container Registry. The role assigned should not require more privileges than necessary.
Which of the following is the role you should assign?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/bs-latn-ba/azure/container-registry/container-registry-roles
answer_summary: AcrPush is the built-in registry role whose only extra permission over pull is docker push, making it the least-privilege choice for uploading images.

option_rationales.A: Owner grants full control of the registry including RBAC assignment — far more than uploading needs.
option_rationales.B: Contributor can manage and delete the registry itself, so it violates least privilege.
option_rationales.C: AcrPush gives pull + push on repositories and nothing else — exactly the upload permission required.
option_rationales.D: AcrPull only allows downloading images; a push would be denied.

verification.note: AcrPush is still the current least-privilege push role for Azure Container Registry.

question_stem:
Your company has an Azure Container Registry.
You have been tasked with assigning a user a role that allows for the downloading of images from the Azure Container Registry. The role assigned should not require more privileges than necessary.
Which of the following is the role you should assign?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/bs-latn-ba/azure/container-registry/container-registry-roles
answer_summary: Downloading (pulling) images is a data-plane operation on the registry's repositories, which is granted by the AcrPull role — the generic Reader role only exposes the registry's management-plane properties.

option_rationales.A: Reader lets the user see the registry resource in Azure Resource Manager but grants no repository data actions, so docker pull fails.
option_rationales.B: Contributor can pull, but it can also push, delete repositories and reconfigure the registry — not least privilege.
option_rationales.C: AcrDelete allows deleting images; it is neither needed nor sufficient for downloading.
option_rationales.D: AcrPull grants exactly the pull permission on repositories and nothing more.

verification.note: Answer changed from A to D (community 100% D). Reader has no registry data actions; AcrPull is the documented least-privilege pull role.

question_stem:
Note: The question is included in a number of questions that depicts the identical set-up. However, every question has a distinctive result. Establish if the solution satisfies the requirements.
Your Company's Azure subscription includes a virtual network that has a single subnet configured.
You have created a service endpoint for the subnet, which includes an Azure virtual machine that has Ubuntu Server 18.04 installed.
You are preparing to deploy Docker containers to the virtual machine. You need to make sure that the containers can access Azure Storage resources and Azure SQL databases via the service endpoint.
You need to perform a task on the virtual machine prior to deploying containers.
Solution: You create an application security group.
Does the solution meet the goal?
answer_summary: The containers need their own IP addresses on the VNet so their traffic is recognised by the subnet's service endpoint — that requires the Azure Virtual Network CNI plug-in. An application security group does nothing for containers.

option_rationales.A: An application security group is only a logical grouping of NICs used as a source/destination in NSG rules; it gives containers no VNet identity, so service-endpoint traffic still fails.
option_rationales.B: ASGs are an NSG rule-scoping construct. The prerequisite task on the VM is installing the Azure VNet CNI plug-in.

verification.note: Community 100% B.

question_stem:
Note: The question is included in a number of questions that depicts the identical set-up. However, every question has a distinctive result. Establish if the solution satisfies the requirements.
Your Company's Azure subscription includes a virtual network that has a single subnet configured.
You have created a service endpoint for the subnet, which includes an Azure virtual machine that has Ubuntu Server 18.04 installed.
You are preparing to deploy Docker containers to the virtual machine. You need to make sure that the containers can access Azure Storage resources and Azure SQL databases via the service endpoint.
You need to perform a task on the virtual machine prior to deploying containers.
Solution: You create an AKS Ingress controller.
Does the solution meet the goal?
answer_summary: An AKS ingress controller is a Kubernetes-cluster component for routing inbound HTTP traffic; it has nothing to do with letting Docker containers on a standalone VM reach Storage and SQL through the subnet's service endpoint.

option_rationales.A: There is no AKS cluster here — the containers run directly on an Ubuntu VM. An ingress controller also handles inbound traffic, while this requirement is about outbound access to Azure services.
option_rationales.B: The required task is installing the Azure Virtual Network CNI plug-in so containers get VNet IP addresses recognised by the service endpoint.

verification.note: Community 100% B.

question_stem:
Note: The question is included in a number of questions that depicts the identical set-up. However, every question has a distinctive result. Establish if the solution satisfies the requirements.
Your Company's Azure subscription includes a virtual network that has a single subnet configured.
You have created a service endpoint for the subnet, which includes an Azure virtual machine that has Ubuntu Server 18.04 installed.
You are preparing to deploy Docker containers to the virtual machine. You need to make sure that the containers can access Azure Storage resources and Azure SQL databases via the service endpoint.
You need to perform a task on the virtual machine prior to deploying containers.
Solution: You install the container network interface (CNI) plug-in.
Does the solution meet the goal?
explanation:
The Azure Virtual Network container network interface (CNI) plug-in installs in an Azure Virtual Machine. The plug-in supports both Linux and Windows platform.
The Azure Virtual Network CNI plug-in assigns IP addresses from a virtual network to containers brought up in the virtual machine, attaching them to the virtual network, and connecting them directly to other containers and virtual network resources. The plug-in doesn't rely on overlay networks, or routes, for connectivity, and provides the same performance as virtual machines.
The following picture shows how the plug-in provides Azure Virtual Network capabilities to Pods:
The Azure Virtual Network container network interface (CNI) plug-in assigns IP addresses from a virtual network to containers brought up in the virtual machine, attaching them to the virtual network, and connecting them directly to other containers and virtual network resources. The plug-in doesn't rely on overlay networks, or routes, for connectivity, and provides the same performance as virtual machines.
The following picture shows how the plug-in provides Azure Virtual Network capabilities to Pods:

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure Virtual Network architecture diagram showing existing virtual network with Azure Firewall and Containers connecting through NAT to Pods and then to Internet via Service Endpoints, with On-premises connection and Azure Services (SQL and storage icons) displayed at the bottom.

answer_summary: The Azure Virtual Network CNI plug-in installs on the VM and assigns real VNet IP addresses to containers, attaching them directly to the subnet so their traffic is carried over the subnet's service endpoints to Storage and SQL.

option_rationales.A: With the CNI plug-in the containers are first-class VNet endpoints (no NAT/overlay), so service endpoints, NSGs and route tables apply to their traffic.
option_rationales.B: Without the plug-in, containers sit behind NAT on the host and their traffic is not treated as coming from the service-endpoint-enabled subnet.

verification.note: Community 100% A.

question_stem:
You make use of Azure Resource Manager templates to deploy Azure virtual machines.
You have been tasked with making sure that Windows features that are not in use, are automatically inactivated when instances of the virtual machines are provisioned.
Which of the following actions should you take?

options.A: You should make use of Azure DevOps.
options.B: You should make use of Azure Automation State Configuration.
options.C: You should make use of network security groups (NSG).
options.D: You should make use of Azure Blueprints.

explanation:
You can use Azure Automation State Configuration to manage Azure VMs (both Classic and Resource Manager), on-premises VMs, Linux machines, AWS VMs, and on-premises physical machines.
Note: Azure Automation State Configuration provides a DSC pull server similar to the Windows Feature DSC-Service so that target nodes automatically receive configurations, conform to the desired state, and report back on their compliance. The built-in pull server in Azure Automation eliminates the need to set up and maintain your own pull server. Azure Automation can target virtual or physical Windows or Linux machines, in the cloud or on-premises.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/automation/automation-dsc-getting-started
answer_summary: Turning off unused Windows features on every newly provisioned VM is desired-state configuration work — Azure Automation State Configuration (DSC) pulls the configuration onto each node and keeps it compliant.

option_rationales.A: Azure DevOps orchestrates pipelines; it does not continuously enforce OS-level feature state on provisioned VMs.
option_rationales.B: Azure Automation State Configuration hosts DSC configurations that nodes pull automatically, so unused features are disabled at provisioning time and drift is reported.
option_rationales.C: NSGs filter network traffic to and from a VM — they cannot change Windows features.
option_rationales.D: Azure Blueprints deploys Azure resources and governance artifacts, not in-guest OS configuration.

verification.note: Correct for the exam as written, but note the direction of travel: Azure Automation State Configuration is being retired (announced end of support 30 September 2027) in favour of Azure Machine Configuration (Azure Policy guest configuration), which is how you would do this today.

question_stem:
Your company's Azure subscription includes Windows Server 2016 Azure virtual machines.
You are informed that every virtual machine must have a custom antimalware virtual machine extension installed. You are writing the necessary code for a policy that will help you achieve this.
Which of the following is an effect that must be included in your code?
explanation:
DeployIfNotExists executes a template deployment when the condition is met.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/policy/concepts/effects
answer_summary: DeployIfNotExists is the only effect that can create something that is missing — here, deploying the antimalware VM extension when a VM does not already have it.

option_rationales.A: Disabled turns the policy rule off entirely.
option_rationales.B: Modify adds, updates or removes properties and tags on the resource itself; it cannot deploy a child resource such as a VM extension.
option_rationales.C: AuditIfNotExists only reports non-compliance — it would flag VMs without the extension but never install it.
option_rationales.D: DeployIfNotExists runs an ARM template deployment when the related resource is missing, which installs the extension automatically.

verification.note: Policy effects are unchanged; DeployIfNotExists still requires a managed identity on the assignment and a remediation task for pre-existing VMs.

question_stem:
Your company makes use of Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) in a hybrid configuration. All users are making use of hybrid Azure AD joined Windows 10 computers.
You manage an Azure SQL database that allows for Azure AD authentication.
You need to make sure that database developers are able to connect to the SQL database via Microsoft SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS). You also need to make sure the developers use their on-premises Active Directory account for authentication. Your strategy should allow for authentication prompts to be kept to a minimum.
Which of the following is the authentication method the developers should use?
explanation:
Azure AD can be the initial Azure AD managed domain. Azure AD can also be an on-premises Active Directory Domain Services that is federated with the Azure AD.
Using an Azure AD identity to connect using SSMS or SSDT
The following procedures show you how to connect to a SQL database with an Azure AD identity using SQL Server Management Studio or SQL Server Database Tools.
Active Directory integrated authentication
Use this method if you are logged in to Windows using your Azure Active Directory credentials from a federated domain.
1. Start Management Studio or Data Tools and in the Connect to Server (or Connect to Database Engine) dialog box, in the Authentication box, select Active Directory - Integrated. No password is needed or can be entered because your existing credentials will be presented for the connection.

diagrams.diagram_description: SQL Server connection dialog screenshot showing Server type: Database Engine, Server name: testus.database.windows.net, Authentication: Active Directory - Integrated, with User name field showing DOMAIN\username and empty Password field with Remember password checkbox, and Connect, Cancel, Help, and Options buttons at the bottom.

answer_summary: On a hybrid-joined Windows 10 device the user is already signed in with the domain account, so Active Directory integrated authentication reuses that Kerberos/token session — connecting with no additional prompt.

option_rationales.A: The access-token method requires the application (or the admin) to obtain and supply a token, which is neither an SSMS single-sign-on flow nor prompt-free for developers.
option_rationales.B: Azure Multi-Factor Authentication (the 'Universal with MFA' option) deliberately adds an interactive prompt, which is the opposite of the requirement.
option_rationales.C: Integrated authentication uses the credentials the user is already logged on with, so SSMS connects silently using the on-premises AD identity federated/synced to the tenant.

verification.note: Still correct; in current SSMS the option is named 'Microsoft Entra MFA' / 'Microsoft Entra Integrated' rather than 'Active Directory - Integrated'.

question_stem:
You have been tasked with enabling Advanced Threat Protection for an Azure SQL Database server.
Advanced Threat Protection must be configured to identify all types of threat detection.
Which of the following will happen if when a faulty SQL statement is generate in the database by an application?

options.A: A Potential SQL injection alert is triggered.
options.B: A Vulnerability to SQL injection alert is triggered.
options.C: An Access from a potentially harmful application alert is triggered.
options.D: A Brute force SQL credentials alert is triggered.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sql-database/sql-database-threat-detection-overview
answer_summary: A faulty SQL statement generated by the application is what Microsoft's threat-detection catalogue describes as 'Vulnerability to SQL injection' — the app has produced a defective statement that could be exploited, but no attack is under way.

option_rationales.A: Potential SQL injection fires when an active exploit attempt is observed against an application vulnerability, not merely a malformed statement.
option_rationales.B: Vulnerability to SQL injection is triggered exactly when an application generates a faulty SQL statement, flagging code that is exposed to injection.
option_rationales.C: Access from a potentially harmful application fires when a known attack tool (for example a SQL injection utility) connects to the database.
option_rationales.D: Brute force SQL credentials fires on a high volume of failed logins with different credentials.

verification.note: Community 59% B. Naming has moved on: SQL Advanced Threat Protection is now Microsoft Defender for SQL under Microsoft Defender for Cloud, and these two alerts are still distinguished the same way.

question_stem:
Note: The question is included in a number of questions that depicts the identical set-up. However, every question has a distinctive result. Establish if the solution satisfies the requirements.
You are in the process of creating an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster. The Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster must be able to connect to an Azure Container Registry.
You want to make sure that Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster authenticates to the Azure Container Registry by making use of the auto-generated service principal.
Solution: You create an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) role assignment.
Does the solution meet the goal?
explanation:
When you create an AKS cluster, Azure also creates a service principal to support cluster operability with other Azure resources. You can use this auto-generated service principal for authentication with an ACR registry. To do so, you need to create an Azure AD role assignment that grants the cluster's service principal access to the container registry.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/bs-latn-ba/azure/container-registry/container-registry-auth-aks
answer_summary: Granting the AKS cluster's auto-generated service principal the AcrPull role on the registry is a role assignment in Microsoft Entra ID/Azure RBAC, which is exactly what the referenced ACR-with-AKS documentation prescribes.

option_rationales.A: A role assignment binding the cluster's service principal to AcrPull on the registry is the documented way to let AKS authenticate to ACR without storing registry credentials.
option_rationales.B: No imagePullSecret or admin credential is needed when the service principal holds AcrPull on the registry.

verification.note: Kept as Yes: the referenced Microsoft doc for this scenario literally says to create the role assignment for the cluster service principal. 73% of community votes say No, most likely objecting that it is an Azure RBAC role assignment on the registry rather than a directory role. Modern practice replaces this entirely: attach the registry with 'az aks update --attach-acr', which assigns AcrPull to the cluster's managed identity (auto-generated service principals are legacy).

question_stem:
Your company has an Azure subscription that includes two virtual machines, named VirMac1 and VirMac2, which both have a status of Stopped (Deallocated).
The virtual machines belong to different resource groups, named ResGroup1 and ResGroup2.
You have also created two Azure policies that are both configured with the virtualMachines resource type. The policy configured for ResGroup1 has a policy definition of Not allowed resource types, while the policy configured for ResGroup2 has a policy definition of Allowed resource types.
You then create a Read-only resource lock on VirMac1, as well as a Read-only resource lock on ResGroup2.
Which of the following is TRUE with regards to the scenario? (Choose all that apply.)

options.A: You will be able to start VirMac1.
options.B: You will NOT be able to start VirMac1.
options.C: You will be able to create a virtual machine in ResGroup2.
options.D: You will NOT be able to create a virtual machine in ResGroup2.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/blueprints/concepts/resource-locking
answer_summary: Both statements about restriction are true, because both stem from the Read-only locks: a ReadOnly lock on VirMac1 blocks the start operation, and a ReadOnly lock on ResGroup2 blocks creating any new resource inside it.

option_rationales.A: Starting a VM is a write-class operation (POST .../start), which a ReadOnly lock explicitly prevents — Microsoft documents this exact case.
option_rationales.B: The ReadOnly lock on VirMac1 stops it being started, so this statement is true.
option_rationales.C: Creating a VM in ResGroup2 is a write operation, and the ReadOnly lock on the resource group blocks it regardless of the 'Allowed resource types' policy.
option_rationales.D: The ReadOnly lock on ResGroup2 prevents new resources being created there, so this statement is true.

verification.note: Answer changed from BC to BD (community 100% BD). A ReadOnly lock blocks all write operations in its scope, including creating child resources and starting a VM.

question_stem:
You have been tasked with delegate administrative access to your company's Azure key vault.
You have to make sure that a specific user can set advanced access policies for the key vault. You also have to make sure that access is assigned based on the principle of least privilege.
Which of the following options should you use to achieve your goal?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/key-vault-secure-your-key-vault
answer_summary: Setting a key vault's advanced access policies is a management-plane operation on the vault resource, so it is granted with Azure RBAC — for least privilege, a scoped role such as Key Vault Contributor on that single vault.

option_rationales.A: Azure Information Protection classifies and labels documents and email; it has no role in Key Vault administration.
option_rationales.B: Azure RBAC assigns the specific management-plane permissions for the vault (for example Key Vault Contributor scoped to that vault), which is what allows advanced access policies to be configured.
option_rationales.C: PIM makes an existing privileged role assignment just-in-time; it still needs the underlying RBAC role, so on its own it does not grant this permission.
option_rationales.D: Azure DevOps is unrelated to delegating Azure resource permissions.

verification.note: Options were repaired: the original scrape merged choices A and B into one line, leaving the stored answer 'B' with no matching option. Also note advanced access policy settings (for Disk Encryption, ARM template deployment, etc.) are toggled on the vault resource, hence a management-plane RBAC role.

question_stem:
You have been tasked with delegate administrative access to your company's Azure key vault.
You have to make sure that a specific user is able to add and delete certificates in the key vault. You also have to make sure that access is assigned based on the principle of least privilege.
Which of the following options should you use to achieve your goal?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/key-vault-secure-your-key-vault
answer_summary: Adding and deleting certificates is a data-plane action inside the vault, so it is granted by a key vault access policy limited to certificate permissions — nothing broader is needed.

option_rationales.A: A key vault access policy can grant only the certificate permissions (create/import/delete) to that one principal, satisfying least privilege on the data plane.
option_rationales.B: Azure Policy audits and enforces resource configuration; it grants no permissions to a user.
option_rationales.C: PIM only makes an existing role assignment time-bound — it does not itself grant certificate permissions.
option_rationales.D: Azure DevOps is unrelated to Key Vault permissions.

verification.note: Correct as written, but the modern equivalent is the Azure RBAC permission model with the 'Key Vault Certificates Officer' role; Microsoft now recommends RBAC over the legacy vault access policy model.

question_stem:
You have an Azure virtual machine that runs Windows Server R2.
You plan to deploy and configure an Azure Key vault, and enable Azure Disk Encryption for the virtual machine.
Which of the following is TRUE with regards to Azure Disk Encryption for a Windows VM?

options.A: It is supported for basic tier VMs.
options.B: It is supported for standard tier VMs.
options.C: It is supported for VMs configured with software-based RAID systems.
options.D: It is supported for VMs configured with Storage Spaces Direct (S2D).

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/disk-encryption-windows
answer_summary: Azure Disk Encryption requires Standard tier (or higher) VM sizes — Basic tier VMs are explicitly unsupported, as are software RAID volumes and Storage Spaces Direct.

option_rationales.A: Basic tier VMs are on the unsupported list for Azure Disk Encryption.
option_rationales.B: Standard tier VM sizes (and above) support Azure Disk Encryption, provided the vault is in the same region and has disk-encryption access enabled.
option_rationales.C: Software-based RAID configurations are not supported by Azure Disk Encryption.
option_rationales.D: Storage Spaces Direct (S2D) is not supported by Azure Disk Encryption.

verification.note: Unsupported-scenario list is unchanged. Note that for many workloads Microsoft now steers you to platform-managed encryption at rest plus encryption at host or confidential-disk encryption rather than ADE.

question_stem:
You have an Azure virtual machine that runs Ubuntu 16.04-DAILY-LTS.
You plan to deploy and configure an Azure Key vault, and enable Azure Disk Encryption for the virtual machine.
Which of the following is TRUE with regards to Azure Disk Encryption for a Linux VM?

options.A: It is NOT supported for basic tier VMs.
options.B: It is NOT supported for standard tier VMs.
options.C: OS drive encryption for Linux virtual machine scale sets is supported.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/linux/disk-encryption-linux
answer_summary: Azure Disk Encryption's unsupported list for Linux starts with Basic tier VM sizes — encryption requires Standard tier or higher.

option_rationales.A: Basic tier VMs cannot use Azure Disk Encryption, so this is the true statement.
option_rationales.B: Standard tier is precisely what ADE does support, so the negative statement is false.
option_rationales.C: For Linux virtual machine scale sets only data disks can be encrypted; OS-drive encryption is not supported.
option_rationales.D: Encrypting custom images is not supported — the image must be an unencrypted platform or generalized image the VM is created from.

verification.note: Unsupported-scenario list for Linux ADE is unchanged.

question_stem:
You need to consider the underlined segment to establish whether it is accurate.
You have configured an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster in your testing environment.
You are currently preparing to deploy the cluster to the production environment.
After disabling HTTP application routing, you want to replace it with an application routing solution that allows for reverse proxy and TLS termination for AKS services via a solitary IP address.
You must create an AKS Ingress controller.
Select 'No adjustment required' if the underlined segment is accurate. If the underlined segment is inaccurate, select the accurate option.
explanation:
An ingress controller is a piece of software that provides reverse proxy, configurable traffic routing, and TLS termination for Kubernetes services.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/aks/ingress-tls
answer_summary: An ingress controller is exactly the component that provides reverse proxy, configurable routing and TLS termination for Kubernetes services behind one IP, so the underlined text needs no change.

option_rationales.A: An AKS ingress controller (NGINX, Application Gateway Ingress Controller, or the managed app routing add-on) is the correct replacement for HTTP application routing.
option_rationales.B: A network security group filters traffic by 5-tuple; it cannot terminate TLS or route by hostname/path.
option_rationales.C: An application security group is only a grouping of NICs used in NSG rules.
option_rationales.D: A Basic Load Balancer works at layer 4 — no TLS termination and no HTTP routing (and Basic SKU load balancers are now retired).

verification.note: Still correct. On current AKS, HTTP application routing is retired and the managed NGINX 'application routing add-on' or AGIC is the supported ingress option.

question_stem:
You want to gather logs from a large number of Windows Server 2016 computers using Azure Log Analytics.
You are configuring an Azure Resource Manager template to deploy the Microsoft Monitoring Agent to all the servers automatically.
Which of the following should be included in the template? (Choose all that apply.)
explanation:
Reference:
https://blogs.technet.microsoft.com/manageabilityguys/2015/11/19/enabling-the-microsoft-monitoring-agent-in-windows-json-templates/
answer_summary: The Microsoft Monitoring Agent extension only needs to know which workspace to report to and how to prove it: the WorkspaceID goes in settings and the WorkspaceKey in protectedSettings.

option_rationales.A: WorkspaceID identifies the Log Analytics workspace the agent should join.
option_rationales.B: No Entra application is involved — the agent authenticates with the workspace key, not an app registration.
option_rationales.C: WorkspaceKey is the shared key the agent uses to authenticate; it belongs in protectedSettings so it is not returned in plain text.
option_rationales.D: A storage account key is used for diagnostics storage, not for onboarding the monitoring agent.

verification.note: Correct for the MMA/Log Analytics agent, which reached end of support on 31 August 2024. The modern equivalent is the Azure Monitor Agent, which uses a managed identity plus data collection rules — there is no workspace key to supply.

question_stem:
Note: The question is included in a number of questions that depicts the identical set-up. However, every question has a distinctive result. Establish if the solution satisfies the requirements.
Your company has Azure subscription linked to their Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant.
As a Global administrator for the tenant, part of your responsibilities involves managing Azure Security Center settings.
You are currently preparing to create a custom sensitivity label.
Solution: You start by altering the pricing tier of the Security Center.
Does the solution meet the goal?
answer_summary: Custom sensitivity labels are an information-protection feature configured in the Microsoft Purview compliance portal, so nothing about Security Center's pricing tier is a step toward creating one.

option_rationales.A: Changing the Security Center pricing tier enables workload-protection features; it creates no labelling capability.
option_rationales.B: The label is created in the compliance/Purview portal (built on a sensitive information type), not from Security Center settings.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Azure Security Center is now Microsoft Defender for Cloud, and labels live in Microsoft Purview Information Protection.

question_stem:
Note: The question is included in a number of questions that depicts the identical set-up. However, every question has a distinctive result. Establish if the solution satisfies the requirements.
Your company has Azure subscription linked to their Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant.
As a Global administrator for the tenant, part of your responsibilities involves managing Azure Security Center settings.
You are currently preparing to create a custom sensitivity label.
Solution: You start by integrating Security Center and Microsoft Cloud App Security.
Does the solution meet the goal?
answer_summary: Connecting Security Center to Cloud App Security shares alerts and cloud-app discovery data; it does not create or define sensitivity labels.

option_rationales.A: The integration surfaces Defender for Cloud Apps alerts and discovery in Security Center — no labelling is configured by it.
option_rationales.B: To create a custom label you start from a custom sensitive information type in the compliance portal.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Microsoft Cloud App Security is now Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps.

question_stem:
Note: The question is included in a number of questions that depicts the identical set-up. However, every question has a distinctive result. Establish if the solution satisfies the requirements.
Your company has Azure subscription linked to their Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant.
As a Global administrator for the tenant, part of your responsibilities involves managing Azure Security Center settings.
You are currently preparing to create a custom sensitivity label.
Solution: You start by creating a custom sensitive information type.
Does the solution meet the goal?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/office365/securitycompliance/customize-a-built-in-sensitive-information-type
answer_summary: A custom sensitivity label needs something to detect: you first define a custom sensitive information type, then reference it from the label's auto-labelling conditions.

option_rationales.A: Creating a custom sensitive information type (a pattern/regex plus confidence level) is the documented starting point for a custom label.
option_rationales.B: This is the one solution in this set that is a genuine first step.

verification.note: Community 100% A. Today the same work is done in Microsoft Purview (custom SIT → sensitivity label → auto-labelling policy).

question_stem:
You have a sneaking suspicion that there are users trying to sign in to resources which are inaccessible to them.
You decide to create an Azure Log Analytics query to confirm your suspicions. The query will detect unsuccessful user sign-in attempts from the last few days.
You want to make sure that the results only show users who had failed to sign-in more than five times.
Which of the following should be included in your query?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/log-query/examples
answer_summary: You group failed sign-in events by user and keep only groups above the threshold, which needs the EventID (4625 = failed logon) to select the events and count() in the summarize to compare against five.

option_rationales.A: Countif() counts rows matching a predicate; the filter here is on the aggregated total, so the query still needs a plain count() plus a where clause.
option_rationales.B: ActivityID is not the field that identifies a Windows security event, and countif() is not what the threshold test needs.
option_rationales.C: Filter on EventID 4625, summarize count() by account, then keep rows where the count exceeds 5.
option_rationales.D: ActivityID relates to correlating operations, not to Windows security events in the Event table.

verification.note: Community 100% C. Note that failed sign-ins to Entra ID resources are queried in SigninLogs, while Windows logon failures come from the Event/SecurityEvent table by EventID.

question_stem:
Your company uses Azure DevOps with branch policies configured.
Which of the following is TRUE with regards to branch policies? (Choose all that apply.)

options.A: It enforces your team's change management standards.
options.B: It controls who can read and update the code in a branch.
options.C: It enforces your team's code quality.
options.D: It places a branch into a read-only state.

explanation:
Branch policies help teams protect their important branches of development. Policies enforce your team's code quality and change management standards.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/branch-policies?view=azure-devops&viewFallbackFrom=vsts
answer_summary: Branch policies exist to enforce quality and process — required reviewers, linked work items, build validation — not to control access. Access is handled by branch permissions and locks.

option_rationales.A: Requiring linked work items and reviewers is exactly change-management enforcement.
option_rationales.B: Who can read or update a branch is set by Git branch permissions (security), not by a policy.
option_rationales.C: Build validation and required successful builds/status checks enforce code quality.
option_rationales.D: Making a branch read-only is done by locking the branch, which is a separate action from policies.

verification.note: Community 100% AC; branch policies vs. permissions vs. locks are still three distinct mechanisms in Azure Repos.

question_stem:
After creating a new Azure subscription, you are tasked with making sure that custom alert rules can be created in Azure Security Center.
You have created an Azure Storage account.
Which of the following is the action you should take?

options.A: You should make sure that Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Identity Protection is removed.
options.B: You should create a DLP policy.
options.C: You should create an Azure Log Analytics workspace.
options.D: You should make sure that Security Center has the necessary tier configured.

explanation:
C: You need write permission in the workspace that you select to store your custom alert.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security-center/security-center-custom-alert
answer_summary: A custom alert rule has to be stored against a workspace, so a Log Analytics workspace (with write permission) must exist before you can create one.

option_rationales.A: Identity Protection is unrelated to Security Center alert rules, and removing it protects nothing.
option_rationales.B: A DLP policy governs data sharing in Microsoft 365 — no relationship to Security Center alerting.
option_rationales.C: The custom alert rule is defined on data in a Log Analytics workspace, so the workspace is the prerequisite.
option_rationales.D: A paid tier is needed for many workload-protection features, but the specific blocker for creating a custom alert rule is having a workspace to store it in.

verification.note: Community 70% C. Historical feature: Security Center custom alert rules have since been retired — the modern equivalent is a Microsoft Sentinel analytics rule or an Azure Monitor log alert over the same workspace.

question_stem:
Your company's Azure subscription includes an Azure Log Analytics workspace.
Your company has a hundred on-premises servers that run either Windows Server 2012 R2 or Windows Server 2016, and is linked to the Azure Log Analytics workspace. The Azure Log Analytics workspace is set up to gather performance counters associated with security from these linked servers.
You have been tasked with configuring alerts according to the information gathered by the Azure Log Analytics workspace.
You have to make sure that alert rules allow for dimensions, and that alert creation time should be kept to a minimum. Furthermore, a single alert notification must be created when the alert is created and when the alert is resolved.
You need to make use of the necessary signal type when creating the alert rules.
Which of the following is the option you should use?

options.A: You should make use of the Activity log signal type.
options.B: You should make use of the Application Log signal type.
options.C: You should make use of the Metric signal type.
options.D: You should make use of the Audit Log signal type.

explanation:
Metric alerts in Azure Monitor provide a way to get notified when one of your metrics cross a threshold. Metric alerts work on a range of multi-dimensional platform metrics, custom metrics, Application Insights standard and custom metrics.
Note: Signals are emitted by the target resource and can be of several types. Metric, Activity log, Application Insights, and Log.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/platform/alerts-metric
answer_summary: Only metric alerts combine all three requirements: multi-dimensional (dimension) support, near-real-time evaluation with quick setup, and stateful behaviour that notifies on fire and again on resolve.

option_rationales.A: Activity log alerts watch control-plane operations and do not support metric dimensions or resolved notifications for performance counters.
option_rationales.B: There is no 'Application Log' signal type for alert rules in Azure Monitor.
option_rationales.C: Metric alerts support dimensions, evaluate every minute, and are stateful — one notification when fired and one when resolved.
option_rationales.D: There is no 'Audit Log' signal type; audit data arrives via the activity log or log queries.

verification.note: Still accurate. Performance counters collected into a workspace can be alerted on as metrics, and log search alerts now also support dimensions but are slower to configure and evaluate.

question_stem:
Your company's Azure subscription includes a hundred virtual machines that have Azure Diagnostics enabled.
You have been tasked with retrieving the identity of the user that removed a virtual machine fifteen days ago. You have already accessed Azure Monitor.
Which of the following options should you use?
explanation:
Azure activity logs provide insight into the operations that were performed on resources in your subscription. Activity logs were previously known as €audit logs€ or €operational logs,€ because they report control-plane events for your subscriptions.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/azure-log-audit
answer_summary: Who deleted a resource is a control-plane operation recorded in the Activity Log, which retains 90 days of subscription-level events — easily covering fifteen days ago.

option_rationales.A: Application logs come from inside the guest workload and would not record an Azure resource deletion.
option_rationales.B: Metrics are numeric time series; they carry no caller identity.
option_rationales.C: The Activity Log records the operation (Delete Virtual Machine), the caller's identity and the timestamp.
option_rationales.D: Logs (workspace queries) can hold activity data only if diagnostic settings export it there; the direct, always-available source is the Activity Log.

verification.note: Activity log retention is still 90 days by default; export to a workspace or storage for longer retention.

question_stem:
Your company's Azure subscription includes a hundred virtual machines that have Azure Diagnostics enabled.
You have been tasked with analyzing the security events of a Windows Server 2016 virtual machine. You have already accessed Azure Monitor.
Which of the following options should you use?
explanation:
Log Integration collects Azure diagnostics from your Windows virtual machines, Azure activity logs, Azure Security Center alerts, and Azure resource provider logs. This integration provides a unified dashboard for all your assets, whether they're on-premises or in the cloud, so that you can aggregate, correlate, analyze, and alert for security events.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/azure-log-audit
answer_summary: Windows security events collected by the agent land in a Log Analytics workspace, so you analyse them with KQL queries under Monitor's Logs section.

option_rationales.A: There is no 'Application Log' blade in Azure Monitor for this purpose.
option_rationales.B: Metrics hold numeric performance data, not event records with detail fields.
option_rationales.C: The Activity Log covers Azure control-plane operations, not in-guest Windows security events.
option_rationales.D: Logs runs KQL over the SecurityEvent/Event tables where the collected Windows security events are stored.

verification.note: Still correct; on current agents, which security events get collected is controlled by a data collection rule (or by Defender for Servers/Sentinel data connectors).

question_stem:
You have been tasked with making sure that you are able to modify the operating system security configurations via Azure Security Center.
To achieve your goal, you need to have the correct pricing tier for Azure Security Center in place.
Which of the following is the pricing tier required?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security-center/security-center-pricing
answer_summary: OS security configuration assessment and remediation was a Standard-tier capability — the Free tier only provided policy and recommendation visibility.

option_rationales.A: There was no Advanced tier in Security Center.
option_rationales.B: There was no Premium tier in Security Center.
option_rationales.C: Standard tier unlocked the workload-protection features, including OS security configuration assessment.
option_rationales.D: Free tier gave only basic policy/recommendation coverage, without OS configuration management.

verification.note: Correct historically. Naming has since changed twice: Security Center became Microsoft Defender for Cloud, and Free/Standard became per-workload plans (for servers, Defender for Servers Plan 1 or Plan 2), with OS baselines now assessed through machine configuration / Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management.

question_stem:
Note: The question is included in a number of questions that depicts the identical set-up. However, every question has a distinctive result. Establish if the solution satisfies the requirements.
Your company's Azure subscription is linked to their Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant.
After an internally developed application is registered in Azure AD, you are tasked with making sure that the application has the ability to access Azure Key Vault secrets on application the users' behalf.
Solution: You configure a delegated permission with admin consent.
Does the solution meet the goal?
answer_summary: The Key Vault delegated permission (user_impersonation) is a user-consentable scope, so the configuration the exam is looking for is a delegated permission without admin consent; requiring admin consent is not the step being asked for.

option_rationales.A: Admin consent is not required for Key Vault's delegated permission, so this is not the configuration the question is after.
option_rationales.B: Correct as graded: the app needs a delegated permission that users themselves can consent to. (Granting admin consent would not break access, but the requirement — acting on behalf of the signed-in user — is satisfied by the delegated permission alone.)

verification.note: Community 100% B; the companion question with 'no admin consent' is the Yes variant.

question_stem:
Note: The question is included in a number of questions that depicts the identical set-up. However, every question has a distinctive result. Establish if the solution satisfies the requirements.
Your company's Azure subscription is linked to their Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant.
After an internally developed application is registered in Azure AD, you are tasked with making sure that the application has the ability to access Azure Key Vault secrets on application the users' behalf.
Solution: You configure a delegated permission with no admin consent.
Does the solution meet the goal?
explanation:
Delegated permissions - Your client application needs to access the web API as the signed-in user, but with access limited by the selected permission. This type of permission can be granted by a user unless the permission requires administrator consent.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/develop/quickstart-configure-app-access-web-apis
answer_summary: Acting on behalf of the signed-in user means a delegated permission, and Key Vault's delegated scope does not require administrator consent — users can consent themselves.

option_rationales.A: A delegated permission gives the app the user's own access to Key Vault, and because the scope is not admin-restricted, no admin consent is needed.
option_rationales.B: An application (app-only) permission would act as itself, not on behalf of users, and that is the configuration that would miss the goal.

verification.note: Community 79% A. In current Key Vault guidance, data-plane access is granted with Azure RBAC roles to the calling identity, with the app requesting the user_impersonation scope for on-behalf-of access.

question_stem:
You need to consider the underlined segment to establish whether it is accurate.
Your Azure Active Directory Azure (Azure AD) tenant has an Azure subscription linked to it.
Your developer has created a mobile application that obtains Azure AD access tokens using the OAuth 2 implicit grant type.
The mobile application must be registered in Azure AD.
You require a redirect URI from the developer for registration purposes.
Select 'No adjustment required' if the underlined segment is accurate. If the underlined segment is inaccurate, select the accurate option.
explanation:
For Native Applications you need to provide a Redirect URI, which Azure AD will use to return token responses.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/develop/v1-protocols-oauth-code
answer_summary: Registration needs the redirect URI from the developer, because that is where Azure AD returns the token in the implicit flow — the client ID is issued by Azure AD during registration, not supplied by the developer.

option_rationales.A: A redirect URI is exactly what you must collect: the implicit grant returns the access token to that URI, and it must match at runtime.
option_rationales.B: A client secret is never used by a public client such as a mobile app — it cannot be kept secret on a device.
option_rationales.C: A login hint is an optional runtime parameter to pre-fill the username, not a registration input.
option_rationales.D: The client (application) ID is generated by Azure AD when the app is registered, so the developer cannot supply it beforehand.

verification.note: Community split 50% A / 46% D, but the redirect URI is the only value the developer must provide. Currency: the OAuth 2.0 implicit grant is deprecated for new apps — mobile and SPA clients should use the authorization code flow with PKCE.

question_stem:
You are in the process of configuring an Azure policy via the Azure portal.
Your policy will include an effect that will need a managed identity for it to be assigned.
Which of the following is the effect in question?
explanation:
When Azure Policy runs the template in the deployIfNotExists policy definition, it does so using a managed identity.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/bs-latn-ba/azure/governance/policy/how-to/remediate-resources
answer_summary: DeployIfNotExists deploys an ARM template on your behalf, so the assignment needs a managed identity with rights to perform that deployment (Modify is the other identity-requiring effect, but it is not offered here).

option_rationales.A: AuditIfNotExists only evaluates and reports compliance — it changes nothing, so no identity is needed.
option_rationales.B: Disabled switches the policy rule off entirely.
option_rationales.C: DeployIfNotExists runs a template deployment during evaluation or remediation, which Policy performs using the assignment's managed identity.
option_rationales.D: EnforceOPAConstraint applied Gatekeeper constraints to AKS clusters and needed no managed identity (the effect is now deprecated).

verification.note: Still true, and Modify also requires a managed identity. EnforceOPAConstraint/EnforceRegoPolicy have since been deprecated in favour of Azure Policy for Kubernetes with Gatekeeper v3.

question_stem:
You have been tasked with creating an Azure key vault using PowerShell. You have been informed that objects deleted from the key vault must be kept for a set period of 90 days.
Which two of the following parameters must be used in conjunction to meet the requirement? (Choose two.)
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/azurerm.keyvault/new-azurermkeyvault https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/key-vault-ovw-soft-delete
answer_summary: Soft delete puts deleted objects into a recoverable state for the retention period, and purge protection stops anyone (including a rogue admin) from purging them early — together they guarantee the full 90 days.

option_rationales.A: EnabledForDeployment lets Azure VMs retrieve certificates from the vault; unrelated to retention.
option_rationales.B: EnablePurgeProtection blocks early permanent deletion, so the retention period cannot be cut short.
option_rationales.C: EnabledForTemplateDeployment lets ARM templates read secrets from the vault; unrelated to retention.
option_rationales.D: EnableSoftDelete keeps deleted vaults and objects recoverable for the configured retention period (7–90 days).

verification.note: Correct as written, but the API has moved on: soft delete is now enabled on every new key vault and cannot be turned off, so the -EnableSoftDelete switch is obsolete. Purge protection remains an explicit opt-in and, once on, cannot be disabled.

question_stem:
DRAG DROP -
Your company has an Azure SQL database that has Always Encrypted enabled.
You are required to make the relevant information available to application developers to allow them to access data in the database.
Which two of the following options should be made available? Answer by dragging the correct options from the list to the answer area.
Select and Place:
explanation:
Always Encrypted uses two types of keys: column encryption keys and column master keys. A column encryption key is used to encrypt data in an encrypted column. A column master key is a key-protecting key that encrypts one or more column encryption keys.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/encryption/always-encrypted-database-engine

diagrams.diagram_description: Drag-drop answer area showing available options (The column encryption key, A DLP policy, A shared access signature (SAS), A key vault access policy, The column master key) on the left and two answer slots on the right.

answer_summary: Always Encrypted is a client-side feature: the application's driver needs the column encryption key to decrypt the data and the column master key that protects (wraps) that CEK.

slot_rationales.Option 1: The column encryption key is what actually encrypts and decrypts the column values, so the client driver must be able to obtain it.
slot_rationales.Option 2: The column master key is the key-protecting key stored outside SQL (typically in Key Vault or the Windows certificate store) that wraps one or more column encryption keys — without access to it, the CEK cannot be unwrapped.

verification.note: The distractors are all wrong for a different reason: a DLP policy classifies content, a SAS grants storage access, and a key vault access policy governs who may reach the CMK but is not itself the key material the developer needs.

question_stem:
Note: This question is part of a series of questions that present the same scenario. Each question in the series contains a unique solution that might meet the stated goals. Some question sets might have more than one correct solution, while others might not have a correct solution.
After you answer a question in this section, you will NOT be able to return to it. As a result, these questions will not appear in the review screen.
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1.
You have an Azure Storage account named sa1 in a resource group named RG1.
Users and applications access the blob service and the file service in sa1 by using several shared access signatures (SASs) and stored access policies.
You discover that unauthorized users accessed both the file service and the blob service.
You need to revoke all access to sa1.
Solution: You create a new stored access policy.
Does this meet the goal?
explanation:
Creating a new (additional) stored access policy will have no effect on the existing policy or the SAS's linked to it.
To revoke a stored access policy, you can either delete it, or rename it by changing the signed identifier. Changing the signed identifier breaks the associations between any existing signatures and the stored access policy. Deleting or renaming the stored access policy immediately affects all of the shared access signatures associated with it.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/storageservices/Establishing-a-Stored-Access-Policy
answer_summary: Adding a new stored access policy leaves every existing policy and its issued SAS tokens intact. To revoke, you delete or rename the existing policy (changing the signed identifier), or rotate the account keys.

option_rationales.A: Creating an additional policy has no effect on already-issued signatures, so unauthorized access continues.
option_rationales.B: Revocation requires deleting/renaming the existing stored access policies and, for ad-hoc SAS, regenerating the account keys.

verification.note: Community 100% B; behaviour unchanged. Note ad-hoc SAS tokens not tied to a stored access policy can only be revoked by rotating the account key (or the user delegation key for user-delegation SAS).

question_stem:
Note: This question is part of a series of questions that present the same scenario. Each question in the series contains a unique solution that might meet the stated goals. Some question sets might have more than one correct solution, while others might not have a correct solution.
After you answer a question in this section, you will NOT be able to return to it. As a result, these questions will not appear in the review screen.
You have a hybrid configuration of Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
You have an Azure HDInsight cluster on a virtual network.
You plan to allow users to authenticate to the cluster by using their on-premises Active Directory credentials.
You need to configure the environment to support the planned authentication.
Solution: You deploy the On-premises data gateway to the on-premises network.
Does this meet the goal?
explanation:
Instead, you connect HDInsight to your on-premises network by using Azure Virtual Networks and a VPN gateway.
Note: To allow HDInsight and resources in the joined network to communicate by name, you must perform the following actions:
=> Create Azure Virtual Network.
=> Create a custom DNS server in the Azure Virtual Network.
=> Configure the virtual network to use the custom DNS server instead of the default Azure Recursive Resolver.
=> Configure forwarding between the custom DNS server and your on-premises DNS server.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/hdinsight/connect-on-premises-network
answer_summary: The on-premises data gateway is a data-movement bridge for services such as Power BI and Logic Apps. HDInsight authentication against on-premises AD needs network connectivity plus name resolution and a domain-joined cluster — not a data gateway.

option_rationales.A: The gateway proxies data queries for SaaS services; it plays no part in Kerberos/LDAP authentication for an HDInsight cluster.
option_rationales.B: You join the cluster's VNet to the on-premises network (VPN/ExpressRoute), point the VNet at a DNS server that resolves the AD domain, and use a domain-joined (ESP) cluster.

verification.note: Community 100% B.

question_stem:
