Note: This question is part of a series of questions that present the same scenario. Each question in the series contains a unique solution that might meet the stated goals. Some question sets might have more than one correct solution, while others might not have a correct solution.
After you answer a question in this section, you will NOT be able to return to it. As a result, these questions will not appear in the review screen.
You have a hybrid configuration of Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
You have an Azure HDInsight cluster on a virtual network.
You plan to allow users to authenticate to the cluster by using their on-premises Active Directory credentials.
You need to configure the environment to support the planned authentication.
Solution: You create a site-to-site VPN between the virtual network and the on-premises network.
Does this meet the goal?
explanation:
You can connect HDInsight to your on-premises network by using Azure Virtual Networks and a VPN gateway.
Note: To allow HDInsight and resources in the joined network to communicate by name, you must perform the following actions:
=> Create Azure Virtual Network.
=> Create a custom DNS server in the Azure Virtual Network.
=> Configure the virtual network to use the custom DNS server instead of the default Azure Recursive Resolver.
=> Configure forwarding between the custom DNS server and your on-premises DNS server.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/hdinsight/connect-on-premises-network
answer_summary: A site-to-site VPN is the connectivity that the referenced Microsoft guidance calls for — joining the HDInsight VNet to the on-premises network so the cluster can reach the domain controllers.

option_rationales.A: Graded as Yes: connecting the VNet to the on-premises network with a VPN gateway is the documented way to let HDInsight use on-premises Active Directory.
option_rationales.B: Marked incorrect by the exam key, though see the note — connectivity alone is not the whole story in practice.

verification.note: Kept as Yes to match the exam key and its cited doc, but be aware of the technical objection behind the 58% community vote for No: a VPN only provides reachability. A production solution also needs custom DNS on the VNet resolving the AD domain and a domain-joined cluster — today that means HDInsight's Enterprise Security Package with Microsoft Entra Domain Services.

question_stem:
Your network contains an Active Directory forest named contoso.com. The forest contains a single domain.
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that is associated to an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com.
You plan to deploy Azure AD Connect and to integrate Active Directory and the Azure AD tenant.
You need to recommend an integration solution that meets the following requirements:
=> Ensures that password policies and user logon restrictions apply to user accounts that are synced to the tenant
=> Minimizes the number of servers required for the solution.
Which authentication method should you include in the recommendation?

options.A: federated identity with Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS)
options.B: password hash synchronization with seamless single sign-on (SSO)
options.C: pass-through authentication with seamless single sign-on (SSO)

explanation:
Password hash synchronization requires the least effort regarding deployment, maintenance, and infrastructure. This level of effort typically applies to organizations that only need their users to sign in to Office 365, SaaS apps, and other Azure AD-based resources. When turned on, password hash synchronization is part of the Azure AD Connect sync process and runs every two minutes.
Incorrect Answers:
A: A federated authentication system relies on an external trusted system to authenticate users. Some companies want to reuse their existing federated system investment with their Azure AD hybrid identity solution. The maintenance and management of the federated system falls outside the control of Azure AD. It's up to the organization by using the federated system to make sure it's deployed securely and can handle the authentication load.
C: For pass-through authentication, you need one or more (we recommend three) lightweight agents installed on existing servers. These agents must have access to your on-premises Active Directory Domain Services, including your on-premises AD domain controllers. They need outbound access to the Internet and access to your domain controllers. For this reason, it's not supported to deploy the agents in a perimeter network.
Pass-through Authentication requires unconstrained network access to domain controllers. All network traffic is encrypted and limited to authentication requests.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/hybrid/how-to-connect-pta
answer_summary: Only pass-through authentication evaluates each sign-in against an on-premises domain controller, which is what makes on-prem password policies and logon-hour restrictions apply — and its lightweight agents run on existing servers, so no new servers are needed.

option_rationales.A: AD FS enforces on-premises policy but requires a federation farm plus proxies, so it fails the 'minimize servers' requirement.
option_rationales.B: Password hash synchronization authenticates in the cloud against synced hashes; on-premises password policy and logon restrictions are not enforced at sign-in.
option_rationales.C: Pass-through authentication forwards each credential validation to a domain controller in real time, so password policy, expiry, lockout and logon hours all apply — with only a lightweight agent on an existing server.

verification.note: Answer changed from B to C (community 100% C). Microsoft's hybrid-identity comparison table lists 'Enforces on-premises account policy at sign-in' as No for PHS and Yes for PTA.

question_stem:
Your network contains an on-premises Active Directory domain named corp.contoso.com.
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that is associated to an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com.
You sync all on-premises identities to Azure AD.
You need to prevent users who have a givenName attribute that starts with TEST from being synced to Azure AD. The solution must minimize administrative effort.
What should you use?
explanation:
Use the Synchronization Rules Editor and write attribute-based filtering rule.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/hybrid/how-to-connect-sync-change-the-configuration
answer_summary: Excluding objects by an attribute value is attribute-based filtering, which is authored in the Synchronization Rules Editor — the wizard offers only OU- and domain-based filtering.

option_rationales.A: The Synchronization Rules Editor lets you add an inbound rule with a scoping filter on givenName, which is the least-effort supported way to filter by attribute.
option_rationales.B: The Web Service Configuration Tool configures FIM/MIM web service endpoints — not Entra Connect filtering.
option_rationales.C: The Azure AD Connect wizard supports domain and OU filtering only; it cannot filter on an arbitrary attribute value.
option_rationales.D: Active Directory Users and Computers manages on-premises objects and has no sync-scope capability.

verification.note: Community 100% A. With Entra Cloud Sync the equivalent is an attribute-based scoping filter in the cloud sync configuration.

question_stem:
DRAG DROP -
You are implementing conditional access policies.
You must evaluate the existing Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) risk events and risk levels to configure and implement the policies.
You need to identify the risk level of the following risk events:
=> Users with leaked credentials
=> Impossible travel to atypical locations
=> Sign-ins from IP addresses with suspicious activity
Which level should you identify for each risk event? To answer, drag the appropriate levels to the correct risk events. Each level may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Select and Place:
explanation:
Azure AD Identity protection can detect six types of suspicious sign-in activities:
=> Users with leaked credentials
=> Sign-ins from anonymous IP addresses
=> Impossible travel to atypical locations

Sign-ins from infected devices -

=> Sign-ins from IP addresses with suspicious activity
=> Sign-ins from unfamiliar locations
These six types of events are categorized in to 3 levels of risks â€" High, Medium & Low:
References:
http://www.rebeladmin.com/2018/09/step-step-guide-configure-risk-based-azure-conditional-access-policies/

diagrams.diagram_description: Drag-drop answer area showing three levels (High, Low, Medium) on the left and three risk event slots (Impossible travel to atypical locations, Users with leaked credentials, Sign-ins from IP addresses with suspicious activity) on the right.

answer_summary: Leaked credentials is the only High-risk detection; impossible travel and suspicious-activity IPs are both Medium — an IP with many failed sign-ins may be shared by many devices, so Microsoft rates it Medium rather than High.

slot_rationales.Impossible travel to atypical locations: Medium — two sign-ins from geographically distant locations too close together is strong behavioural evidence, but it is legitimately triggered by VPNs and travel.
slot_rationales.Users with leaked credentials: High — the actual username/password pair has been found exposed publicly, so the account is presumed compromised.
slot_rationales.Sign-ins from IP addresses with suspicio: Medium — a high number of failed sign-ins across multiple accounts came from that IP, but several devices can share one address, so it is not rated High.

verification.note: Changed this slot from Low to Medium after checking Microsoft's risk-event-types reference, which rates suspicious-activity IPs as Medium and only 'sign-ins from infected devices' as Low. The exam key follows a widely-copied blog table that swaps those two. The question allows a level to be used more than once, so High/Medium/Medium is a valid answer shape.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com that contains the users shown in the following table.

| Name | Member of | Mobile phone | Multi-factor authentication (MFA) status |
|------|-----------|--------------|------------------------------------------|
| User1 | Group1 | 123 555 7890 | Disabled |
| User2 | Group1, Group2 | None | Enabled |
| User3 | Group1 | 123 555 7891 | Required |

You create and enforce an Azure AD Identity Protection user risk policy that has the following settings:
=> Assignment: Include Group1, Exclude Group2
=> Conditions: Sign-in risk of Medium and above
=> Access: Allow access, Require password change
For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: If User1 signs in from an unfamiliar location, he must change his password.
hotspot_rows.rationale: User1 is in Group1 and nothing excludes him. An unfamiliar sign-in location is a Medium detection, so the policy fires and forces a password change (his MFA status is irrelevant — the policy allows access with a password change).

hotspot_rows.statement: If User2 signs in from an anonymous IP address, she must change her password.
hotspot_rows.rationale: User2 is in Group1 but also in Group2, which the policy excludes — and an exclusion always overrides an inclusion. The policy never evaluates User2, so no password change is required even though anonymous-IP is a Medium detection.

hotspot_rows.statement: If User3 signs in from a computer containing malware that is communicating with known bot servers, he must change his password.
hotspot_rows.rationale: A device talking to known bot servers is the 'sign-ins from infected devices' detection, which Microsoft rates Low. The policy only triggers at Medium and above, so nothing happens.

explanation:
Box 1: Yes -
User1 is member of Group1. Sign in from unfamiliar location is risk level Medium.

Box 2: Yes -
User2 is member of Group1. Sign in from anonymous IP address is risk level Medium.

Box 3: No -
Sign-ins from IP addresses with suspicious activity is low.
Note:
answer_summary: The policy applies to Group1 but excludes Group2, and exclusions always win. So it applies to User1 and User3 but not User2 — and it only fires at Medium risk and above, which rules out the infected-device detection (Low).

verification.note: Row 2 changed from Yes to No. The bank's own explanation says 'User2 is member of Group1' and ignores that User2 is also in the excluded Group2; in Microsoft Entra ID, an exclusion takes precedence over an inclusion. Row 3 stays No, and Microsoft's reference confirms the reason is that infected-device sign-ins are a Low detection.

question_stem:
DRAG DROP -
You need to configure an access review. The review will be assigned to a new collection of reviews and reviewed by resource owners.
Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
Select and Place:
explanation:
Step 1: Create an access review program
Step 2: Create an access review control
Step 3: Set Reviewers to Group owners
In the Reviewers section, select either one or more people to review all the users in scope. Or you can select to have the members review their own access. If the resource is a group, you can ask the group owners to review.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/governance/create-access-review https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/governance/manage-programs-controls

diagrams.diagram_description: Drag-drop answer area showing available actions (Create an access review program, Set Reviewers to Selected users, Create an access review audit, Create an access review control, Set Reviewers to Group owners, Set Reviewers to Members) on the left and three sequential answer slots on the right, with a screenshot showing the Reviewers dropdown options (Group owners, Group owners, Selected users, Members (self)).

answer_summary: You build the container first, then the review itself, then choose who reviews: create the access review program, create the access review control inside it, and set Reviewers to Group owners so resource owners do the attestation.

slot_rationales.Step 1: Create an access review program — the collection that the new review will be assigned to.
slot_rationales.Step 2: Create an access review control — the review definition (scope, resource, schedule) inside that program.
slot_rationales.Step 3: Set Reviewers to Group owners — this is what makes the resource owners the reviewers, rather than named users or the members themselves.

verification.note: Correct for the portal generation this question was written for. In current Microsoft Entra ID Governance the 'program/control' terminology is gone: you create an access review directly (optionally inside an access package) and pick reviewers there.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that is associated to an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com.
An administrator named Admin1 has access to the following identities:
=> An OpenID-enabled user account
=> A Hotmail account
=> An account in contoso.com
=> An account in an Azure AD tenant named fabrikam.com
You plan to use Azure Account Center to transfer the ownership of Sub1 to Admin1.
To which accounts can you transfer the ownership of Sub1?

options.D: contoso.com, fabrikam.com, Hotmail, and OpenID-enabled user account

explanation:
When you transfer billing ownership of your subscription to an account in another Azure AD tenant, you can move the subscription to the new account's tenant. If you do so, all users, groups, or service principals who had role based access (RBAC) to manage subscriptions and its resources lose their access. Only the user in the new account who accepts your transfer request will have access to manage the resources.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/billing/billing-subscription-transfer https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/billing/billing-subscription-transfer#transferring-subscription-to-an-account-in-another-azure-ad-tenant
answer_summary: Billing ownership can only be transferred to a work or school (Entra ID) account — the Hotmail and OpenID identities are out — and the target account may live in another tenant, which is what makes fabrikam.com eligible alongside contoso.com.

option_rationales.A: This would be right only if cross-tenant transfer were blocked; Microsoft explicitly documents transferring to an account in another Entra ID tenant (the subscription then moves to that tenant).
option_rationales.B: A personal Microsoft account such as Hotmail cannot receive a billing-ownership transfer.
option_rationales.C: Both contoso.com and fabrikam.com are Entra ID work accounts, so both are valid transfer targets.
option_rationales.D: OpenID-enabled and Hotmail accounts are not supported transfer targets.

verification.note: Kept as C, matching the cited documentation on transferring billing ownership across tenants; 77% of community votes say contoso.com only. Currency: Azure Account Center is retired — billing-ownership transfers are now done in Cost Management + Billing, and for Microsoft Customer Agreement / EA accounts the rules differ (transfers happen at billing-profile level, and the recipient may need to be invited to the tenant first).

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
Your company has two offices in Seattle and New York. Each office connects to the Internet by using a NAT device. The offices use the IP addresses shown in the following table.

| Location | IP address space | Public NAT segment |
|----------|-----------------|--------------------|
| Seattle | 10.10.0.0/16 | 190.15.1.0/24 |
| New York | 172.16.0.0/16 | 194.25.2.0/24 |

The company has an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com. The tenant contains the users shown in the following table.

| Name | Multi-factor authentication (MFA) status |
|------|------------------------------------------|
| User1 | Enabled |
| User2 | Enforced |

The MFA service settings are configured as shown in the exhibit. (Click the Exhibit tab.)

trusted ips (learn more)

Skip multi-factor authentication for requests from federated users on my intranet

Skip multi-factor authentication for requests from following range of IP address subnets

10.10.0.0/16
194.25.2.0/24

verification options (learn more)

Methods available to users:
☑ Call to phone
☑ Text message to phone
☐ Notification through mobile app
☐ Verification code from mobile app or hardware token

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: If User1 signs in to Azure from a device that uses an IP address of 134.18.14.10, User1 must be authenticated by using a phone.
hotspot_rows.rationale: 134.18.14.10 is in neither trusted range, so User1 is challenged. Only 'Call to phone' and 'Text message to phone' are enabled as verification options, so the challenge is satisfied with a phone — the statement is true.

hotspot_rows.statement: If User2 signs in to Azure from a device in the Seattle office, User2 must be authenticated by using the Microsoft Authenticator app.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Seattle's public NAT segment is 190.15.1.0/24, which is not in the trusted list (the listed 10.10.0.0/16 is Seattle's private space and never appears as the source of an Internet sign-in), so User2 is challenged — but the Microsoft Authenticator app option is not enabled, so authentication by app is not what happens.

hotspot_rows.statement: If User2 signs in to Azure from a device in the New York office, User2 must be authenticated by using a phone
hotspot_rows.rationale: New York's public NAT segment 194.25.2.0/24 is in the trusted-IP list, so MFA is skipped entirely and no phone authentication occurs.

explanation:
Box 1: Yes -

Box 2: No -
Use of Microsoft Authenticator is not required. Either a text or phone call is required for MFA.
Note: Microsoft Authenticator is a multifactor app for mobile devices that generates time-based codes used during the Two-Step Verification process.

Box 3: No -
The New York IP address subnet is included in the 'skip multi-factor authentication for request.
Reference:
https://www.cayosoft.com/difference-enabling-enforcing-mfa/

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure Portal screenshot showing MFA service settings with two sections: trusted ips (with checkbox for 'Skip multi-factor authentication for requests from federated users on my intranet' and text box showing '10.10.0.0/16' and '194.25.2.0/24') and verification options (with checkboxes for 'Call to phone', 'Text message to phone', 'Notification through mobile app', and 'Verification code from mobile app or hardware token', with first two checked).

answer_summary: Trusted IPs skip MFA only for the listed ranges — 10.10.0.0/16 (a private range, so it matches nothing for Internet sign-ins) and 194.25.2.0/24 (New York's public NAT). Seattle sign-ins therefore still need MFA, New York sign-ins do not, and the enabled verification options limit the method to a phone call or text.

verification.note: Answers unchanged. Currency: per-user MFA with the legacy 'trusted IPs' service setting is deprecated — the modern equivalent is Conditional Access with named locations, and Microsoft is enforcing MFA for admin portal sign-ins regardless of such exclusions.

question_stem:
Your company plans to create separate subscriptions for each department. Each subscription will be associated to the same Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant.
You need to configure each subscription to have the same role assignments.
What should you use?
explanation:
Just as a blueprint allows an engineer or an architect to sketch a project's design parameters, Azure Blueprints enables cloud architects and central information technology groups to define a repeatable set of Azure resources that implements and adheres to an organization's standards, patterns, and requirements.
Blueprints are a declarative way to orchestrate the deployment of various resource templates and other artifacts such as:
=> Role Assignments
=> Policy Assignments
=> Azure Resource Manager templates
=> Resource Groups
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/blueprints/overview
answer_summary: Azure Blueprints packages role assignments, policy assignments, resource groups and ARM templates into one artifact set that you assign to each subscription, producing identical RBAC everywhere.

option_rationales.A: Azure Security Center (now Defender for Cloud) assesses and protects workloads; it does not provision role assignments.
option_rationales.B: Azure Policy can audit or enforce resource configuration and can even deploy resources, but role assignments across subscriptions are a Blueprints artifact, not a policy definition.
option_rationales.C: PIM governs activation and review of existing privileged roles — it does not replicate assignments to new subscriptions.
option_rationales.D: Blueprints is purpose-built for repeatable, subscription-level governance including RBAC role assignments.

verification.note: Community 100% D. Currency: Azure Blueprints is deprecated — Microsoft now recommends Template Specs plus deployment stacks (with Azure landing zones as the pattern) for the same outcome.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription.
You create an Azure web app named Contoso1812 that uses an S1 App Service plan.

You plan to -
create a CNAME DNS record for www.contoso.com that points to Contoso1812.
You need to ensure that users can access Contoso1812 by using the https://www.contoso.com URL.
Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

A. Turn on the system-assigned managed identity for Contoso1812.
B. Add a hostname to Contoso1812.
C. Scale out the App Service plan of Contoso1812.
D. Add a deployment slot to Contoso1812.
E. Scale up the App Service plan of Contoso1812.
F. Upload a PFX file to Contoso1812.

options.A: Turn on the system-assigned managed identity for Contoso1812.
options.C: Scale out the App Service plan of Contoso1812.
options.D: Add a deployment slot to Contoso1812.
options.E: Scale up the App Service plan of Contoso1812.
options.F: Upload a PFX file to Contoso1812.

explanation:
B: You can configure Azure DNS to host a custom domain for your web apps. For example, you can create an Azure web app and have your users access it using either www.contoso.com or contoso.com as a fully qualified domain name (FQDN).
To do this, you have to create three records:
A root "A" record pointing to contoso.com
A root "TXT" record for verification
A "CNAME" record for the www name that points to the A record
F: To use HTTPS, you need to upload a PFX file to the Azure Web App. The PFX file will contain the SSL certificate required for HTTPS.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/dns/dns-web-sites-custom-domain

Community vote distribution
BF (100%)
answer_summary: Two things are needed for https on a custom domain: bind the name to the app (add the hostname) and give the app a certificate for that name (upload the PFX and create the TLS binding). An S1 plan already supports both, so no scaling is involved.

option_rationales.A: A managed identity lets the app authenticate to Azure services; it has nothing to do with serving a custom hostname over TLS.
option_rationales.B: Adding www.contoso.com as a custom hostname is what makes App Service answer for that name once the CNAME resolves to it.
option_rationales.C: Scaling out adds instances for load — custom domains and TLS work on a single instance.
option_rationales.D: A deployment slot is a staging copy of the app; irrelevant to hostname or TLS.
option_rationales.E: Scaling up would be needed only if the plan were below Basic; S1 (Standard) already supports custom domains and SNI TLS bindings.
option_rationales.F: Uploading the PFX certificate for www.contoso.com (then binding it) is what enables https rather than plain http.

verification.note: Community 100% BF. Currency: you would normally skip the PFX today and use a free App Service managed certificate or import one from Key Vault — the exam still tests the upload-and-bind flow.

Solution: You create a lock on sa1.
Does this meet the goal?

A. Yes
B. No
explanation:
To revoke a stored access policy, you can either delete it, or rename it by changing the signed identifier. Changing the signed identifier breaks the associations between any existing signatures and the stored access policy. Deleting or renaming the stored access policy immediately affects all of the shared access signatures associated with it.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/storageservices/Establishing-a-Stored-Access-Policy

Community vote distribution
B (100%)
answer_summary: Resource locks are a management-plane control: they stop the storage account being modified or deleted, but they do not touch data-plane access, so every existing SAS keeps working.

option_rationales.A: A CanNotDelete or ReadOnly lock protects the account resource itself; unauthorized readers using a SAS are unaffected.
option_rationales.B: To cut off SAS-based access you delete or rename the stored access policies and regenerate the account keys.

verification.note: Community 100% B.

options.B: the Security administrator role in Azure AD

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/hybrid/reference-connect-accounts-permissions

You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com that contains the users shown in the following table.

| Name | Member of | Multi-factor authentication (MFA) status |
|------|-----------|------------------------------------------|
| User1 | None | Disabled |
| User2 | Group1 | Disabled |
| User3 | Group1 | Enforced |

Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM) is used in contoso.com.
In PIM, the Password Administrator role has the following settings:
=> Maximum activation duration (hours): 2
=> Send email notifying admins of activation: Disable
=> Require incident/request ticket number during activation: Disable
=> Require Azure Multi-Factor Authentication for activation: Enable
=> Require approval to activate this role: Enable
=> Selected approver: Group1
You assign users the Password Administrator role as shown in the following table.

| Name | Assignment type |
|------|----------------|
| User1 | Active |
| User2 | Eligible |
| User3 | Eligible |

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: When User1 signs in, the user is assigned the Password Administrator role automatically.
hotspot_rows.rationale: User1 has an Active assignment, so the role's privileges apply at all times with no activation step — signing in is enough.

hotspot_rows.statement: User2 can request to activate the Password Administrator role.
hotspot_rows.rationale: User2 is Eligible, so requesting activation is exactly what they are meant to do. Per-user MFA being Disabled does not block the request: the 'Require MFA for activation' setting makes User2 complete an MFA challenge (registering if needed) as part of activating.

hotspot_rows.statement: If User3 wants to activate the Password Administrator role, the user can approve their own request.
hotspot_rows.rationale: User3 is in Group1, the selected approver group, but PIM does not allow self-approval — another member of the approver group must approve User3's request.

explanation:
Box 1: Yes -
Active assignments don't require the member to perform any action to use the role. Members assigned as active have the privileges assigned to the role at all times.

Box 2: Yes -
While Multi-Factor Authentication is disabled for User2 and the setting Require Azure Multi-Factor Authentication for activation is enabled, User2 can request the role but will need to enable MFA to use the role.
Note: Eligible assignments require the member of the role to perform an action to use the role. Actions might include performing a multi-factor authentication
(MFA) check, providing a business justification, or requesting approval from designated approvers.

Box 3: No -
User3 is Group1, which is a Selected Approver Group, however, self-approval is not allowed and someone else from group is required to approve the request.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/privileged-identity-management/pim-resource-roles-assign-roles
answer_summary: Active assignments are permanent, eligible assignments must be activated (MFA is enforced at activation, not pre-registered), and an approver cannot approve their own activation request.

verification.note: PIM still blocks self-approval, and role-setting names have only changed cosmetically (for example 'Require Azure AD Multifactor Authentication on activation').

question_stem:
You have a hybrid configuration of Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) that has Single Sign-On (SSO) enabled. You have an Azure SQL Database instance that is configured to support Azure AD authentication.
Database developers must connect to the database instance from the domain joined device and authenticate by using their on-premises Active Directory account.
You need to ensure that developers can connect to the instance by using Microsoft SQL Server Management Studio. The solution must minimize authentication prompts.
Which authentication method should you recommend?

A. Active Directory - Password
B. Active Directory - Universal with MFA support
C. SQL Server Authentication
D. Active Directory - Integrated

options.B: Active Directory - Universal with MFA support

explanation:
Active Directory - Integrated -
Azure Active Directory Authentication is a mechanism of connecting to Microsoft Azure SQL Database by using identities in Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
Use this method for connecting to SQL Database if you are logged in to Windows using your Azure Active Directory credentials from a federated domain.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/ssms/f1-help/connect-to-server-database-engine?view=sql-server-2017 https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sql-database/sql-database-aad-authentication-configure

Community vote distribution
D (100%)
answer_summary: On a domain-joined device with SSO configured, 'Active Directory - Integrated' reuses the Windows logon session, so developers connect with their on-premises account and see no extra prompt.

option_rationales.A: Active Directory - Password makes the user type their credentials each time — more prompts than necessary.
option_rationales.B: Universal with MFA support deliberately adds an interactive MFA challenge.
option_rationales.C: SQL Server Authentication uses a separate SQL login, not the on-premises AD account.
option_rationales.D: Integrated authentication passes the existing Windows/Kerberos session through, satisfying both 'use their on-premises account' and 'minimize prompts'.

verification.note: Community 100% D. In current SSMS the entry is named 'Microsoft Entra Integrated'.

question_stem:
You plan to use Azure Resource Manager templates to perform multiple deployments of identically configured Azure virtual machines. The password for the administrator account of each deployment is stored as a secret in different Azure key vaults.
You need to identify a method to dynamically construct a resource ID that will designate the key vault containing the appropriate secret during each deployment.
The name of the key vault and the name of the secret will be provided as inline parameters.
What should you use to construct the resource ID?

A. a key vault access policy
B. a linked template
C. a parameters file
D. an automation account
explanation:
You reference the key vault in the parameter file, not the template. The following image shows how the parameter file references the secret and passes that value to the template.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/resource-manager-keyvault-parameter

Community vote distribution
B (91%)    9%

diagrams.diagram_description: Diagram showing template, parameter file, and Azure Key Vault with arrows indicating how the parameter file passes secret reference to template.

answer_summary: A parameters file can only reference a key vault secret by a static resource ID. When the vault name and secret name arrive as parameters and the ID has to be built at deploy time, you must pass them to a linked (nested) template, which can construct the ID with resourceId() and use it in a static reference.

option_rationales.A: An access policy controls who may read the secret; it does not build a resource ID.
option_rationales.B: A linked template is Microsoft's documented answer for a dynamic secret ID: the parent template computes or forwards the values and the linked template forms the key vault reference.
option_rationales.C: A parameters file supports only the static-ID pattern — template functions such as resourceId() and concat() cannot be evaluated there.
option_rationales.D: An Automation account runs runbooks; it plays no part in an ARM template's parameter resolution.

verification.note: Answer changed from C to B (community 91% B). Microsoft's Key Vault parameter documentation distinguishes 'reference secret with static ID' (parameters file) from 'reference secret with dynamic ID', and states that the dynamic case requires a linked template because functions cannot be used in a parameters file.

explanation:
Box 1: Yes -

Box 2: No -

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant that contains the users shown in the following table.

| Name | Member of | Multi-factor authentication (MFA) status |
|------|-----------|------------------------------------------|
| User1 | Group1, Group2 | Disabled |
| User2 | Group2 | Disabled |

The tenant contains the named locations shown in the following table.

| Name | IP address range | Trusted location |
|------|-----------------|------------------|
| Seattle | 193.77.10.0/24 | Yes |
| Boston | 154.12.18.0/24 | No |

You create the conditional access policies for a cloud app named App1 as shown in the following table.

| Name | Include | Exclude | Condition | Grant |
|------|---------|---------|-----------|-------|
| Policy1 | Group1 | Group2 | Locations: Boston | Block access |
| Policy2 | Group1 | None | Locations: Any location | Grant access, Require multi-factor authentication |
| Policy3 | Group2 | Group1 | Locations: Boston | Block access |
| Policy4 | User2 | None | Locations: Any location | Grant access, Require multi-factor authentication |

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: User1 can access App1 from an IP address of 154.12.18.10.
hotspot_rows.rationale: 154.12.18.10 is Boston. Policy1 excludes Group2 and Policy3 excludes Group1, so neither applies to User1 (a member of both). Policy2 does apply and requires MFA, which User1 — with MFA Disabled — cannot complete, so access fails.

hotspot_rows.statement: User2 can access App1 from an IP address of 193.77.10.15.
hotspot_rows.rationale: 193.77.10.15 is Seattle, a trusted location. Policy1/Policy2 target Group1 only and Policy3 is scoped to Boston, so the only policy in play is Policy4; from the trusted Seattle location the MFA requirement is treated as satisfied, so User2 gets in.

hotspot_rows.statement: User2 can access App1 from an IP address of 154.12.18.34.
hotspot_rows.rationale: 154.12.18.34 is Boston. User2 is in Group2 and is not in the excluded Group1, so Policy3 applies and blocks access outright — and Block always wins over any Grant.

answer_summary: Work each policy's include/exclude first: exclusions win, so Policy1 and Policy3 never apply to User1 (who is in both groups). What is left is Policy2 for User1 (MFA required, which she cannot satisfy with MFA disabled), Policy4 for User2 everywhere, and Policy3 blocking User2 from Boston.

verification.note: Answers kept as graded, but two of the mechanics are dated: in current Conditional Access, marking a named location 'trusted' does not by itself satisfy or bypass a Require-MFA grant (you must exclude the location in the policy), and a user who hits a Require-MFA policy without a registered method is prompted to register rather than silently denied. Block-over-Grant precedence and exclusion-over-inclusion are still exactly as shown.

Box 2: Yes -

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the users shown in the following table.

| User1 | Owner | Authentication administrator | Enabled |

Which users can enable Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM)?
explanation:
For Azure AD roles in PIM, only a user who is in the Privileged Role Administrator or Global Administrator role can manage assignments for other administrators.
Global Administrators, Security Administrators, Global Readers, and Security Readers can also view assignments to Azure AD roles in PIM.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/privileged-identity-management/pim-deployment-plan
answer_summary: Enabling PIM is reserved for Global Administrators, so only User2 and User3 qualify. A subscription Owner role grants nothing in the directory, and a user's MFA status does not change who can enable the service.

option_rationales.A: User2 and User3 are both Global Administrators, which is the role that can onboard/enable PIM.
option_rationales.B: User1 is a subscription Owner and Authentication administrator — neither grants the directory-wide rights to enable PIM.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription.
You plan to create a custom role-based access control (RBAC) role that will provide permission to read the Azure Storage account.
Which property of the RBAC role definition should you configure?
explanation:
To 'Read a storage account', ie. list the blobs in the storage account, you need an 'Action' permission.
To read the data in a storage account, ie. open a blob, you need a 'DataAction' permission.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/role-definitions
answer_summary: Reading the storage account itself (its properties, listing containers through the management plane) is a control-plane operation, so it belongs in Actions. DataActions is only for reaching the data inside — for example opening a blob.

option_rationales.A: NotActions subtracts permissions from those already granted in Actions; it cannot grant read access.
option_rationales.B: DataActions covers data-plane operations such as reading blob content, which is not what 'read the Azure Storage account' means here.
option_rationales.C: AssignableScopes controls where the role may be assigned, not what it permits.
option_rationales.D: Actions is where you list the management-plane permission, for example Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/read.

verification.note: Role definition structure is unchanged. Remember that adding any DataAction restricts the role's assignable scopes and that NotDataActions is the data-plane equivalent of NotActions.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription linked to an Azure Active Directory Premium Plan 1 tenant.
You plan to implement Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Identity Protection.
You need to ensure that you can configure a user risk policy and a sign-in risk policy.
What should you do first?

options.A: Purchase Azure Active Directory Premium Plan 2 licenses for all users.
options.B: Register all users for Azure Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA).
options.C: Enable security defaults for Azure AD.
options.D: Enable Azure Defender in Azure Security Center.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/authentication/tutorial-risk-based-sspr-mfa
answer_summary: The user risk and sign-in risk policies are Identity Protection features that require Entra ID P2 licensing — with only P1 the policies cannot be configured, so licensing is the first blocker to clear.

option_rationales.A: Identity Protection risk policies need Microsoft Entra ID P2 for every user in scope, so acquiring P2 is the prerequisite.
option_rationales.B: Registering users for MFA is useful once the policy exists, but it does not make the policy configurable.
option_rationales.C: Security defaults are a fixed baseline and are mutually exclusive with custom Conditional Access/risk policies — enabling them does not unlock risk policies.
option_rationales.D: Defender plans protect workloads in Defender for Cloud; they grant nothing in Identity Protection.

verification.note: Community 100% A. Still true: risk-based policies (now normally authored as Conditional Access policies using the risk conditions) require Microsoft Entra ID P2.

question_stem:

question_stem:

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.

| Name | Type | Description |
|------|------|-------------|
| RG1 | Resource group | Used to store virtual machines |
| RG2 | Resource group | Used to store virtual networks |
| ServerAdmins | Security group | Used to manage virtual machines |

You need to ensure that ServerAdmins can perform the following tasks:
=> Create virtual machines in RG1 only.
=> Connect the virtual machines to the existing virtual networks in RG2 only.
The solution must use the principle of least privilege.
Which two role-based access control (RBAC) roles should you assign to ServerAdmins? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.A: a custom RBAC role for RG2
options.B: the Network Contributor role for RG2
options.C: the Contributor role for the subscription
options.D: a custom RBAC role for the subscription
options.E: the Network Contributor role for RG1
options.F: the Virtual Machine Contributor role for RG1

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles
answer_summary: Creating VMs in RG1 is Virtual Machine Contributor on RG1; attaching them to existing VNets in RG2 only needs the subnet join permission, which no built-in role provides in isolation — hence a custom role on RG2.

option_rationales.A: A custom role on RG2 containing just Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/subnets/join/action (plus reads) is the least-privilege way to let the group attach NICs to existing subnets.
option_rationales.B: Network Contributor on RG2 would work but grants full management of virtual networks — more than joining a subnet, so it fails least privilege.
option_rationales.C: Contributor at the subscription is vastly more than required.
option_rationales.D: A custom role at the subscription would be broader in scope than the two resource groups involved.
option_rationales.E: Network Contributor on RG1 is the wrong resource group — the virtual networks live in RG2.
option_rationales.F: Virtual Machine Contributor on RG1 gives exactly the ability to create and manage VMs there.

verification.note: Community 71% AF. Still the standard pattern: the subnet 'join' action is the classic least-privilege gap that forces a custom role.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
Your network contains an on-premises Active Directory domain named adatum.com that syncs to Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
The Azure AD tenant contains the users shown in the following table.

| Name | Source | Password |
|------|--------|----------|
| User1 | Azure AD | Adatum123 |
| User2 | Azure AD | N3w3r10Gue33 |
| User3 | On-premises Active Directory | ComplexPassword33 |

You configure the Authentication methods " Password Protection settings for adatum.com as shown in the following exhibit.

Custom smart lockout
Lockout threshold ⓘ  10  ✓
Lockout duration in seconds ⓘ  60  ✓

Custom banned passwords
Enforce custom list ⓘ  Yes  No
  Adatum  ✓
Custom banned password list ⓘ

Password protection for Windows Server Active Directory
Enable password protection on Windows Server Active Directory ⓘ  Yes  No
Mode ⓘ  Enforced  Audit

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: User1 will be prompted to change the password on the next sign-in.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Password protection never invalidates an existing password. User1's 'Adatum123' contains a banned term, but it is only evaluated the next time the password is changed — no forced change is triggered.

hotspot_rows.statement: User2 can change the password to @d@tum_C0mplexX123.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Normalization turns '@d@tum_C0mplexX123' into 'adatum_complexx123', so the banned term is found — but that is 1 point plus 12 points for the remaining characters, which is well over the 5-point threshold, so the change is allowed.

hotspot_rows.statement: User3 can change the password to Adatum123!.
hotspot_rows.rationale: 'Adatum123!' normalizes to 'adatum123!': 1 point for the banned term plus 4 points for '123!' equals exactly 5, which meets the threshold, so it is accepted — even though on-premises protection is in Enforced mode.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/authentication/howto-password-ban-bad-on-premises-deploy
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-password-ban-bad

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure Portal screenshot of Password Protection settings showing custom smart lockout configuration, custom banned password list with 'Adatum' entry, and Windows Server Active Directory password protection enabled in Enforced mode.

answer_summary: Banned-password rules apply only when a password is set or changed, never retroactively — and the scoring algorithm gives one point per banned term found plus one per remaining character, accepting anything that scores five or more.

verification.note: The normalization plus 5-point scoring algorithm is still how Microsoft Entra Password Protection evaluates passwords, and the custom banned list still holds up to 1,000 terms.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
Your company has an Azure subscription named Subscription1. Subscription1 is associated with the Azure Active Directory tenant that includes the users shown in the following table.

| Name | Role |
|------|------|
| User1 | Global administrator |
| User2 | Billing administrator |
| User3 | Owner |

The company is sold to a new owner.
The company needs to transfer ownership of Subscription1.
Which user can transfer the ownership and which tool should the user use? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/manage/billing-subscription-transfer
answer_summary: Transferring a subscription because the company was sold is a billing-ownership transfer, and the documented requirement is the Account Administrator (the subscription's billing owner) — carried out, for this subscription generation, in Azure Account Center.

slot_rationales.User: User4, the Account Admin: Microsoft documents that only the Account Administrator of a subscription can transfer its billing ownership. Global administrator (User1) is a directory role, Owner (User3) is an Azure RBAC role, and neither confers billing rights.
slot_rationales.Tool: Azure Account Center is where the Transfer subscription action lived for this generation of subscriptions.

verification.note: Corrected from User1 to User4. This bank contains the same question twice with two different keys (this copy said User1, the other said User2), so at least one was wrong; the documented answer for a MOSP/pay-as-you-go subscription is the Account Administrator. question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that uses Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Privileged Identity Management (PIM).
A PIM user that is assigned the User Access Administrator role reports receiving an authorization error when performing a role assignment or viewing the list of assignments.
You need to resolve the issue by ensuring that the PIM service principal has the correct permissions for the subscription. The solution must use the principle of least privilege.
Which role should you assign to the PIM service principle?
answer_summary: PIM performs role assignments on your behalf, so its service principal needs the one role that can read and write role assignments: User Access Administrator. Anything less cannot manage assignments; anything more breaks least privilege.

option_rationales.A: Contributor can manage resources but explicitly cannot create or read role assignments, so the authorization error would persist.
option_rationales.B: User Access Administrator grants Microsoft.Authorization/* — exactly the permission needed to view and manage role assignments, and nothing more.
option_rationales.C: Managed Application Operator only allows actions on managed applications.
option_rationales.D: Resource Policy Contributor manages Azure Policy artifacts, not role assignments.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Granting the PIM service principal User Access Administrator on the subscription is still the documented fix, and Role Based Access Control Administrator is now a narrower alternative for delegating role assignment.

question_stem:
You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant that contains a user named Admin1. Admin1 is assigned the Application developer role.
You purchase a cloud app named App1 and register App1 in Azure AD.
Admin1 reports that the option to enable token encryption for App1 is unavailable.
You need to ensure that Admin1 can enable token encryption for App1 in the Azure portal.
What should you do?

options.B: Modify the API permissions of App1.
options.C: Add App1 as an enterprise application.
options.D: Assign Admin1 the Cloud application administrator role.

explanation:
This is a tricky one because uploading a certificate is also required. However, the question states that the Token Encryption option is unavailable. This is because the app is not added as an enterprise application. When the app is added as an enterprise application, the Token Encryption option will be available.
Then you can upload the certificate.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/manage-apps/howto-saml-token-encryption
answer_summary: Token encryption is driven by a public-key certificate: Entra ID uses it to encrypt the SAML token it issues. Until a certificate is uploaded to the application there is nothing to activate, which is why the option is unavailable.

option_rationales.A: Uploading (importing) a certificate is the prerequisite — the activation control only becomes usable once the app has a certificate whose public key can encrypt the token.
option_rationales.B: API permissions govern what the app can call; they have no bearing on token encryption.
option_rationales.C: Registering the app already created its enterprise application/service principal entry, so there is nothing further to add — and the exam's own explanation concedes a certificate is required anyway.
option_rationales.D: The Application Developer role is enough to manage an app the user owns; a higher role does not create the missing certificate.

verification.note: Answer changed from C to A, matching the 61% community vote and Microsoft's 'Configure SAML token encryption' procedure, whose first step is importing the certificate. Two caveats: token encryption applies to apps using SAML-based single sign-on, and it requires a Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 licence.

question_stem:
You plan to deploy an app that will modify the properties of Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) users by using Microsoft Graph.
You need to ensure that the app can access Azure AD.
What should you configure first?

options.C: a custom role-based access control (RBAC) role

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/develop/active-directory-how-applications-are-added
answer_summary: Before an app can call Microsoft Graph it needs an identity in the directory — that starts with an app registration, which produces the application object, the service principal, and the place where Graph permissions are requested.

option_rationales.A: The app registration is the first step: it creates the identity, then you add Microsoft Graph permissions (for example User.ReadWrite.All) and consent to them.
option_rationales.B: External identities are for guest/B2B users, not for an application's own access.
option_rationales.C: A custom Azure RBAC role grants permissions on Azure resources, not on directory objects via Graph.
option_rationales.D: Application Proxy publishes on-premises web apps; it grants no Graph access.

verification.note: Community 100% A. Directory writes via Graph need directory permissions plus an appropriate Entra role for the app where required.

question_stem:
You have a Microsoft 365 tenant that uses an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant. The Azure AD tenant syncs to an on-premises Active Directory domain by using an instance of Azure AD Connect.
You create a new Azure subscription.
You discover that the synced on-premises user accounts cannot be assigned roles in the new subscription.
You need to ensure that you can assign Azure and Microsoft 365 roles to the synced Azure AD user accounts.
What should you do first?

options.A: Configure the Azure AD tenant used by the new subscription to use pass-through authentication.
options.B: Configure the Azure AD tenant used by the new subscription to use federated authentication.
options.C: Change the Azure AD tenant used by the new subscription.
options.D: Configure a second instance of Azure AD Connect.

answer_summary: A brand-new subscription is created in its own new directory, so the synced accounts simply do not exist in that tenant. You have to point the subscription at the existing tenant that holds those users.

option_rationales.A: Changing the sign-in method does nothing if the users are not in the subscription's directory at all.
option_rationales.B: Federation has the same problem — it is an authentication choice, not a directory-membership fix.
option_rationales.C: Changing the subscription's directory to the existing tenant makes the synced users (and Microsoft 365 roles) available for assignment.
option_rationales.D: A second Entra Connect instance would sync into the wrong directory and is unsupported for the same source objects.

verification.note: Community 100% C. Still true, and remember that changing a subscription's directory removes all existing role assignments on it.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains an app named App1. App1 has the app registration shown in the following table.

| API | Permission | Type | Admin consent required | Status |
|-----|------------|------|------------------------|--------|
| Microsoft.Graph | User.Read | Delegated | No | None |
| Microsoft.Graph | Calendars.Read | Delegated | No | None |

You need to ensure that App1 can read all user calendars and create appointments. The solution must use the principle of least privilege.
What should you do?

options.A: Add a new Delegated API permission for Microsoft.Graph Calendars.ReadWrite.
options.B: Add a new Application API permission for Microsoft.Graph Calendars.ReadWrite.
options.D: Add new Delegated API permission for Microsoft.Graph Calendars.ReadWrite.Shared.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/permissions-reference#calendars-permissions
answer_summary: Reading every user's calendar and creating appointments without a signed-in user is app-only work, so it needs the Application permission Calendars.ReadWrite (with admin consent) — a delegated permission would only reach the calendar of whoever is signed in.

option_rationales.A: A delegated Calendars.ReadWrite acts on behalf of the signed-in user, so it cannot read all users' calendars.
option_rationales.B: The Application permission Calendars.ReadWrite grants app-only access to all mailboxes' calendars, which is exactly what is required (and is normally narrowed with an application access policy in Exchange).
option_rationales.C: Granting admin consent to the existing permissions changes nothing — Calendars.Read cannot create appointments.
option_rationales.D: Calendars.ReadWrite.Shared extends delegated access to calendars shared with the signed-in user, which is still not all users.

verification.note: Answer changed from A to B (community 65% B). Delegated permissions are always bounded by the signed-in user's own access; 'all user calendars' with no user present requires an application permission. Best practice today is to pair it with an Exchange application access policy so the app can only touch the mailboxes it needs.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant that contains the users shown in the following table.

| Name | Member of group | Multi-factor authentication (MFA) status |
|------|----------------|------------------------------------------|
| User1 | Group1, Group2 | Enabled |
| User2 | Group1 | Disabled |

You create and enforce an Azure AD Identity Protection sign-in risk policy that has the following settings:
=> Assignments: Include Group1, exclude Group2
=> Conditions: Sign-in risk level: Low and above
=> Access: Allow access, Require multi-factor authentication
You need to identify what occurs when the users sign in to Azure AD.
What should you identify for each user? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
Reference:
http://www.rebeladmin.com/2018/09/step-step-guide-configure-risk-based-azure-conditional-access-policies/ https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/concept-identity-protection-policies https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/concept-identity-protection-risks
answer_summary: User1 is excluded from the risk policy (she is in the excluded Group2), so the policy never fires for her — but her per-user MFA is Enabled, so she is challenged anyway. User2 is in scope, and because he has no registered MFA method he cannot satisfy the requirement and is blocked.

slot_rationales.When User1 signs in from an anonymous IP: Be prompted for MFA — not because of the risk policy (Group2 is excluded, and exclusions win) but because User1's per-user MFA status is Enabled, so MFA is requested at sign-in.
slot_rationales.When User2 signs in from an unfamiliar l: Be blocked — an unfamiliar location is Medium risk, so the policy applies to this Group1 member and requires MFA; a user who is not registered for MFA cannot satisfy a risk-based MFA requirement and is blocked rather than prompted to register.

verification.note: Both still hold, and the blocking behaviour is specific to risk-based policies: Microsoft documents that users not registered for MFA are blocked when a risk policy requires it, whereas an ordinary Conditional Access MFA grant normally interrupts the user to register. Currency: the standalone Identity Protection sign-in risk policy is superseded by Conditional Access policies using the sign-in risk condition.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure SQL database named SQL1.
You plan to deploy a web app named App1.
You need to provide App1 with read and write access to SQL1. The solution must meet the following requirements:
=> Provide App1 with access to SQL1 without storing a password.
=> Use the principle of least privilege.
=> Minimize administrative effort.
Which type of account should App1 use to access SQL1, and which database roles should you assign to App1? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/tutorial-connect-msi-sql-database?tabs=windowsclient%2Cdotnet
answer_summary: A managed identity removes the stored password entirely, and inside the database the least-privilege pairing for read plus write is db_datareader with db_datawriter — not db_owner.

slot_rationales.Account type: Managed identity — the web app authenticates to SQL with a token from its own identity, so there is no password anywhere and nothing to rotate.
slot_rationales.Roles: Db_datareader and db_datawriter together give SELECT plus INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on all tables and nothing more; db_owner would grant schema and security control the app does not need.

verification.note: Still the recommended pattern: create the contained database user FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER for the managed identity, then add it to those two roles.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant that contains two users named User1 and User2 and a registered app named App1.
You create an app-specific role named Role1.
You need to assign Role1 to User1 and enable User2 to request access to App1.
Which two settings should you modify? To answer, select the appropriate settings in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
Box 1: Roles and administrators -
Here you will find Role1 and be able to assign User1 to the role.
Box 2: Self Service -
Under Self Service, there is an option to "Allow users to request access to this application".

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure Portal screenshot of App1 Enterprise Application blade showing navigation menu with Overview, Deployment Plan, Manage section (Properties, Owners, Roles and administrators, Users and groups, Single sign-on, Provisioning, Application proxy, Self-service) and Security section (Conditional Access, Permissions, Token encryption).

answer_summary: Two different blades on the enterprise application: the app-scoped role is granted from Roles and administrators, and letting a user ask for access is switched on under Self-service.

slot_rationales.Box 1: Roles and administrators — where the app-specific role appears and where User1 is assigned to it.
slot_rationales.Box 2: Self-service — contains 'Allow users to request access to this application?', which is what enables User2 to request access (optionally with approval).

verification.note: The blade is now simply 'Roles and administrators' (no longer flagged Preview). Note the distinction that trips people up: application roles defined in the app manifest are granted under Users and groups, whereas app-scoped directory roles are granted under Roles and administrators.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table. | Name | Type | |------|------| | storage1 | Storage account | | Vault1 | Azure Key vault | | Vault2 | Azure Key vault | You plan to deploy the virtual machines shown in the following table. | Name | Role | |------|------| | VM1 | • Storage Blob Data Reader for storage1
• Key Vault Reader for Vault1 | | VM2 | • Storage Blob Data Reader for storage1
• Key Vault Reader for Vault1 | | VM3 | • Storage Blob Data Reader for storage1
• Key Vault Reader for Vault1
• Key Vault Reader for Vault2 | | VM4 | • Storage Blob Data Reader for storage1
• Key Vault Reader for Vault1
• Key Vault Reader for Vault2 | You need to assign managed identities to the virtual machines. The solution must meet the following requirements: => Assign each virtual machine the required roles. => Use the principle of least privilege. What is the minimum number of managed identities required?
explanation:
We have two different sets of required permissions. VM1 and VM2 have the same permission requirements. VM3 and VM4 have the same permission requirements.
A user-assigned managed identity can be assigned to one or many resources. By using user-assigned managed identities, we can create just two managed identities: one with the permission requirements for VM1 and VM2 and the other with the permission requirements for VM3 and VM4.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/managed-identities-azure-resources/overview
answer_summary: Two distinct permission sets are needed (VM1/VM2 versus VM3/VM4), and a user-assigned managed identity can be shared by many resources — so two user-assigned identities cover all four VMs with the fewest identities and the least privilege.

option_rationales.A: One identity would have to hold the union of both permission sets, giving VM1 and VM2 access to Vault2 that they should not have.
option_rationales.B: Two user-assigned managed identities — one with the roles for VM1/VM2 and one with the roles for VM3/VM4 — match the requirements exactly.
option_rationales.C: Three identities means at least one duplicate permission set, adding administrative overhead for no benefit.
option_rationales.D: Four (for example system-assigned identities on each VM) would need the same role assignments repeated four times.

verification.note: Community 78% B. User-assigned managed identities can still be attached to multiple resources, which is what makes the count two rather than four.

question_stem:

question_stem:

You need to create a new Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) directory named 12345678.onmicrosoft.com. The new directory must contain a new user named user1@12345678.onmicrosoft.com.
