|------|------|
| User1 | Role1 |
| User2 | Role2 |
| User3 | Role1, Role2 |

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: User1 can read data in storage1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Role1 includes Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action, so User1 can retrieve the account key and use it to read any data in storage1 — a classic reason to prefer Entra ID authorization over key access.

hotspot_rows.statement: User2 can read data in storage1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Role2's Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/* wildcard includes listKeys, so User2 can do the same.

hotspot_rows.statement: User3 can restore storage1 from a backup in Azure Backup.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Restoring from Azure Backup requires Recovery Services vault permissions (Microsoft.RecoveryServices/*). Neither role grants them, so User3 cannot perform the restore despite holding both roles.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/custom-roles
answer_summary: The listKeys permission is the giveaway: anyone who can list the account keys can read all the data, whatever their data-plane assignments say. Both roles grant it (Role2 via Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/*), but neither grants anything under Microsoft.RecoveryServices.

verification.note: Still accurate. If you want to close the listKeys loophole in practice, disable shared key authorization on the storage account so only Entra ID identities can access data.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains a storage account named storage1 and two web apps named app1 and app2.
Both apps will write data to storage1.
You need to ensure that each app can read only the data that it has written.
What should you do?

options.A: Provide each app with a system-assigned identity and configure storage1 to use Azure AD User account authentication.
options.B: Provide each app with a separate Storage account key and configure the app to send the key with each request.
options.C: Provide each app with a user-managed identity and configure storage1 to use Azure AD User account authentication.
options.D: Provide each app with a unique Base64-encoded AES-256 encryption key and configure the app to send the key with each request.

explanation:
A user-assigned identity is a standalone Azure resource that can be assigned to your app. An app can have multiple user-assigned identities.
Incorrect:
Not A: A system-assigned identity is tied to your application and is deleted if your app is deleted. An app can only have one system-assigned identity.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/overview-managed-identity
answer_summary: With both apps writing into the same account, the only thing that guarantees an app can read just its own data is encrypting each app's blobs with its own customer-provided key: without that key the other app's requests fail even if RBAC would allow the read.

option_rationales.A: A system-assigned identity plus Entra ID authorization controls who can reach the account or container, but by itself does not stop app1 reading blobs app2 wrote into the same container.
option_rationales.B: Account keys are account-wide — either key grants full access to everything, which is the opposite of isolation.
option_rationales.C: Same limitation as A: identities determine access, but the isolation asked for would still need per-container scoping, which is not part of the proposal.
option_rationales.D: Supplying a unique Base64-encoded AES-256 customer-provided key on each request means blobs written by one app can only be read by a request presenting that same key, so each app can read only its own data.

verification.note: Answer changed from C to D, matching the 72% community vote. The stored key's own explanation only compares system-assigned with user-assigned identities and never addresses the read-only-your-own-data requirement. Note the trade-off with customer-provided keys: Azure Storage never stores the key, so losing it means losing the data.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure Files share named share1 and a user named User1. Identity-based authentication is configured for share1.
User1 attempts to access share1 from a Windows 10 device by using SMB.
Which type of token will Azure Files use to authorize the request?
explanation:
Azure Files‰Ûª supports identity-based authentication over Server Message Block (SMB) through two types of Domain Services: on-premises Active Directory Domain
Services (AD DS) and Azure Active Directory Domain Services (Azure AD DS).
Supported scenarios and restrictions include:
Supports Kerberos authentication with AD with AES 256 encryption (recommended) and RC4-HMAC.
Note: Kerberos is an authentication protocol that is used to verify the identity of a user or host.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/files/storage-files-identity-auth-active-directory-enable
answer_summary: Identity-based authentication for Azure Files over SMB is built on Kerberos — the client obtains a Kerberos ticket from AD DS (or Microsoft Entra Domain Services / Entra Kerberos) and presents it to the file share.

option_rationales.A: OAuth 2.0 is used by the REST/data-plane APIs with Entra ID tokens, not by the SMB protocol.
option_rationales.B: A JWT is the token format Entra ID issues for REST calls; SMB cannot present one.
option_rationales.C: SAML is for web single sign-on between identity providers and applications.
option_rationales.D: Kerberos tickets are what SMB uses for identity-based authorization, which is why the client must be able to reach a domain controller.

verification.note: Community 100% D. Still Kerberos, and the supported identity sources have since expanded to include Microsoft Entra Kerberos for hybrid identities and Entra Domain Services.

question_stem:
DRAG DROP -
You have an Azure subscription.
You plan to create two custom roles named Role1 and Role2.
The custom roles will be used to perform the following tasks:
• Members of Role1 will manage application security groups.
• Members of Role2 will manage Azure Bastion.
You need to add permissions to the custom roles.
Which resource provider should you use for each role? To answer, drag the appropriate resource providers to the correct roles. Each resource provider may be used, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Select and Place:

diagrams.diagram_description: Drag-drop answer area showing available resource providers (Microsoft.Compute, Microsoft.Network, Microsoft.Security, Microsoft.Solutions) on the left and Role1/Role2 target slots on the right.

answer_summary: Both features belong to the networking provider: application security groups are Microsoft.Network/applicationSecurityGroups and Azure Bastion hosts are Microsoft.Network/bastionHosts.

slot_rationales.Role1: Microsoft.Network — application security groups are a networking resource type (Microsoft.Network/applicationSecurityGroups), not a compute or security one.
slot_rationales.Role2: Microsoft.Network — Azure Bastion is deployed as Microsoft.Network/bastionHosts, so managing it also needs this provider (plus reads on the VMs you connect to).

verification.note: Both resource types are still under Microsoft.Network. Microsoft.Security covers Defender for Cloud and Microsoft.Solutions covers managed applications, which is why they are distractors here.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription linked to an Azure Active Directory Premium Plan 1 tenant.
You plan to implement Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Identity Protection.
You need to ensure that you can configure a user risk policy and a sign-in risk policy.
What should you do first?

options.A: Purchase Azure Active Directory Premium Plan 2 licenses for all users.
options.B: Register all users for Azure Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA).
options.C: Enable security defaults for Azure Active Directory.
options.D: Enable enhanced security features in Microsoft Defender for Cloud.

answer_summary: User risk and sign-in risk policies are Identity Protection features licensed under Microsoft Entra ID P2 — with P1 you cannot configure them, so the licences come first.

option_rationales.A: Entra ID P2 for the users in scope is the prerequisite for risk policies.
option_rationales.B: MFA registration matters for the policy's outcome, not for whether the policy can be created.
option_rationales.C: Security defaults are a fixed baseline that conflicts with custom policies rather than enabling them.
option_rationales.D: Defender for Cloud plans protect Azure workloads and grant nothing in Identity Protection.

verification.note: Community 100% A. This is a near-duplicate of Topic 2 Q52 in the same bank.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT
-
You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.

| Name | Type |
|------|------|
| RG1 | Resource group |
| VM1 | Virtual machine |

You perform the following tasks:
• Create a managed identity named Managed1.
• Create a Microsoft 365 group named Group1.
• Register an enterprise application named App1.
• Enable a system-assigned managed identity for VM1.
You need to identify which service principals were created and which identities can be assigned the Reader role for RG1.
What should you identify? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
answer_summary: Service principals are created for the managed identity, for the VM's system-assigned identity and for the registered application — a Microsoft 365 group is not a service principal. The second box asks which of them can hold an Azure RBAC role.

slot_rationales.Service Principles: Managed1, VM1 and App1: every managed identity (standalone or system-assigned) has a service principal, and registering an enterprise application creates one. Group1, a Microsoft 365 group, is a group object, not a service principal.
slot_rationales.Identities: The stored key limits this to the two managed identities, Managed1 and VM1 — see the note, because in current Azure the app's service principal and the group can also be given the Reader role.

verification.note: The first box is solid. The second is questionable: Azure RBAC role assignments support users, groups (including Microsoft 365 groups), service principals and managed identities, so App1 and Group1 could also be assigned Reader on RG1. The original dropdown choices are not preserved in this bank, so the stored value has been left in place rather than guessed at — treat 'Managed1 and VM1 only' as the exam key, not as a limitation of Azure.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT
-
You have an Azure Active directory tenant that syncs with an Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) domain.
You plan to create an Azure file share that will contain folders and files.
Which identity store can you use to assign permissions to the Azure file share and folders within the share? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
answer_summary: Azure Files has two independent permission layers: share-level access is Azure RBAC granted to Microsoft Entra identities, while permissions on folders and files inside the share are Windows ACLs evaluated with domain (AD DS) identities.

slot_rationales.Azure file share: Entra ID (Azure AD): share-level permissions are Azure RBAC roles such as Storage File Data SMB Share Reader/Contributor/Elevated Contributor, assigned to Entra identities.
slot_rationales.Folders in the file share: Directory and file permissions are standard Windows ACLs, which are set and enforced using the AD DS identities (that are synchronized with Entra ID in this hybrid tenant).

verification.note: Kept as stored. Be aware of the precise mechanics for the real exam: NTFS/Windows ACLs on directories and files are evaluated against the AD DS (domain) identity via Kerberos, so many sources give 'AD DS only' for the second box; Entra ID appears only because the same users are synchronized from AD DS.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription.
You plan to deploy a new Conditional Access policy named CAPolicy1.
You need to use the What if tool to evaluate how CAPolicy1 will affect users. The solution must minimize the impact of CAPolicy1 on the users.
To what should you set the Enable policy setting for CAPolicy1?
answer_summary: Report-only mode evaluates the policy for every sign-in and records what would have happened without enforcing it — exactly what you want when using What If to assess impact.

option_rationales.A: Off means the policy is disabled entirely, so no evaluation data is produced.
option_rationales.B: On enforces the policy immediately, which is the maximum impact on users, not the minimum.
option_rationales.C: Report only logs the result of the policy in the sign-in logs while letting users through, so you can measure impact safely before enforcing.

verification.note: Community 100% C. Report-only is still the recommended rollout step, and the What If tool remains available for point-in-time evaluation.

question_stem:
You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant that contains 500 users and an administrative unit named AU1.
From the Azure Active Directory admin center, you plan to add the users to AU1 by using Bulk add members.
You need to create and upload a file for the bulk add.
What should you include in the file?

options.A: only the display name of each user
options.B: only the user principal name (UPN) of each user
options.C: only the user principal name (UPN) and display name of each user
options.D: only the user principal name (UPN) and object identifier of each user
options.E: only the object identifier of each user

answer_summary: The bulk-add template for administrative unit members takes a single identifying column — each user's UPN (or object ID) — so nothing else needs to be in the file.

option_rationales.A: Display name is not unique and is not part of the template.
option_rationales.B: The CSV needs only the member identifier per row, and the user principal name is what the downloaded template asks for.
option_rationales.C: Including display name adds a column the import does not use.
option_rationales.D: Only one identifier is required — either the UPN or the object ID, not both.
option_rationales.E: The object identifier alone would also work, but the template's documented column is the user principal name, and the question asks what to include.

verification.note: Answer changed from C to B (community 100% B). The bulk operation CSV for administrative units contains one member-identifier column plus the template's header rows — no display name.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains a user named User1.
You need to ensure that User1 can create managed identities. The solution must use the principle of least privilege.
What should you do?

options.A: Create a management group and assign User1 the Hybrid Identity Administrator Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) role.
options.B: Create a management group and assign User1 the Managed Identity Operator role.
options.C: Create a resource group and assign User1 to the Managed Identity Contributor role.
options.D: Create an organizational unit (OU) and assign User1 the User administrator Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) role.

answer_summary: Creating user-assigned managed identities is a resource-creation right in a resource group, granted by Managed Identity Contributor — Managed Identity Operator only lets you use an existing identity, and the directory roles are irrelevant.

option_rationales.A: Hybrid Identity Administrator is a directory role for Entra Connect; it cannot create Azure resources.
option_rationales.B: Managed Identity Operator allows reading and assigning an existing user-assigned identity, not creating one.
option_rationales.C: Managed Identity Contributor allows create, read, update and delete of user-assigned managed identities, scoped to a resource group for least privilege.
option_rationales.D: OUs are an on-premises AD concept, and User administrator manages users, not Azure resources.

verification.note: Community 100% C. Both roles still exist with the same split: Contributor creates identities, Operator assigns them to resources.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT
-
You have an Azure subscription that contains a resource group named RG1. RG1 contains a virtual machine named VM1 that uses Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) authentication.
You have two custom Azure roles named Role1 and Role2 that are scoped to RG1.
The permissions for Role1 are shown in the following JSON code.

```json
"permissions": [
  {
    "actions": [
      "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/*"
    ],
    "notActions": [
      "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete"
    ],
    "dataActions": [],
    "notDataActions": []
  }
]
```

The permissions for Role2 are shown in the following JSON code.

```json
"permissions": [
  {
    "actions": [
      "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/*"
    ],
    "notActions": [],
    "dataActions": [],
    "notDataActions": []
  }
]
```

You assign the roles to the users shown in the following table.

| Name | Role |
|------|------|
| User1 | Role1 |
| User2 | Role1, Role2 |
| User3 | Role1, Role2 |

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

hotspot_rows.statement: User1 can delete VM1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: User1 holds only Role1, whose NotActions removes Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete, so the delete is not permitted.

hotspot_rows.statement: User2 can delete VM1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: User2 holds Role1 and Role2. Effective permissions are the union of role assignments, and Role2 grants Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/* with no NotActions — so the delete Role1 withheld is granted by Role2.

hotspot_rows.statement: User3 can sign in to VM1 by using Azure AD credentials.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Signing in with Entra ID credentials requires the data actions Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/login/action (or loginAsAdmin), which are what the Virtual Machine User Login and Administrator Login roles provide. Both custom roles have empty dataActions, and an Actions wildcard does not cover DataActions, so sign-in is denied.

answer_summary: NotActions is subtractive only inside its own role definition — it is not a deny rule — so a second role that allows delete wins. And the Entra ID sign-in permission is a DataAction, which a wildcard in Actions never covers.

verification.note: Rows 2 and 3 changed (No→Yes and Yes→No). Microsoft's RBAC documentation is explicit on both points: NotActions is not a deny rule and can be overridden by another role assignment (only deny assignments actually block), and control-plane Actions and data-plane DataActions are evaluated separately, so Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/* does not grant the VM login data action.

question_stem:
DRAG DROP
-
You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.

| Name | Type |
|------|------|
| VM1 | Virtual machine |
| VM2 | Virtual machine |
| st1 | Storage account |
| Vault1 | Azure Key Vault |

You plan to perform the following actions:
• Deploy a new app named App1 that will require access to Vault1.
• Configure a shared identity for VM1 and VM2 to access st1.
You need to configure identities for each requirement. The solution must minimize administrative effort.
Which type of identity should you configure for each requirement? To answer, drag the appropriate identity types to the correct requirements. Each identity type may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

diagrams.diagram_description: Drag-drop answer area showing available identity types (Security group, System-assigned managed identity, User account, User-assigned managed identity) on the left and two requirement slots on the right (VM1 and VM2 access to st1, App1 access to Vault1).

answer_summary: One identity shared by two VMs can only be a user-assigned managed identity (a system-assigned identity belongs to exactly one resource), while a single new app that just needs Key Vault access is simplest with a system-assigned identity.

slot_rationales.VM1 and VM2 access to st1: A user-assigned managed identity is a standalone resource that can be attached to many VMs, so one identity — and one role assignment on st1 — covers both machines.
slot_rationales.App1 access to Vault1: A system-assigned managed identity is created and deleted with the app and needs no separate lifecycle management, which is the least-effort choice for a single consumer of Vault1.

verification.note: First slot changed from system-assigned to user-assigned. A system-assigned managed identity is bound one-to-one to its resource, so it cannot be the 'shared identity for VM1 and VM2' the requirement asks for.

question_stem:
You have an Azure AD tenant. The tenant contains users that are assigned Azure AD Premium P2 licenses.
You have a partner company that has a domain named fabrikam.com. The fabrikam.com domain contains a user named User1. User1 has an email address of user1@fabrikam.com
You need to provide User1 with access to the resources in the tenant. The solution must meet the following requirements:
• User1 must be able to sign in by using the user1@fabrikam.com credentials.
• You must be able to grant User1 access to the resources in the tenant.
• Administrative effort must be minimized.
What should you do?

options.A: Create a user account for User1.
options.B: To the tenant, add fabrikam.com as a custom domain.
options.D: Set Enable guest self-service sign up via user flows to Yes for the tenant.

answer_summary: Inviting User1 as a B2B guest lets them sign in with their own user1@fabrikam.com credentials while giving you a guest object in your tenant to assign access to — with almost no administrative work.

option_rationales.A: A local user account would mean new credentials in your tenant, not sign-in with user1@fabrikam.com.
option_rationales.B: Adding fabrikam.com as a custom domain would require you to own and verify that domain, and it would not import the partner's users.
option_rationales.C: A B2B invitation creates a guest user backed by the partner's own identity, so User1 authenticates at fabrikam.com and you can grant them resources.
option_rationales.D: Self-service sign-up flows let unknown users register themselves — more configuration and less control than a direct invite for one known person.

verification.note: Community 100% C. Still the standard approach (now Microsoft Entra External ID B2B collaboration); cross-tenant access settings let you tighten what invited guests can do.

question_stem:
You have an Azure AD tenant that contains the identities shown in the following table.

| Type | Amount |
|------|--------|
| User | 1,000 |
| Microsoft 365 group | 200 |
| Mail-enabled security group | 65 |
| Security group | 25 |

You plan to implement Azure AD Identity Protection.
What is the maximum number of user risk policies you can configure?
answer_summary: Identity Protection exposes exactly one user risk policy for the tenant — the numbers in the table are a distraction, because the limit has nothing to do with how many users or groups exist.

option_rationales.A: There is a single built-in user risk policy per tenant (as there is a single sign-in risk policy and one MFA registration policy).
option_rationales.B: 90 has no basis — it is derived from adding group counts.
option_rationales.C: 200 is the number of Microsoft 365 groups, not a policy limit.
option_rationales.D: 265 is just 200 + 65 groups; policy count is not driven by group count.
option_rationales.E: 1,000 is the user count.

verification.note: Answer changed from D to A (community 91% A). Currency: the built-in Identity Protection policies are now superseded by Conditional Access policies that use the user-risk and sign-in-risk conditions — and of those you can create many, so a modern exam item would phrase this differently.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains a resource group named RG1 and the identities shown in the following table.

| Name | Type | Azure AD roles can be assigned to the group |
|------|------|--------------------------------------------|
| User1 | User | Not applicable |
| Group1 | Microsoft 365 group | Yes |
| Group2 | Security group | No |
| Group3 | Security group | Yes |
| Group4 | Security group | Yes |

You assign Group4 the Contributor role for RG1.
Which identities can you add to Group4 as members?
answer_summary: Group4 is role-assignable (Azure AD roles can be assigned to it), and a role-assignable group can only contain users and service principals — no nested groups of any kind.

option_rationales.A: Only User1 can be added: role-assignable groups do not support group membership, so Group1, Group2 and Group3 are all ineligible regardless of their own settings.
option_rationales.B: Group3 is itself role-assignable, but that does not make it addable — nesting is blocked for role-assignable groups.
option_rationales.C: Group1 is a Microsoft 365 group and also a group, so it fails on both counts.
option_rationales.D: Group2 is a plain security group, still a group, so it cannot be nested here.
option_rationales.E: All three groups are excluded for the same reason.

verification.note: Answer changed from B to A (community 63% A). Microsoft documents that groups cannot be members of a role-assignable group (isAssignableToRole = true); such groups also cannot be created dynamically and their membership is protected by the Privileged Role Administrator boundary.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT
-

You have an Azure subscription that contains a storage account named contoso2023.

You need to perform the following tasks:

• Verify that identity-based authentication over SMB is enabled.
• Only grant users access to contoso2023 in the year 2023.

Which two settings should you use? To answer, select the appropriate settings in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure Portal screenshot of contoso2023 Storage account navigation menu showing sections for Diagnose and solve problems, Access Control (IAM), Data migration, Events, Storage browser, Data storage (Containers, File shares, Queues, Tables), Security + networking (Networking, Azure CDN, Access keys, Shared access signature, Encryption, Microsoft Defender for Cloud), and Data management (Geo-replication, Data protection).

answer_summary: Identity-based (Entra ID / AD DS) authentication over SMB is a File shares setting on the storage account, and time-boxing access to a specific year means issuing a shared access signature with matching start and expiry times.

slot_rationales.Box 1: File shares — the Active Directory/identity-based access configuration for SMB is shown and enabled from this blade.
slot_rationales.Box 2: Shared access signature — a SAS lets you set the start and expiry date/time, which is how access is limited to 2023 only.

verification.note: Both settings are still in those places. A stored access policy on the share is the more manageable way to enforce and later revoke such a window.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains a user named User1 and an Azure Container Registry named ContReg1.
You enable content trust for ContReg1.
You need to ensure that User1 can create trusted images in ContReg1. The solution must use the principle of least privilege.
Which two roles should you assign to User1? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

A. AcrQuarantineReader

B. Contributor

C. AcrPush

D. AcrImageSigner

E. AcrQuarantineWriter
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-content-trust https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-roles
answer_summary: Creating a trusted image means two things: pushing the image (AcrPush) and signing it (AcrImageSigner) — neither role includes the other, and Contributor would be excessive.

option_rationales.A: AcrQuarantineReader only allows pulling quarantined images.
option_rationales.B: Contributor grants full registry management, violating least privilege.
option_rationales.C: AcrPush is required to push the image to ContReg1.
option_rationales.D: AcrImageSigner is required to sign the image so it becomes trusted under Docker content trust.
option_rationales.E: AcrQuarantineWriter relates to the quarantine workflow, not to signing.

verification.note: Community 100% CD. Note for currency: ACR's Docker content trust feature is deprecated in favour of image signing with Notation/Notary v2 and verification through Azure Policy or Ratify.

question_stem:
You have an Azure Container Registry named ContReg1 that contains a container image named image1.
You enable content trust for ContReg1.
After content trust is enabled, you push two images to ContReg1 as shown in the following table.

| Name | Details |
|------|----------|
| image2 | Image was pushed with client content trust enabled. |
| image3 | Image was pushed with client content trust disabled. |

Which images are trusted images?
explanation:
Azure Container Registry implements Docker's content trust model, enabling pushing and pulling of signed images.
To push a trusted image tag to your container registry, enable content trust and push the image with docker push.
To work with trusted images, both image publishers and consumers need to enable content trust for their Docker clients. As a publisher, you can sign the images you push to a content trust-enabled registry.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-content-trust
answer_summary: An image is trusted only if it was signed at push time. image2 was pushed with client content trust enabled, so it is signed; image1 predates content trust and image3 was pushed with trust disabled, so neither is signed.

option_rationales.A: Image1 was pushed before content trust was enabled, so it carries no signature.
option_rationales.B: Only image2 was pushed with client-side content trust on, so only image2 is signed and therefore trusted.
option_rationales.C: Image3 was explicitly pushed with content trust disabled, so it is unsigned.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Enabling content trust on the registry does not retroactively sign existing images — the same is true of the newer Notation-based signing.

Reference:

answer_summary: On the storage account's networking settings, switch Public network access to 'Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses', add 131.107.0.0/16 as the only IP rule, and save — the default action then denies everything else.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Location | Virtual network name |
|------|----------|---------------------|
| VM1 | East US | VNET1 |
| VM2 | West US | VNET2 |
| VM3 | East US | VNET1 |
| VM4 | West US | VNET3 |

All the virtual networks are peered.
You deploy Azure Bastion to VNET2.
Which virtual machines can be protected by the bastion host?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/bastion/vnet-peering
answer_summary: A bastion host can reach any VM it has network line-of-sight to, and all four VNets are peered — so one Bastion deployment in VNET2 covers VMs in VNET1, VNET2 and VNET3, in either region.

option_rationales.A: With VNet peering in place (including global peering across regions), the bastion host in VNET2 can connect to VM1, VM2, VM3 and VM4.
option_rationales.B: There is no reason to exclude VM4 — VNET3 is peered too.
option_rationales.C: Bastion is not limited to VMs in its own region.
option_rationales.D: Bastion is not limited to its own virtual network when peering exists.

verification.note: Community 100% A. Peering-based access still works this way; in practice the bastion SKU matters (Basic and above support peered VNets, and IP-based connection or shareable links require Standard/Premium), and NSGs must allow the bastion subnet to reach port 3389/22.

question_stem:
You have Azure Resource Manager templates that you use to deploy Azure virtual machines.
You need to disable unused Windows features automatically as instances of the virtual machines are provisioned.
What should you use?

options.A: device configuration policies in Microsoft Intune
options.C: security policies in Azure Security Center
options.D: device compliance policies in Microsoft Intune

explanation:
You can use Azure Automation State Configuration to manage Azure VMs (both Classic and Resource Manager), on-premises VMs, Linux machines, AWS VMs, and on-premises physical machines.
Note: Azure Automation State Configuration provides a DSC pull server similar to the Windows Feature DSC-Service so that target nodes automatically receive configurations, conform to the desired state, and report back on their compliance. The built-in pull server in Azure Automation eliminates the need to set up and maintain your own pull server. Azure Automation can target virtual or physical Windows or Linux machines, in the cloud or on-premises.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/automation/automation-dsc-getting-started
answer_summary: Turning off unused Windows features on every provisioned VM is desired-state work, and Azure Automation State Configuration is the DSC service that pulls that configuration onto each node and keeps it compliant.

option_rationales.A: Intune device configuration policies manage enrolled client devices via MDM, not Azure IaaS VMs being provisioned by templates.
option_rationales.B: Azure Automation State Configuration hosts the DSC configuration that nodes pull automatically, disabling the unwanted features and reporting drift.
option_rationales.C: Security Center policies assess and recommend; they do not apply in-guest Windows configuration.
option_rationales.D: Intune compliance policies only evaluate and report device state — they change nothing on the machine.

verification.note: Correct as written. Azure Automation State Configuration is being retired (end of support announced for 30 September 2027); the modern replacement is Azure Machine Configuration via Azure Policy guest configuration.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1. Sub1 contains a virtual network named VNet1 that contains one subnet named Subnet1.
Subnet1 contains an Azure virtual machine named VM1 that runs Ubuntu Server 18.04.
You create a service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage in Subnet1.
You need to ensure that when you deploy Docker containers to VM1, the containers can access Azure Storage resources by using the service endpoint.
What should you do on VM1 before you deploy the container?

options.A: Create an application security group and a network security group (NSG).
options.C: Install the container network interface (CNI) plug-in.

explanation:
The Azure Virtual Network container network interface (CNI) plug-in installs in an Azure Virtual Machine. The plug-in supports both Linux and Windows platform.
The plug-in assigns IP addresses from a virtual network to containers brought up in the virtual machine, attaching them to the virtual network, and connecting them directly to other containers and virtual network resources. The plug-in doesn't rely on overlay networks, or routes, for connectivity, and provides the same performance as virtual machines.
The following picture shows how the plug-in provides Azure Virtual Network capabilities to Pods:

Existing vitual network

Azure Firewall

Containers
Pod   Pod
Pod   Pod

Internet

Service Endpoints

Azure Services

On-premises

References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/container-networking-overview

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure architecture diagram showing an existing virtual network with Azure Firewall connected to Containers (four Pods arranged in a 2x2 grid), which connect to the Internet, Service Endpoints leading to Azure Services (SQL and storage icons), and On-premises infrastructure.

answer_summary: The containers need VNet IP addresses of their own so their traffic is recognised as coming from the service-endpoint-enabled subnet — that is what the Azure Virtual Network CNI plug-in provides.

option_rationales.A: ASGs and NSGs filter traffic; they cannot give containers a VNet identity, so service-endpoint traffic still would not work.
option_rationales.B: Docker-compose defines how containers run, not how the host's virtual network is presented to them.
option_rationales.C: The CNI plug-in assigns VNet IP addresses to the containers and attaches them directly to the subnet, so service endpoints, NSGs and routes apply to their traffic.

verification.note: Community 100% C; same scenario as Topic 1 Q15.

question_stem:
You have Azure Resource Manager templates that you use to deploy Azure virtual machines.
You need to disable unused Windows features automatically as instances of the virtual machines are provisioned.
What should you use?

options.A: device configuration policies in Microsoft Intune
options.B: an Azure Desired State Configuration (DSC) virtual machine extension
options.D: device compliance policies in Microsoft Intune

explanation:
The primary use case for the Azure Desired State Configuration (DSC) extension is to bootstrap a VM to the Azure Automation State Configuration (DSC) service.
The service provides benefits that include ongoing management of the VM configuration and integration with other operational tools, such as Azure Monitoring.
Using the extension to register VM's to the service provides a flexible solution that even works across Azure subscriptions.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/extensions/dsc-overview
answer_summary: The Azure DSC virtual machine extension is what runs at provisioning time to apply the configuration (and to bootstrap the VM into Automation State Configuration), so features can be disabled as each instance comes up.

option_rationales.A: Intune device configuration policies apply to MDM-enrolled devices, not to VMs deployed by ARM templates.
option_rationales.B: The DSC extension is deployed as part of the template and applies the configuration during provisioning.
option_rationales.C: Application security groups are a networking construct for NSG rules.
option_rationales.D: Intune compliance policies report on state rather than enforcing OS configuration.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Same currency caveat as the Automation State Configuration questions: Azure Machine Configuration is the current mechanism, and the DSC extension is legacy.

question_stem:
DRAG DROP -
You have an Azure subscription that contains the virtual networks shown in the following table.

| Name | Region | Description |
|------|--------|-------------|
| HubVNet | East US | HubVNet is a virtual network connected to the on-premises network by using a site-to-site VPN that has BGP route propagation enabled. HubVNet contains subnets named HubVNetSubnet0, AzureFirewallSubnet and GatewaySubnet. Virtual network gateway is connected to GatewaySubnet. |
| SpokeVNet | East US | SpokeVNet is a virtual network connected to HubVNet by using VNet peering. SpokeVNet contains a subnet named SpokeVNetSubnet0. |

The Azure virtual machines on SpokeVNetSubnet0 can communicate with the computers on the on-premises network.
You plan to deploy an Azure firewall to HubVNet.
You create the following two routing tables:
=> RT1: Includes a user-defined route that points to the private IP address of the Azure firewall as a next hop address
=> RT2: Disables BGP route propagation and defines the private IP address of the Azure firewall as the default gateway
You need to ensure that traffic between SpokeVNetSubnet0 and the on-premises network flows through the Azure firewall.
To which subnet should you associate each route table? To answer, drag the appropriate subnets to the correct route tables. Each subnet may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Select and Place:
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/tutorial-hybrid-portal#create-the-routes

diagrams.diagram_description: Drag-drop answer area showing available subnets (AzureFirewallSubnet, GatewaySubnet, SpokeVNetSubnet0) on the left and RT1/RT2 target slots on the right.

answer_summary: Traffic has to be forced through the firewall in both directions: the gateway subnet needs a route sending on-premises-bound-to-spoke traffic to the firewall, and the spoke subnet needs a default route to the firewall with BGP propagation disabled so the VPN routes do not bypass it.

slot_rationales.RT1: GatewaySubnet — RT1 only adds a user-defined route pointing at the firewall's private IP, which is what redirects traffic arriving from the on-premises network (through the VPN gateway) into the firewall.
slot_rationales.RT2: SpokeVNetSubnet0 — RT2 makes the firewall the default gateway and disables BGP route propagation, so the spoke's outbound traffic goes to the firewall instead of following the routes advertised by the VPN gateway.

verification.note: Matches Microsoft's hybrid-network firewall tutorial. Note that the AzureFirewallSubnet itself must not get a route table that overrides its default route to the Internet.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription. The subscription contains Azure virtual machines that run Windows Server 2016.
You need to implement a policy to ensure that each virtual machine has a custom antimalware virtual machine extension installed.
How should you complete the policy? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
Box 1: DeployIfNotExists -
DeployIfNotExists executes a template deployment when the condition is met.

Box 2: Template -
The details property of the DeployIfNotExists effects has all the subproperties that define the related resources to match and the template deployment to execute.
Deployment [required]
This property should include the full template deployment as it would be passed to the Microsoft.Resources/deployment
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/policy/concepts/effects

diagrams.diagram_description: JSON policy code snippet showing dropdown menus for 'effect' field (options: Append, Deny, DeployIfNotExists) and a nested field in 'details' section (options: existenceCondition, resources, template).

answer_summary: The policy has to install something that is missing, which is the DeployIfNotExists effect, and the ARM deployment it runs lives in the details.deployment.properties.template property.

question_stem:
You are configuring an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster that will connect to an Azure Container Registry.
You need to use the auto-generated service principal to authenticate to the Azure Container Registry.
What should you create?

options.A: an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) group
options.B: an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) role assignment
options.C: an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) user
options.D: a secret in Azure Key Vault

explanation:
When you create an AKS cluster, Azure also creates a service principal to support cluster operability with other Azure resources. You can use this auto-generated service principal for authentication with an ACR registry. To do so, you need to create an Azure AD role assignment that grants the cluster's service principal access to the container registry.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/bs-latn-ba/azure/container-registry/container-registry-auth-aks
answer_summary: Authentication is granted by giving the cluster's auto-generated service principal the AcrPull role on the registry — a role assignment, not a new user, group or stored secret.

option_rationales.A: A group adds nothing: the service principal already exists and is the identity to authorize.
option_rationales.B: A role assignment (AcrPull on the registry, for the cluster's service principal) is what allows the cluster to pull images without credentials.
option_rationales.C: A user account is not used by a cluster's non-interactive image pulls.
option_rationales.D: A Key Vault secret would mean storing registry credentials — the opposite of using the service principal's identity.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Currency: new AKS clusters use a managed identity rather than an auto-generated service principal, and the standard command is 'az aks update --attach-acr', which creates exactly this role assignment for you.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the Azure virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Operating system |
|------|------------------|
| VM1 | Windows 10 |
| VM2 | Windows Server 2016 |
| VM3 | Windows Server 2019 |
| VM4 | Ubuntu Server 18.04 LTS |

You create an MDM Security Baseline profile named Profile1.
You need to identify to which virtual machines Profile1 can be applied.
Which virtual machines should you identify?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/mem/intune/protect/security-baselines
answer_summary: MDM security baselines are an Intune feature for Windows 10/11 client devices, so only VM1 qualifies — Windows Server and Linux cannot be targeted by them.

option_rationales.A: VM1 (Windows 10) is the only supported target for an MDM Security Baseline profile.
option_rationales.B: Windows Server 2016 and 2019 are not managed by Intune MDM security baselines.
option_rationales.C: VM3 is Windows Server 2019, so it cannot be included.
option_rationales.D: Ubuntu is out of scope entirely — Linux has no MDM security baseline in Intune.

verification.note: Community 100% A. Still true: Intune security baselines target Windows 10/11 (and specific Defender/Edge baselines). Server hardening is done through Azure machine configuration, Defender for Servers or Group Policy instead.

question_stem:
SIMULATION -
You need to ensure that connections from the Internet to VNET1\subnet0 are allowed only over TCP port 7777. The solution must use only currently deployed resources.
To complete this task, sign in to the Azure portal.
explanation:
You need to configure the Network Security Group that is associated with subnet0.
1. In the Azure portal, type Virtual Networks in the search box, select Virtual Networks from the search results then select VNET1. Alternatively, browse to Virtual Networks in the left navigation pane.
2. In the properties of VNET1, click on Subnets. This will display the subnets in VNET1 and the Network Security Group associated to each subnet. Note the name of the Network Security Group associated with Subnet0.
3. Type Network Security Groups into the search box and select the Network Security Group associated with Subnet0.
4. In the properties of the Network Security Group, click on Inbound Security Rules.
5. Click the Add button to add a new rule.
6. In the Source field, select Service Tag.
7. In the Source Service Tag field, select Internet.
8. Leave the Source port ranges and Destination field as the default values (* and All).
9. In the Destination port ranges field, enter 7777.
10.Change the Protocol to TCP.
11.Leave the Action option as Allow.
12.Change the Priority to 100.
13.Change the Name from the default Port_8080 to something more descriptive such as Allow_TCP_7777_from_Internet. The name cannot contain spaces.
14.Click the Add button to save the new rule.
answer_summary: Edit the NSG already associated with subnet0: add an inbound Allow rule for TCP 7777 from Internet (or Any) at a low priority number, and make sure any broader inbound Allow rules are removed so the default DenyAllInbound covers everything else.

verification.note: Still correct; 'use only currently deployed resources' is the hint that you must reuse the existing NSG rather than deploying a firewall or Bastion.

question_stem:
SIMULATION -
You need to prevent administrators from performing accidental changes to the Homepage app service plan.
To complete this task, sign in to the Azure portal.
explanation:
You need to configure a 'lock' for the app service plan. A read-only lock ensures that no one can make changes to the app service plan without first deleting the lock.
1. In the Azure portal, type App Service Plans in the search box, select App Service Plans from the search results then select Homepage. Alternatively, browse to App Service Plans in the left navigation pane.
2. In the properties of the app service plan, click on Locks.
3. Click the Add button to add a new lock.
4. Enter a name in the Lock name field. It doesn't matter what name you provide for the exam.
5. For the Lock type, select Read-only.
6. Click OK to save the changes.
answer_summary: Add a ReadOnly lock to the Homepage app service plan (Settings → Locks → Add), which stops administrators changing or deleting it until the lock is removed.

verification.note: Correct: 'accidental changes' means ReadOnly, whereas CanNotDelete would still allow modification. Note that a ReadOnly lock on an App Service plan can block operations that write to it, including some scaling and app changes.

question_stem:
SIMULATION -
You need to ensure that a user named Danny1234578 can sign in to any SQL database on a Microsoft SQL server named web1234578 by using SQL Server
Management Studio (SSMS) and Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) credentials.
To complete this task, sign in to the Azure portal.
explanation:
You need to provision an Azure AD Admin for the SQL Server.
1. In the Azure portal, type SQL Server in the search box, select SQL Server from the search results then select the server named web1234578. Alternatively, browse to SQL Server in the left navigation pane.
2. In the SQL Server properties page, click on Active Directory Admin.
3. Click the Set Admin button.
4. In the Add Admin window, search for and select Danny1234578.
5. Click the Select button to add Danny1234578.
6. Click the Save button to save the changes.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/authentication-aad-configure?tabs=azure-powershell
answer_summary: Set Danny1234578 as the Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) admin for the logical server web1234578 — the server's Entra admin can sign in to every database on that server with Entra credentials from SSMS.

verification.note: Still the right lever for 'any database on the server'. In current practice you would then create contained database users FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER for everyday users rather than making them server admins, and the blade is now 'Microsoft Entra ID' admin.

question_stem:
SIMULATION -
You need to configure a Microsoft SQL server named Web1234578 only to accept connections from the Subnet0 subnet on the VNET01 virtual network.
To complete this task, sign in to the Azure portal.
explanation:
You need to allow access to Azure services and configure a virtual network rule for the SQL Server.
1. In the Azure portal, type SQL Server in the search box, select SQL Server from the search results then select the server named web1234578. Alternatively, browse to SQL Server in the left navigation pane.
2. In the properties of the SQL Server, click Firewalls and virtual networks.
3. In the Virtual networks section, click on Add existing. This will open the Create/Update virtual network rule window.
4. Give the rule a name such as Allow_VNET01-Subnet0 (it doesn't matter what name you enter for the exam).
5. In the Virtual network box, select VNET01.
6. In the Subnet name box, select Subnet0.
7. Click the OK button to save the rule.
8. Back in the Firewall / Virtual Networks window, set the Allow access to Azure services option to On.
answer_summary: On the server's networking/firewall settings, add a virtual network rule for VNET01\Subnet0 (which enables the Microsoft.Sql service endpoint on that subnet) and remove any IP firewall rules and the 'Allow Azure services' exception so nothing else can connect.

verification.note: Still valid. A private endpoint plus 'Public network access: Disabled' is the stronger modern equivalent.

question_stem:
You have Azure Resource Manager templates that you use to deploy Azure virtual machines.
You need to disable unused Windows features automatically as instances of the virtual machines are provisioned.
What should you use?

options.A: device configuration policies in Microsoft Intune
options.B: an Azure Desired State Configuration (DSC) virtual machine extension
options.C: security policies in Azure Security Center

explanation:
The primary use case for the Azure Desired State Configuration (DSC) extension is to bootstrap a VM to the Azure Automation State Configuration (DSC) service.
The service provides benefits that include ongoing management of the VM configuration and integration with other operational tools, such as Azure Monitoring.
Using the extension to register VM's to the service provides a flexible solution that even works across Azure subscriptions.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/extensions/dsc-overview
answer_summary: The Azure DSC virtual machine extension applies the desired-state configuration as each VM is provisioned, which is how unused Windows features get disabled automatically.

option_rationales.A: Intune device configuration policies apply to MDM-enrolled devices, not template-deployed Azure VMs.
option_rationales.B: The DSC extension runs at provisioning time inside the VM and can disable Windows features.
option_rationales.C: Security Center policies assess configuration; they do not apply it.
option_rationales.D: Logic Apps orchestrate workflows and have no in-guest configuration capability.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Third near-duplicate of this item in the bank; the modern approach is Azure Machine Configuration.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription that contains the virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Resource group | Status |
|------|----------------|--------|
| VM1 | RG1 | Stopped (Deallocated) |
| VM2 | RG2 | Stopped (Deallocated) |

You create the Azure policies shown in the following table.

| Policy definition | Resource type | Scope |
|-------------------|---------------|-------|
| Not allowed resource types | virtualMachines | RG1 |
| Allowed resource types | virtualMachines | RG2 |

You create the resource locks shown in the following table.

| Name | Type | Created on |
|------|------|------------|
| Lock1 | Read-only | VM1 |
| Lock2 | Read-only | RG2 |

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: You can start VM1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Starting a VM is a write-class operation (Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/start/action), which the ReadOnly lock on VM1 prevents — Microsoft documents this specific example.

hotspot_rows.statement: You can start VM2.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Lock2 is a ReadOnly lock on RG2 and locks are inherited by the resources inside, so VM2 cannot be started either.

hotspot_rows.statement: You can create a virtual machine in RG2.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Creating a virtual machine in RG2 is a write operation in the locked scope, so the ReadOnly lock blocks it regardless of the 'Allowed resource types' policy permitting virtualMachines.

explanation: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/blueprints/concepts/resource-locking
answer_summary: A ReadOnly lock blocks every write operation in its scope, and it is inherited by child resources. Lock1 stops VM1 starting, and Lock2 on RG2 stops both starting VM2 and creating anything new in RG2.

verification.note: Rows 2 and 3 changed from Yes to No. A ReadOnly lock applies to all write operations within its scope and is inherited by child resources; the equivalent question in Topic 1 (Q21) is keyed consistently with this correction.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com. The tenant contains the users shown in the following table.

| Name | Subscription role | Azure AD user role |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| User1 | Owner | None |
| User2 | Contributor | None |
| User3 | Security Admin | None |
| User4 | None | Service administrator |

You create a resource group named RG1.
Which users can modify the permissions for RG1 and which users can create virtual networks in RG1? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
Box 1: Only an owner can change permissions on resources.
Box 2: A Contributor can create/modify/delete anything in the subscription but cannot change permissions.
answer_summary: Changing permissions needs Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, which only Owner has here; creating virtual networks needs resource write, which both Owner and Contributor have — Contributor is specifically barred from granting access.

slot_rationales.Users who can modify the permissions for: User1 (Owner) only. Contributor explicitly excludes role-assignment writes, and a Security Admin cannot delegate access either.
slot_rationales.Users who can create virtual networks in: User1 and User2 — Owner and Contributor both have full resource write in the subscription, inherited by RG1.

verification.note: Kept as stored, with one caveat: the table lists User4 as 'Service administrator', and the classic Service Administrator had Owner-equivalent access to everything in the subscription, which would have let that user modify permissions too. The point is moot on current Azure — classic subscription administrators (Service Administrator and Co-Administrator) were retired on 31 August 2024.

question_stem:
SIMULATION -
You need to configure network connectivity between a virtual network named VNET1 and a virtual network named VNET2. The solution must ensure that virtual machines connected to VNET1 can communicate with virtual machines connected to VNET2.
To complete this task, sign in to the Azure portal and modify the Azure resources.
explanation:
You need to configure VNet Peering between the two networks. The questions states, xThe solution must ensure that virtual machines connected to VNET1 can communicate with virtual machines connected to VNET2x£ It doesn't say the VMs on VNET2 should be able to communicate with VMs on VNET1. Therefore, we need to configure the peering to allow just the one-way communication.
1. In the Azure portal, type Virtual Networks in the search box, select Virtual Networks from the search results then select VNET1. Alternatively, browse to
Virtual Networks in the left navigation pane.
2. In the properties of VNET1, click on Peerings.
3. In the Peerings blade, click Add to add a new peering.
4. In the Name of the peering from VNET1 to remote virtual network box, enter a name such as VNET1-VNET2 (this is the name that the peering will be displayed as in VNET1)
5. In the Virtual Network box, select VNET2.
6. In the Name of the peering from remote virtual network to VNET1 box, enter a name such as VNET2-VNET1 (this is the name that the peering will be displayed as in VNET2).
There is an option Allow virtual network access from VNET to remote virtual network. This should be left as Enabled.
7. For the option Allow virtual network access from remote network to VNET1, click the slider button to Disabled.
8. Click the OK button to save the changes.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-manage-peering
answer_summary: Create VNet peering between VNET1 and VNET2 (Virtual network → Peerings → Add), leaving 'Allow traffic to remote virtual network' enabled on both links — the portal creates the link in each direction for you, and both links must exist before traffic flows.

verification.note: One correction to the stored explanation: peering is not one-directional in effect. A peering link created on only one side stays in the Initiated state and carries no traffic — the reciprocal link must exist (the portal adds it automatically) before VMs on VNET1 can reach VNET2.

question_stem:
SIMULATION -
You need to deploy an Azure firewall to a virtual network named VNET3.
To complete this task, sign in to the Azure portal and modify the Azure resources.
This task might take several minutes to complete. You can perform other tasks while the task completes.
explanation:
To add an Azure firewall to a VNET, the VNET must first be configured with a subnet named AzureFirewallSubnet (if it doesn't already exist).
Configure VNET3.
1. In the Azure portal, type Virtual Networks in the search box, select Virtual Networks from the search results then select VNET3. Alternatively, browse to
Virtual Networks in the left navigation pane.
2. In the Overview section, note the Location (region) and Resource Group of the virtual network. We'll need these when we add the firewall.
3. Click on Subnets.
4. Click on + Subnet to add a new subnet.
5. Enter AzureFirewallSubnet in the Name box. The subnet must be named AzureFirewallSubnet.
6. Enter an appropriate IP range for the subnet in the Address range box.
7. Click the OK button to create the subnet.
Add the Azure Firewall.
1. In the settings of VNET3 click on Firewall.
2. Click the Click here to add a new firewall link.
3. The Resource group will default to the VNET3 resource group. Leave this default.
4. Enter a name for the firewall in the Name box.
5. In the Region box, select the same region as VNET3.
6. In the Public IP address box, select an available public IP address if one exists, or click Add new to add a new public IP address.
7. Click the Review + create button.
8. Review the settings and click the Create button to create the firewall.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/tutorial-firewall-deploy-portal
answer_summary: Azure Firewall can only be deployed into a subnet named AzureFirewallSubnet, so add that subnet (at least /26) to VNET3 first, then create the firewall in VNET3 with a public IP.

verification.note: Still required: the subnet name must be exactly AzureFirewallSubnet and /26 or larger. A second subnet named AzureFirewallManagementSubnet is needed only for forced-tunnelling deployments.

question_stem:
SIMULATION -
You need to configure a virtual network named VNET2 to meet the following requirements:
=> Administrators must be prevented from deleting VNET2 accidentally.
=> Administrators must be able to add subnets to VNET2 regularly.
To complete this task, sign in to the Azure portal and modify the Azure resources.
explanation:
Locking prevents other users in your organization from accidentally deleting or modifying critical resources, such as Azure subscription, resource group, or resource.
Note: In Azure, the term resource refers to an entity managed by Azure. For example, virtual machines, virtual networks, and storage accounts are all referred to as Azure resources.
1. In the Azure portal, type Virtual Networks in the search box, select Virtual Networks from the search results then select VNET2. Alternatively, browse to
Virtual Networks in the left navigation pane.
2. In the Settings blade for virtual network VNET2, select Locks.
3. To add a lock, select Add.
4. For Lock type select Delete lock, and click OK
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/resource-group-lock-resources

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure Portal screenshot showing the Settings blade for VNET2 with navigation menu including Tags, Locks (highlighted with red box), Users, and Automation script options, plus a Management locks interface showing Add, Resource group, Subscription, and Refresh buttons.

answer_summary: Add a CanNotDelete (Delete) lock to VNET2 — it blocks deletion while still allowing administrators to modify the network, such as adding subnets. A ReadOnly lock would block the subnet additions too.

verification.note: Correct: the two requirements together rule out ReadOnly. Locks are inherited by child resources, so the lock also protects the subnets from deletion.

question_stem:
You have an Azure virtual machine named VM1.
From Microsoft Defender for Cloud, you get the following high-severity recommendation: `Install endpoint protection solutions on virtual machine`.
You need to resolve the issue causing the high-severity recommendation.
What should you do?

options.A: Add the Microsoft Antimalware extension to VM1.
options.B: Install Microsoft System Center Security Management Pack for Endpoint Protection on VM1.
options.C: Add the Network Watcher Agent for Windows extension to VM1.
options.D: Onboard VM1 to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.

explanation: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security-center/security-center-endpoint-protection
answer_summary: The 'Install endpoint protection solutions' recommendation is satisfied by deploying an endpoint protection agent to the VM, and on Azure the direct fix is the Microsoft Antimalware extension.

option_rationales.A: Adding the Microsoft Antimalware (IaaSAntimalware) extension installs a supported endpoint protection solution, which clears the recommendation.
option_rationales.B: The System Center Security Management Pack is a monitoring pack for SCOM, not an endpoint protection agent.
option_rationales.C: The Network Watcher agent supports network diagnostics such as connection monitor — nothing to do with antimalware.
option_rationales.D: Onboarding to Defender for Endpoint is the modern answer (see the note) but is not what this exam item treats as the fix for this recommendation.

verification.note: Kept as A (community 67%), but 33% vote D with good reason: in current Defender for Cloud, endpoint protection is delivered by the integrated Microsoft Defender for Endpoint sensor that Defender for Servers deploys automatically, and Windows Server 2016+ already includes Defender Antivirus. Treat the Antimalware extension as the legacy answer.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have a file named File1.yaml that contains the following contents.
apiVersion: 2018-10-01
location: eastus
name: containergroup1
properties:
  containers:
    - name: container1
      properties:
        environmentVariables:
          - name: 'Variable1'
            value: 'Value1'
          - name: 'Variable2'
            secureValue: 'Value2'
        image: nginx
        ports: []
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 1.0
            memoryInGB: 1.5
        osType: Linux
        restartPolicy: Always
  tags: null
  type: Microsoft.ContainerInstance/containerGroups

You create an Azure container instance named container1 by using File1.yaml.
You need to identify where you can access the values of Variable1 and Variable2.
What should you identify? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

dragdrop_slots.Variable1: Can be accessed from inside container1 and the Azure portal
dragdrop_slots.Variable2: Can be accessed from inside container1 only

explanation: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-instances/container-instances-environment-variables
answer_summary: A plain environment variable is stored in the container group's properties and is therefore visible in the portal and CLI as well as inside the container; a secureValue is write-only — it is delivered to the container but never returned by the management plane.

slot_rationales.Variable1: Declared with 'value', so it is part of the container group's readable properties: visible from inside container1 and in the Azure portal.
slot_rationales.Variable2: Declared with 'secureValue', so Azure will not display it in the portal, CLI output or API responses — only the process inside the container can read it.

verification.note: Still accurate. For genuinely sensitive material, mounting a secret volume or referencing Key Vault is preferred over secureValue.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains a virtual network. The virtual network contains the subnets shown in the following table.

| Name | Has a network security group (NSG) associated to the virtual subnet |
|------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Subnet1 | Yes |
| Subnet2 | No |

The subscription contains the virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Has an NSG associated to the network adaptor of the virtual machine | Connected to |
|------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------|
| VM1 | No | Subnet1 |
| VM2 | No | Subnet2 |
| VM3 | No | Subnet1 |
| VM4 | Yes | Subnet2 |

You enable just in time (JIT) VM access for all the virtual machines.
You need to identify which virtual machines are protected by JIT.
Which virtual machines should you identify?
explanation:
An NSG needs to be enabled, either at the VM level or the subnet level.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security-center/security-center-just-in-time
answer_summary: Just-in-time access works by editing NSG (and Azure Firewall) rules, so a VM is only protected if it has an NSG attached to its NIC or to its subnet. VM2 has neither.

option_rationales.A: VM4 qualifies via its NIC-level NSG, but it is not the only one.
option_rationales.B: VM1 and VM3 qualify via Subnet1's NSG, but VM4 also qualifies.
option_rationales.C: VM1 and VM3 are covered by the subnet NSG and VM4 by its NIC NSG; VM2 has no NSG at either level, so JIT has nothing to lock down.
option_rationales.D: VM2 cannot be protected until an NSG is associated with its NIC or with Subnet2.

verification.note: Community 100% C. Still true, and JIT now also programs Azure Firewall rules where the VM sits behind one; it requires Defender for Servers Plan 2.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription that contains the virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Connected to | Private IP address | Public IP address |
|------|--------------|--------------------|-----------------|
| VM1 | VNET1/Subnet1 | 10.1.1.4 | 13.80.73.87 |
| VM2 | VNET2/Subnet2 | 10.2.1.4 | 213.199.133.190 |
| VM3 | VNET2/Subnet2 | 10.2.1.5 | None |

Subnet1 and Subnet2 have a Microsoft.Storage service endpoint configured.
You have an Azure Storage account named storageacc1 that is configured as shown in the following exhibit.
Allow access from
© All networks © Selected networks

Configure network security for your storage accounts. Learn more.

Virtual networks
Secure your storage account with virtual networks. + Add existing virtual network
+ Add new virtual network

VIRTUAL NETWORK    SUBNET    ADDRESS RANGE    ENDPOINT STATUS    RESOURCE GROUP    SUBSCRIPTION

No network selected.

13.80.73.87
IP address or CIDR

Exceptions
