☐ Allow read access to storage metrics from any network

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: From VM1, you can upload a blob to storageacc1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Subnet1 has a Microsoft.Storage service endpoint, so VM1's requests reach the account over that endpoint from the subnet's private IP — Microsoft documents that IP network rules do not apply to such traffic. With no virtual network rule for Subnet1, the request is denied despite VM1's public IP being listed.

hotspot_rows.statement: From VM2, you can upload a blob to storageacc1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: The virtual network list is empty, so Subnet2's service endpoint grants nothing, and VM2's public IP 213.199.133.190 is not in the firewall list — the request is denied.

hotspot_rows.statement: From VM3 , you can upload a blob to storageacc1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: VM3 has no public IP and no virtual network rule covers Subnet2, so it has no allowed path to the account.

explanation:
Box 1: Yes -
The public IP of VM1 is allowed through the firewall.

Box 2: No -
The allowed virtual network list is empty so VM2 cannot access storageacc1 directly. The public IP address of VM2 is not in the allowed IP list so VM2 cannot access storageacc1 over the Internet.

Box 3: No -
The allowed virtual network list is empty so VM3 cannot access storageacc1 directly. VM3 does not have a public IP address so it cannot access storageacc1 over the Internet.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/storage/common/storage-network-security

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure Portal screenshot of Storage Account firewall configuration showing 'Selected networks' option enabled, with an empty Virtual Networks list and a Firewall section containing IP address 13.80.73.87, plus 'Allow trusted Microsoft services' checkbox enabled.

answer_summary: The account allows only selected networks and has no virtual network rules at all — so the Microsoft.Storage service endpoints on Subnet1 and Subnet2 grant nothing, and every request is denied. Once a subnet has a storage service endpoint, its traffic arrives from a private address, so the firewall's IP rule for 13.80.73.87 never matches either.

verification.note: Row 1 changed from Yes to No. Enabling a Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on the subnet switches that traffic to the private path, and Microsoft's storage firewall documentation states IP network rules do not apply to it — a virtual network rule for the subnet is then mandatory. The same bank keys the equivalent situation as No in Topic 3 Q153, so this also removes an internal inconsistency.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have Azure virtual machines that have Update Management enabled. The virtual machines are configured as shown in the following table.

| Name | Operating system | Region | Resource group |
|------|------------------|--------|----------------|
| VM1 | Windows Server 2012 | East US | RG1 |
| VM2 | Windows Server 2012 R2 | West US | RG1 |
| VM3 | Windows Server 2016 | West US | RG2 |
| VM4 | Ubuntu Server 18.04 LTS | West US | RG2 |
| VM5 | Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7.4 | East US | RG1 |
| VM6 | CentOS 7.5 | East US | RG1 |

You schedule two update deployments named Update1 and Update2. Update1 updates VM3. Update2 updates VM6.
Which additional virtual machines can be updated by using Update1 and Update2? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
An update deployment can apply to Windows VMs or Linux VMs but not both. The VMs can be in different regions, different subscriptions and different resource groups.

Update1: VM1 and VM2 only -
VM3: Windows Server 2016.

Update2: VM4 and VM5 only -
VM6: CentOS 7.5.
For Linux, the machine must have access to an update repository. The update repository can be private or public.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/automation/update-management/overview
answer_summary: An update deployment targets one OS family only, but region, subscription and resource group are irrelevant. Update1 is a Windows deployment (VM3), so it can add the other Windows machines; Update2 is a Linux deployment (VM6), so it can add the other Linux machines.

slot_rationales.Update1: VM1 and VM2 only — the other Windows Server machines. VM4, VM5 and VM6 are Linux and cannot be mixed into a Windows deployment.
slot_rationales.Update2: VM4 and VM5 only — the remaining Linux machines (Ubuntu and RHEL); the Windows VMs cannot join a Linux deployment.

verification.note: The one-OS-family-per-deployment rule still applies, but the product has changed: Azure Automation Update Management retired in 2024 and this work is now done with Azure Update Manager (maintenance configurations), which also separates Windows and Linux schedules.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1.
You create a virtual network that contains one subnet. On the subnet, you provision the virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Network interface | Application security group assignment | IP address |
|------|-------------------|--------------------------------------|------------|
| VM1 | NIC1 | AppGroup12 | 10.0.0.10 |
| VM2 | NIC2 | AppGroup12 | 10.0.0.11 |
| VM3 | NIC3 | AppGroup3 | 10.0.0.100 |
| VM4 | NIC4 | AppGroup4 | 10.0.0.200 |

Currently, you have not provisioned any network security groups (NSGs).
You need to implement network security to meet the following requirements:
=> Allow traffic to VM4 from VM3 only.
=> Allow traffic from the Internet to VM1 and VM2 only.
=> Minimize the number of NSGs and network security rules.
How many NSGs and network security rules should you create? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
NSGs: 2 -

Network security rules: 3 -

Not 2: You cannot specify multiple service tags or application groups) in a security rule.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/security-overview
answer_summary: Application security groups let one NSG on the subnet express all the requirements: allow Internet to AppGroup12, allow AppGroup3 to AppGroup4, then deny everything else to AppGroup4 (needed because the default AllowVnetInBound rule would otherwise let VM1/VM2 reach VM4).

slot_rationales.NSGs: One NSG associated with the subnet is enough — ASGs are used as the source and destination inside its rules, so there is no need for per-NIC NSGs.
slot_rationales.Network security rules: Three: (1) Allow Internet → AppGroup12, (2) Allow AppGroup3 → AppGroup4, (3) Deny Any → AppGroup4. The default DenyAllInbound already blocks Internet traffic to VM3/VM4, but the default AllowVnetInBound must be overridden for VM4.

verification.note: NSG count changed to 1. This item was internally inconsistent in the source bank — the stored answer said 3 while its own explanation said 2. With all four VMs in a single subnet and ASG-based rules, one subnet-level NSG plus the three rules above satisfies every requirement, which is also what 'minimize the number of NSGs' asks for. A rule still cannot list multiple ASGs as its source or destination, which is why three separate rules are needed.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure key vault.
You need to delegate administrative access to the key vault to meet the following requirements:
=> Provide a user named User1 with the ability to set advanced access policies for the key vault.
=> Provide a user named User2 with the ability to add and delete certificates in the key vault.
=> Use the principle of least privilege.
What should you use to assign access to each user? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
User1: RBAC -
RBAC is used as the Key Vault access control mechanism for the management plane. It would allow a user with the proper identity to:
=> set Key Vault access policies
=> create, read, update, and delete key vaults
=> set Key Vault tags
Note: Role-based access control (RBAC) is a system that provides fine-grained access management of Azure resources. Using RBAC, you can segregate duties within your team and grant only the amount of access to users that they need to perform their jobs.

User2: A Key vault access policy
A key vault access policy is the access control mechanism to get access to the key vault data plane. Key Vault access policies grant permissions separately to keys, secrets, and certificates.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/key-vault-secure-your-key-vault
answer_summary: Two different planes: setting advanced access policies is a management-plane operation on the vault resource (Azure RBAC), while adding and deleting certificates is a data-plane operation granted by a key vault access policy.

slot_rationales.User1: RBAC — advanced access policies are properties of the vault resource, so User1 needs a management-plane role (for example Key Vault Contributor scoped to the vault).
slot_rationales.User2: A key vault access policy — grant only the certificate permissions needed to create/import and delete certificates, with no key or secret permissions.

verification.note: Correct as written. Microsoft now recommends the Azure RBAC permission model for the data plane too, where User2's equivalent is the Key Vault Certificates Officer role.

question_stem:
You have Azure Resource Manager templates that you use to deploy Azure virtual machines.
You need to disable unused Windows features automatically as instances of the virtual machines are provisioned.
What should you use?

options.A: device compliance policies in Microsoft Intune

explanation: You can use Azure Automation State Configuration to manage Azure VMs (both Classic and Resource Manager), on-premises VMs, Linux machines, AWS VMs, and on-premises physical machines. Note: Azure Automation State Configuration provides a DSC pull server similar to the Windows Feature DSC Service so that target nodes automatically receive configurations, conform to the desired state, and report back on their compliance. The built-in pull server in Azure Automation eliminates the need to set up and maintain your own pull server. Azure Automation can target virtual or physical Windows or Linux machines, in the cloud or on- premises.
answer_summary: Disabling unused Windows features as VMs are provisioned is desired-state configuration, delivered by Azure Automation State Configuration (DSC).

option_rationales.A: Intune compliance policies only report device state; they enforce nothing in-guest.
option_rationales.B: Azure Automation State Configuration applies and continuously enforces the DSC configuration that disables the features.
option_rationales.C: Application security groups are a networking construct.
option_rationales.D: Azure Advisor makes recommendations; it changes no configuration.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Azure Automation State Configuration is slated for retirement (30 September 2027); Azure Machine Configuration is the successor.

question_stem:
You have an Azure Container Registry named Registry1.
From Azure Security Center, you enable Azure Container Registry vulnerability scanning of the images in Registry1.
You perform the following actions:
=> Push a Windows image named Image1 to Registry1.
=> Push a Linux image named Image2 to Registry1.
=> Push a Windows image named Image3 to Registry1.
=> Modify Image1 and push the new image as Image4 to Registry1.
Modify Image2 and push the new image as Image5 to Registry1.
•
Which two images will be scanned for vulnerabilities? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
explanation:
Only Linux images are scanned. Windows images are not scanned.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security-center/azure-container-registry-integration
answer_summary: The registry scanner in this generation of Security Center only assessed Linux images, so of the five pushes only the Linux ones — Image2 and its modified copy Image5 — were scanned.

option_rationales.A: Image4 is derived from the Windows Image1, so it is still a Windows image and not scanned.
option_rationales.B: Image2 is a Linux image that was pushed after scanning was enabled, so it is scanned.
option_rationales.C: Image1 is Windows.
option_rationales.D: Image3 is Windows.
option_rationales.E: Image5 is the modified Linux image, and each new push triggers a fresh scan.

verification.note: Community 100% BE for the exam as written. Currency: registry scanning has moved to Microsoft Defender for Containers with Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management, which now covers Windows images as well as Linux — so the Linux-only limitation is historical.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have two Azure virtual machines in the East US 2 region as shown in the following table.

| Name | Operating system | Type | Tier |
|------|------------------|------|------|
| VM1 | Windows Server 2008 R2 | A3 | Basic |
| VM2 | Ubuntu 16.04-DAILY-LTS | L4s | Standard |

You deploy and configure an Azure Key vault.
You need to ensure that you can enable Azure Disk Encryption on VM1 and VM2.
What should you modify on each virtual machine? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
VM1: The Tier -
The Tier needs to be upgraded to standard.
Disk Encryption for Windows and Linux IaaS VMs is in General Availability in all Azure public regions and Azure Government regions for Standard VMs and VMs with Azure Premium Storage.

VM2: The type -
Need to change the VMtype to any of A, D, DS, G, GS, F, and so on, series IaaS VMs.
Not the operating system version: Ubuntu 16.04 is supported.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/azure-security-disk-encryption-overview https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/azure-security-disk-encryption-faq#bkmk_LinuxOSSupport
answer_summary: Azure Disk Encryption has two blockers here: VM1 is on the Basic tier (unsupported, so the tier must change) and VM2 is an L-series size (an unsupported VM type, so the size must change).

slot_rationales.VM1: The tier — Basic tier VMs cannot use Azure Disk Encryption; it must be upgraded to Standard.
slot_rationales.VM2: The type — the Ls-series (L4s) size is not supported for Azure Disk Encryption, so the VM must be resized to a supported family.

verification.note: Both restrictions still hold for ADE. Note that Windows Server 2008 R2 (VM1) is also out of support today, and encryption at host or confidential-disk encryption is now often preferred over ADE.

question_stem:
You have the Azure virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Operating system | Region | Resource group |
|------|------------------|--------|----------------|
| VM1 | Windows Server 2012 | East US | RG1 |
| VM2 | Windows Server 2012 R2 | West Europe | RG1 |
| VM3 | Windows Server 2016 | West Europe | RG2 |
| VM4 | Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7.4 | East US | RG2 |

You create an Azure Log Analytics workspace named Analytics1 in RG1 in the East US region.
Which virtual machines can be enrolled in Analytics1?
explanation:
Note: Create a workspace -
=> In the Azure portal, click All services. In the list of resources, type Log Analytics. As you begin typing, the list filters based on your input. Select Log Analytics.
Click Create, and then select choices for the following items:
•
Provide a name for the new Log Analytics workspace, such as DefaultLAWorkspace. OMS workspaces are now referred to as Log Analytics workspaces.
Select a Subscription to link to by selecting from the drop-down list if the default selected is not appropriate.
For Resource Group, select an existing resource group that contains one or more Azure virtual machines.
•
Select the Location your VMs are deployed to. For additional information, see which regions Log Analytics is available in.
•
Select a Subscription in the drop-down list if the default selected is not appropriate.
Select the Location the VMs are deployed to. For additional information, see which regions Log Analytics is available in.
If you are creating a workspace in a new subscription created after April 2, 2018, it will automatically use the Per GB pricing plan and the option to select a pricing tier will not be available.
Incorrect Answers:
B, C: A Log Analytics workspace provides a geographic location for data storage. VM2 and VM3 are at a different location.
D: VM4 is a different resource group.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/platform/manage-access
answer_summary: A Log Analytics workspace has no region or resource-group affinity for the machines that report to it — any of the four VMs, Windows or Linux, in any region, can be connected to Analytics1.

option_rationales.A: Nothing restricts enrollment to VMs in the workspace's own region and resource group.
option_rationales.B: The Linux VM is equally eligible — the agent supports supported Linux distributions.
option_rationales.C: All four VMs can report to Analytics1 regardless of region, resource group or operating system.
option_rationales.D: There is no reason to exclude VM2 and VM3.

verification.note: Answer changed from A to C (community 100% C). Cross-region and cross-subscription reporting to a workspace has always been supported; you pay egress in some cases, but there is no eligibility restriction. With the Azure Monitor Agent the association is made by a data collection rule, which must be in the same region as the workspace — the machines still need not be.

question_stem:
You are testing an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster. The cluster is configured as shown in the exhibit. (Click the Exhibit tab.)
Basics

Subscription                  Azure Pass - Sponsorship
Resource group                RG1
Region                        (US) East US
Kubernetes cluster name       AKScluster
Kubernetes version            1.12.8
DNS name prefix               AKScluster
Node count                    3
Node size                     Standard_DS2_v2

Scale

Virtual nodes                 Disabled
VM scale sets (preview)       Disabled

Authentication

Enable RBAC                   No

Networking

HTTP application routing      No
Network configuration         Basic

Monitoring

Enable container monitoring   No

Tags

(none)

You plan to deploy the cluster to production. You disable HTTP application routing.
You need to implement application routing that will provide reverse proxy and TLS termination for AKS services by using a single IP address.
What should you do?

options.B: Install the container network interface (CNI) plug-in.
options.C: Create an Azure Standard Load Balancer.
options.D: Create an Azure Basic Load Balancer.

explanation:
An ingress controller is a piece of software that provides reverse proxy, configurable traffic routing, and TLS termination for Kubernetes services.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/aks/ingress-tls

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure Portal screenshot of AKS cluster configuration showing settings including Subscription (Azure Pass - Sponsorship), Resource group (RG1), Region (US East US), Kubernetes cluster name (AKScluster), version 1.12.8, 3 nodes with Standard_DS2_v2 size, RBAC disabled, HTTP application routing disabled, and Basic network configuration.

answer_summary: Replacing HTTP application routing with reverse proxy, hostname/path routing and TLS termination behind a single IP is exactly what an ingress controller does.

option_rationales.A: An AKS ingress controller (NGINX, AGIC or the managed app-routing add-on) provides the reverse proxy and TLS termination required.
option_rationales.B: The CNI plug-in is about IP addressing for pods, not HTTP routing.
option_rationales.C: A Standard Load Balancer works at layer 4 — it cannot terminate TLS or route by host/path.
option_rationales.D: A Basic Load Balancer has the same layer-4 limitation, and the Basic SKU is now retired.

verification.note: Community 100% A. Note the cluster in the exhibit also has RBAC disabled, which would itself be unacceptable for production on any current AKS version (Kubernetes RBAC is always on now).

question_stem:
Note: This question is part of a series of questions that present the same scenario. Each question in the series contains a unique solution that might meet the stated goals. Some question sets might have more than one correct solution, while others might not have a correct solution.
After you answer a question in this section, you will NOT be able to return to it. As a result, these questions will not appear in the review screen.
You have an Azure subscription. The subscription contains 50 virtual machines that run Windows Server 2012 R2 or Windows Server 2016.
You need to deploy Microsoft Antimalware to the virtual machines.
Solution: You add an extension to each virtual machine.
Does this meet the goal?
explanation:
You can use Visual Studio to enable and configure the Microsoft Antimalware service. This entails selecting Microsoft Antimalware extension from the dropdown list under Installed Extensions and click Add to configure with default antimalware configuration.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/fundamentals/antimalware
answer_summary: Microsoft Antimalware for Azure VMs is delivered as a VM extension, so adding the extension to each machine is exactly the supported deployment method.

option_rationales.A: The IaaSAntimalware extension is the documented way to deploy Microsoft Antimalware, whether from the portal, a template, PowerShell or a policy.
option_rationales.B: This is the solution in the series that does meet the goal.

verification.note: Community 100% A. At scale you would use a DeployIfNotExists policy so new VMs get the extension automatically — and on Windows Server 2016+ Defender Antivirus is already built in.

question_stem:
Note: This question is part of a series of questions that present the same scenario. Each question in the series contains a unique solution that might meet the stated goals. Some question sets might have more than one correct solution, while others might not have a correct solution.
After you answer a question in this section, you will NOT be able to return to it. As a result, these questions will not appear in the review screen.
You have an Azure subscription. The subscription contains 50 virtual machines that run Windows Server 2012 R2 or Windows Server 2016.
You need to deploy Microsoft Antimalware to the virtual machines.
Solution: You connect to each virtual machine and add a Windows feature.
Does this meet the goal?
explanation:
Microsoft Antimalware is deployed as an extension and not a feature.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/fundamentals/antimalware
answer_summary: Microsoft Antimalware for Azure is an extension, not an in-box Windows feature, so adding a Windows feature on each VM does not deploy it.

option_rationales.A: There is no Windows feature that installs the Azure Microsoft Antimalware solution.
option_rationales.B: Deployment is via the antimalware VM extension. (Windows Server 2016 and later do include Microsoft Defender Antivirus as a feature, but that is a different product from the Azure extension this scenario asks for.)

verification.note: Community 100% B.

question_stem:
You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named Contoso.com and an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster AKS1.
You discover that AKS1 cannot be accessed by using accounts from Contoso.com.
You need to ensure AKS1 can be accessed by using accounts from Contoso.com. The solution must minimize administrative effort.
What should you do first?

options.B: From AKS1, upgrade the version of Kubernetes.
options.C: From Azure AD, implement Azure AD Premium P2
options.D: From Azure AD, configure the User settings.

explanation: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/aks/azure-ad-integration-cli
answer_summary: With the legacy Azure AD integration, directory authentication could only be turned on while the cluster was being created — so an existing cluster that cannot accept tenant accounts has to be recreated.

option_rationales.A: Recreating AKS1 with Azure AD integration enabled was the only supported way to add it to a cluster that was built without it.
option_rationales.B: A Kubernetes version upgrade changes the cluster's API version, not its identity provider.
option_rationales.C: Entra ID P2 is not required for AKS directory integration; licensing is not the blocker.
option_rationales.D: Tenant User settings control things like app registration and guest permissions, not cluster authentication.

verification.note: Community 100% A for the legacy integration. Currency: with AKS-managed Microsoft Entra integration you can now enable it on an existing cluster ('az aks update --enable-aad'), so recreating is no longer necessary — treat this item as historical.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure Container Registry named Registry1. Microsoft Defender for Cloud is enabled in the subscription.
You upload several container images to Registry1.
You discover that vulnerability security scans were not performed.
You need to ensure that the container images are scanned for vulnerabilities when they are uploaded to Registry1.
What should you do?

options.A: From the Azure portal, modify the Pricing tier settings.
options.B: From Azure CLI, lock the container images.
options.C: Upload the container images by using AzCopy.
options.D: Push the container images to Registry1 by using Docker.

explanation: https://charbelnemnom.com/scan-container-images-in-azure-container-registry-with-azure-security-center/
answer_summary: Registry vulnerability scanning is a paid Defender plan feature, so it only starts once the relevant Defender plan is turned on in the pricing/plan settings — and it then scans images on push.

option_rationales.A: Enabling the Defender plan for container registries in the pricing tier settings is what activates scanning on push.
option_rationales.B: Locking images prevents changes; it triggers no scanning.
option_rationales.C: AzCopy moves blobs and files — it cannot push container images at all.
option_rationales.D: Pushing with Docker is already how the images arrived; the push is not the missing piece.

verification.note: Community 100% A. Currency: the plan is now Microsoft Defender for Containers, and assessment is performed by Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management (which also rescans images already in the registry, not only on push).

question_stem:
From Azure Security Center, you create a custom alert rule.
You need to configure which users will receive an email message when the alert is triggered.
What should you do?

options.A: From Azure Monitor, create an action group.
options.B: From Security Center, modify the Security policy settings of the Azure subscription.
options.C: From Azure Active Directory (Azure AD), modify the members of the Security Reader role group.
options.D: From Security Center, modify the alert rule.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/platform/action-groups
answer_summary: Who gets notified is defined by an Azure Monitor action group — the alert rule references the action group, which holds the email recipients (and any webhooks, SMS or ITSM actions).

option_rationales.A: An action group holds the notification targets and is what the alert rule fires; adding email recipients there is the answer.
option_rationales.B: Security policy settings define which recommendations and standards apply, not alert recipients.
option_rationales.C: Membership of Security Reader controls who can view security data, not who receives email.
option_rationales.D: The alert rule itself defines the detection logic and points at an action group; the recipients are configured in that group.

verification.note: Community 100% A. Note that Defender for Cloud separately has 'Email notifications' settings for security contacts, used for its own built-in alerts.

question_stem:
You are configuring and securing a network environment.
You deploy an Azure virtual machine named VM1 that is configured to analyze network traffic.
You need to ensure that all network traffic is routed through VM1.
What should you configure?
explanation:
Although the use of system routes facilitates traffic automatically for your deployment, there are cases in which you want to control the routing of packets through a virtual appliance. You can do so by creating user defined routes that specify the next hop for packets flowing to a specific subnet to go to your virtual appliance instead, and enabling IP forwarding for the VM running as the virtual appliance.

Note: User Defined Routes -
For most environments you will only need the system routes already defined by Azure. However, you may need to create a route table and add one or more routes in specific cases, such as:
=> Force tunneling to the Internet via your on-premises network.
=> Use of virtual appliances in your Azure environment.
=> In the scenarios above, you will have to create a route table and add user defined routes to it.
Reference:
https://github.com/uglide/azure-content/blob/master/articles/virtual-network/virtual-networks-udr-overview.md
answer_summary: Forcing traffic through a network virtual appliance means overriding Azure's default routing, which is done with a user-defined route whose next hop is the appliance's private IP.

option_rationales.A: System routes are created by Azure automatically and cannot be authored to point at your VM.
option_rationales.B: An NSG can allow or deny traffic but cannot redirect it through an appliance.
option_rationales.C: A user-defined route on the subnet sets the next hop type to Virtual appliance with VM1's private IP, so traffic is steered through it.

verification.note: Community 100% C. Remember the appliance VM also needs IP forwarding enabled on its NIC for this to work.

Use the drop-down menus to select the answer choice that completes each statement based on the information presented in the graphic.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

Answer Area

able to connect to East US

dragdrop_slots.Traffic destined for an Azure Storage ac: able to connect to East US 2

explanation:
Box 1: able to connect to East US 2
The StorageE2Allow has DestinationAddressPrefix (Storage/EastUS2)

Box 2: allowed -
TCP Port 21 controls the FTP session. Contoso_FTP has SourceAddressPrefix (1.2.3.4/32) and DestinationAddressPrefix (10.0.0.5/32)
Note:
The Get-AzureRmNetworkSecurityRuleConfig cmdlet gets a network security rule configuration for an Azure network security group.
Security rules in network security groups enable you to filter the type of network traffic that can flow in and out of virtual network subnets and network interfaces.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/manage-network-security-group

diagrams.diagram_description: PowerShell output showing NSG security rules configuration with three rules: DenyStorageAccess, StorageE2Allow, and Contoso_FTP, displaying ports, protocols, addresses, access, priority, and direction.

answer_summary: Rules are evaluated in priority order: StorageE2Allow at 104 permits port 443 to Storage.EastUS2 before DenyStorageAccess at 105 blocks the rest, and the only inbound FTP allow rule targets 10.0.0.5/32 — so traffic to 10.0.0.10/32 hits DenyAllInBound.

slot_rationales.Traffic destined for an Azure Storage ac: Able to connect to East US 2: the allow rule for the Storage.EastUS2 tag on port 443 has priority 104, which is evaluated before the broader Storage deny at 105. Storage in every other region is blocked.

verification.note: Second box changed from 'allowed' to 'dropped'. The bank's own explanation quotes the rule's destination as 10.0.0.5/32 while the statement asks about 10.0.0.10/32, so the rule cannot match — the stored answer contradicted its own reasoning.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the virtual networks shown in the following table.

| Name | Region | Subnet |
|------|--------|--------|
| VNET1 | West US | Subnet11 and Subnet12 |
| VNET2 | West US 2 | Subnet21 |
| VNET3 | East US | Subnet31 |

The subscription contains the virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Network interface | Connected to |
|------|------------------|-------------|
| VM1 | NIC1 | Subnet11 |
| VM2 | NIC2 | Subnet11 |
| VM3 | NIC3 | Subnet12 |
| VM4 | NIC4 | Subnet21 |
| VM5 | NIC5 | Subnet31 |

On NIC1, you configure an application security group named ASG1.
On which other network interfaces can you configure ASG1?
explanation:
Only network interfaces in VNET1, which consists of Subnet11 and Subnet12, can be configured in ASG1, as all network interfaces assigned to an application security group have to exist in the same virtual network that the first network interface assigned to the application security group is in.
Reference:
https://azure.microsoft.com/es-es/blog/applicationsecuritygroups/
answer_summary: Every network interface in an application security group must live in the same virtual network as the first interface added — so only NIC2 and NIC3, which are in VNET1, are eligible.

option_rationales.A: NIC3 is also in VNET1 (Subnet12), so it can join too — ASG membership is per-virtual-network, not per-subnet.
option_rationales.B: NIC4 (VNET2) and NIC5 (VNET3) are in different virtual networks and cannot be added.
option_rationales.C: NIC2 and NIC3 are both in VNET1, which is the constraint that matters.
option_rationales.D: NIC4 is in VNET2, so it is excluded.

verification.note: Community 100% C. The same-virtual-network restriction on ASGs still applies, as does the rule that both source and destination ASGs in one rule must be in that VNet.

question_stem:
You have 15 Azure virtual machines in a resource group named RG1.
All the virtual machines run identical applications.
You need to prevent unauthorized applications and malware from running on the virtual machines.
What should you do?

options.A: Apply an Azure policy to RG1.
options.B: From Azure Security Center, configure adaptive application controls.
options.C: Configure Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Identity Protection.
options.D: Apply a resource lock to RG1.

explanation:
Adaptive application control is an intelligent, automated end-to-end application whitelisting solution from Azure Security Center. It helps you control which applications can run on your Azure and non-Azure VMs (Windows and Linux), which, among other benefits, helps harden your VMs against malware. Security
Center uses machine learning to analyze the applications running on your VMs and helps you apply the specific whitelisting rules using this intelligence.
answer_summary: Adaptive application controls build an allowlist of the applications normally seen on a group of similar machines and alert on anything else — exactly the control for a fleet of identical VMs.

option_rationales.A: Azure Policy governs the configuration of Azure resources, not which processes may execute inside a VM.
option_rationales.B: Adaptive application controls learn the known-good application set per VM group and flag or block deviations.
option_rationales.C: Identity Protection detects risky sign-ins; it has no view of processes on a VM.
option_rationales.D: A resource lock only stops management-plane changes to the resources.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Adaptive application controls are still part of Microsoft Defender for Cloud and require Defender for Servers Plan 2.

question_stem:
You have a web app hosted on an on-premises server that is accessed by using a URL of https://www.contoso.com.
You plan to migrate the web app to Azure. You will continue to use https://www.contoso.com.
You need to enable HTTPS for the Azure web app.
What should you do first?

options.A: Export the public key from the on-premises server and save the key as a P7b file.
options.B: Export the private key from the on-premises server and save the key as a PFX file that is encrypted by using TripleDES.
options.C: Export the public key from the on-premises server and save the key as a CER file.
options.D: Export the private key from the on-premises server and save the key as a PFX file that is encrypted by using AES256.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/configure-ssl-certificate#private-certificate-requirements
answer_summary: App Service needs the certificate with its private key, so you export a password-protected PFX — and its documented requirement is that the PFX be encrypted with triple DES.

option_rationales.A: A P7B contains certificates without the private key, so TLS cannot be bound.
option_rationales.B: A password-protected PFX encrypted with triple DES is what App Service's private-certificate requirements specify.
option_rationales.C: A CER file holds only the public key.
option_rationales.D: AES256-encrypted PFX files are the modern default from newer OpenSSL/Windows tooling, but App Service's documented requirement is triple DES — which is why exports from newer tools often have to be re-encrypted.

verification.note: Community 65% B. The triple-DES requirement is genuinely still in Microsoft's private-certificate requirements list, which is why 29% voting D is understandable: newer OpenSSL versions default to AES-256 and you must pass -legacy (or -keypbe/-certpbe with tripleDES) to produce an accepted file.

question_stem:
You plan to deploy Azure container instances.
You have a containerized application that is comprised of two containers: an application container and a validation container. The application container is monitored by the validation container. The validation container performs security checks by making requests to the application container and waiting for responses after every transaction.
You need to ensure that the application container and the validation container are scheduled to be deployed together. The containers must communicate to each other only on ports that are not externally exposed.
What should you include in the deployment?
explanation:
Azure Container Instances supports the deployment of multiple containers onto a single host using a container group. A container group is useful when building an application sidecar for logging, monitoring, or any other configuration where a service needs a second attached process.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-instances/container-instances-container-groups
answer_summary: A container group co-schedules containers on the same host, where they share a network namespace and can talk over localhost on ports that are never exposed externally.

option_rationales.A: Application security groups are a VNet/NSG construct and do not co-schedule containers.
option_rationales.B: NSGs filter traffic between network resources; they do not group containers into one deployment.
option_rationales.C: Management groups organize subscriptions for governance.
option_rationales.D: A container group deploys both containers together on one host with a shared local network, which is the sidecar pattern this scenario describes.

verification.note: Community 100% D. Container groups still share lifetime, local network and (optionally) volumes; only explicitly exposed ports are reachable from outside.

answer_summary: Basic is ruled out because it does not support BGP, and VpnGw1 already allows up to 30 site-to-site tunnels — so the cheapest SKU that meets both requirements is VpnGw1 for each network.

question_stem:
You are securing access to the resources in an Azure subscription.
A new company policy states that all the Azure virtual machines in the subscription must use managed disks.
You need to prevent users from creating virtual machines that use unmanaged disks.
What should you use?
answer_summary: Preventing a resource configuration outright is Azure Policy's Deny effect — the built-in policy requiring managed disks blocks any VM creation that uses unmanaged disks.

option_rationales.A: Azure Monitor observes and alerts; it cannot block a deployment.
option_rationales.B: An Azure Policy assignment with a Deny effect stops non-compliant VM creations before they happen.
option_rationales.C: Defender for Cloud would flag the configuration as a recommendation after the fact.
option_rationales.D: Service Health reports on Azure platform incidents.

verification.note: Community 100% B. The built-in definition 'Audit VMs that do not use managed disks' is audit-only; use the deny-effect managed-disk policy (or a custom deny) to actually prevent creation.

hotspot_rows.statement: VM1 can connect to storage1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Subnet1 has a Microsoft.Storage service endpoint, so VM1's requests come from a private address and cannot match an IP rule — and Subnet1 is not in the allowed virtual network list, so access is denied.

hotspot_rows.statement: VM2 can connect to storage1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Subnet2 has no service endpoint, so VM2 reaches the account over its public IP 52.233.129.82, which falls inside the allowed 52.233.129.0/24 range.

hotspot_rows.statement: VM3 can connect to storage1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: VM3's subnet is listed as a virtual network rule, but its service endpoint is Microsoft.KeyVault — without a Microsoft.Storage endpoint the rule does not take effect, and VM3's public IP is outside the allowed range.

explanation:
Box 1: No -
VNet1 has a service endpoint configure for Azure Storage. However, the Azure storage does not allow access from VNet1 or the public IP address of VM1.

Box 2: Yes -
VNet2 does not have a service endpoint configured. However, the Azure storage allows access from the public IP address of VM2.

Box 3: No -

answer_summary: Only two things are allowed: the VNET3\Subnet3 virtual network rule and the IP range 52.233.129.0/24. Subnet3's service endpoint is for Key Vault, not Storage, so the virtual network rule cannot carry VM3's traffic — while VM2 matches the IP range.

verification.note: Answers kept as graded, and rows 1 and 3 are the two classic traps (service endpoint replaces the public source IP; the endpoint must be for the right service). One caveat on row 2: Microsoft's storage firewall documentation notes that IP network rules have no effect on requests originating in the same region as the storage account, which is the case here — so in a real deployment you would add a virtual network rule instead of relying on the IP range.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

Answer Area

Statements                                                               Yes    No
VM1 can ping VM3 successfully.                                            O      O
VM2 can ping VM4 successfully.                                            O      O
VM3 can be accessed by using Remote Desktop from the internet.            O      O

hotspot_rows.statement: VM1 can ping VM3 successfully.
hotspot_rows.rationale: VM1 and VM3 are in peered virtual networks, and Rule1 allows any protocol from ASG1 to any destination — peered address space is included in the VirtualNetwork tag, so the ping succeeds.

hotspot_rows.statement: VM2 can ping VM4 successfully.
hotspot_rows.rationale: VNET4 is not peered with VNET2, so there is no private path; and because application security groups are scoped to a single virtual network, Rule2's ASG2 source cannot match traffic arriving at VM4 in VNET4 — Rule4 denies it.

hotspot_rows.statement: VM3 can be accessed by using Remote Desktop from the internet.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Allow_RDP (priority 110) permits TCP 3389 from any source to any destination, and VM3 has a public IP, so Remote Desktop from the internet reaches it — well ahead of Rule4's deny at 160.

explanation:
Box 1: Yes -
VM1 and VM3 are on peered VNets. The firewall rules with a source of ASG1 and ASG2 allow 'any' traffic on 'any' protocol so pings are allowed between VM1 and VM3.

Box 2: No -
VM2 and VM4 are on separate VNets and the VNets are not peered. Therefore, the pings would have to go over the Internet. VM4 does have a public IP and the firewall allows pings. However, VM2 would also need a public IP address. In Azure, pings don't go out through the default gateway as they would in a physical network. For an Azure VM to ping external IPs, the VM must have a public IP address assigned to it.

Box 3: Yes -
VM3 has a public IP address and the firewall allows traffic on port 3389.

diagrams.diagram_description: NSG1 firewall configuration showing inbound security rules (Allow_RDP on port 3389, Rule1 from ASG1, Rule2 from ASG2, Rule3 from ASG4, Rule4 deny all, default VNet and Azure Load Balancer allow rules) and outbound security rules (AllowVnetOutBound, AllowInternetOutBound, DenyAllOutBound).

answer_summary: ASG-based rules only work inside one virtual network, and NSG1's Rule4 denies anything the ASG rules do not allow. VM1→VM3 works across the VNET1/VNET2 peering, VM2→VM4 has no peering (and ASG2 means nothing in VNET4), and Allow_RDP at priority 110 lets RDP in from anywhere.

verification.note: Behaviour unchanged. Note that the Allow_RDP rule as written exposes 3389 to the entire internet, which is precisely what JIT access or Bastion exists to avoid.

question_stem:
You have multiple development teams that will create apps in Azure.
You plan to create a standard development environment that will be deployed for each team.
You need to recommend a solution that will enforce resource locks across the development environments and ensure that the locks are applied in a consistent manner.
What should you include in the recommendation?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/blueprints/concepts/resource-locking
answer_summary: Resource locks are a first-class blueprint capability: a blueprint assignment can apply Read Only or Do Not Delete locks to the resources it deploys and keeps re-applying them, which gives every team's environment identical protection.

option_rationales.A: Azure Policy can audit and even deploy things, but it has no native lock artifact — you would have to hand-roll a deployIfNotExists template.
option_rationales.B: An ARM template can create locks, but nothing keeps them consistent afterwards; a redeployment or manual removal is not corrected.
option_rationales.C: A management group organizes scopes for policy and RBAC inheritance; it applies no locks.
option_rationales.D: Azure Blueprints deploys the standard environment and locks its resources as part of the assignment, enforcing consistency across teams.

verification.note: Kept as D, matching the cited resource-locking documentation, though community votes are split (45% A / 38% D). Currency matters here: Azure Blueprints is deprecated, and the modern successor for exactly this behaviour is a deployment stack with deny settings, which protects the stack's resources from modification or deletion.

You have an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster that will connect to an Azure Container Registry.
You need to use the automatically generated service principal for the AKS cluster to authenticate to the Azure Container Registry.
What should you create?

options.A: a secret in Azure Key Vault
options.C: an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) user
options.D: an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) group

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/aks/kubernetes-service-principal
answer_summary: The cluster's service principal is authorized by giving it the AcrPull role on the registry — a role assignment, so no credentials are stored anywhere.

option_rationales.A: A Key Vault secret would mean storing registry credentials instead of using the cluster's own identity.
option_rationales.B: A role assignment granting the service principal AcrPull on the registry is the documented mechanism.
option_rationales.C: A user account is not used for a cluster's automated image pulls.
option_rationales.D: A group adds indirection but no permission by itself.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Current clusters use a managed identity and 'az aks update --attach-acr', which creates this role assignment automatically.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains two virtual machines named VM1 and VM2 that run Windows Server 2019.
You are implementing Update Management in Azure Automation.
You plan to create a new update deployment named Update1.
You need to ensure that Update1 meets the following requirements:
=> Automatically applies updates to VM1 and VM2.
=> Automatically adds any new Windows Server 2019 virtual machines to Update1.
What should you include in Update1?

options.A: a security group that has a Membership type of Assigned
options.B: a security group that has a Membership type of Dynamic Device

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/automation/update-management/configure-groups
answer_summary: A dynamic group query defines the deployment's targets by criteria (subscription, resource group, tag, OS), so new Windows Server 2019 machines that match are picked up automatically at each run.

option_rationales.A: An assigned security group is a static list — new VMs would have to be added by hand.
option_rationales.B: Dynamic Device groups are an Entra ID/Intune concept for devices, not something an update deployment targets.
option_rationales.C: A dynamic group query is evaluated when the deployment runs, so machines matching the criteria are always included.
option_rationales.D: A KQL query can list machines but is not what an update deployment accepts as its target definition.

verification.note: Community 81% C. Currency: Azure Automation Update Management retired in 2024 — the same idea now exists in Azure Update Manager as a 'dynamic scope' on a maintenance configuration.

question_stem:
You have the Azure virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Operating system | State |
|------|------------------|-------|
| VM1 | Windows Server 2012 | Running |
| VM2 | Windows Server 2012 R2 | Running |
| VM3 | Windows Server 2016 | Stopped |
| VM4 | Ubuntu Server 18.04 LTS | Running |

For which virtual machines can you enable Update Management?
explanation:
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/automation/automation-update-management?toc=%2Fazure%2Fautomation%2Ftoc.json
answer_summary: Onboarding requires the machine to be running so the agent can be installed and register with the workspace — VM3 is stopped, which is why it is excluded while the two older Windows versions and the Linux VM are all supported.

option_rationales.A: VM1 (Windows Server 2012) is supported and VM3 cannot be onboarded while stopped.
option_rationales.B: VM3 is stopped, so it cannot be enabled now.
option_rationales.C: VM1, VM2 and VM4 are running and on supported operating systems, so Update Management can be enabled for them.
option_rationales.D: Including VM3 assumes a stopped VM can be onboarded, which it cannot — the agent installation would fail.
option_rationales.E: VM4 (Ubuntu) is supported, so excluding Linux is wrong.

verification.note: Community split 60% C / 40% D. The distinction is onboarding versus staying enrolled: an already-onboarded machine can be stopped and still appear (as Not assessed), but you cannot enable Update Management on a deallocated VM. Currency: this is Azure Update Manager's job now, and it no longer needs an Automation account or Log Analytics workspace.

You have an Azure subscription that contains the following resources:
A virtual network named VNET1 that contains two subnets named Subnet1 and Subnet2.
•

Actions

Configure a network security group (NSG).

Create a network rule collection.

Create a NAT rule collection.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription that is linked to an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD). The tenant contains the users shown in the following table.

| Name | Role | Member of |
|------|------|----------|
| User1 | Security administrator | Group1 |
| User2 | Network Contributor | Group2 |
| User3 | Key Vault Contributor | Group1, Group2 |

You have an Azure key vault named Vault1 that has Purge protection set to Disable. Vault1 contains the access policies shown in the following table.

| Name | Key permission | Secret permission | Certificate permission |
|------|----------------|-------------------|-----------------------|
| Group1 | Purge | Purge | Purge |
| Group2 | Select all | Select all | Select all |

You create role assignments for Vault1 as shown in the following table.

| Name | Role |
|------|------|
| User1 | None |
| User2 | Key Vault Reader |
| User3 | User Access Administrator |

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

Statements                                                   Yes    No
User1 can set Purge protection to Enable for Vault1.         O      O
User2 can configure firewalls and virtual networks for Vault1. O    O
User3 can add access policies to Vault1.                     O      O

Correct Answer:

Statements                                                   Yes    No
User1 can set Purge protection to Enable for Vault1.         O      O
User2 can configure firewalls and virtual networks for Vault1. O    O
User3 can add access policies to Vault1.                     O      O

hotspot_rows.statement: User1 can set Purge protection to Enable for Vault1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: User1 has the Security administrator directory role and no role assignment on Vault1. Purge protection is a property of the vault, so changing it needs vault write permission — the access policy's Purge data-plane permission is unrelated.

hotspot_rows.statement: User2 can configure firewalls and virtual networks for Vault1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Configuring a vault's firewall and virtual network rules also updates the vault resource, which needs Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write. Key Vault Reader is read-only and Network Contributor grants only Microsoft.Network permissions, so User2 cannot do it.

hotspot_rows.statement: User3 can add access policies to Vault1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: User3 holds Key Vault Contributor, which manages the vault including its access policies (but grants no data-plane access to keys, secrets or certificates).

explanation:
Box 1: No -
Resource Policy Contributor or Security Administrator is required.
User1 is Security Administrator only with the no specific permission granted to Vault1.
The Security Admin can view and update permissions for Security Center. Same permissions as the Security Reader role and can also update the security policy and dismiss alerts and recommendations.
However:

Last but not least, you need to have the appropriate permissions to assign the Contributor role for the Managed Identity (Application ID) created during the assignment of the policy either on a management group or a subscription, so the policy with "DeployIfNotExists" can remediate and modify your Key Vault settings. Azure Policy creates a managed identity for each assignment but must have details about what roles to grant the managed identity.

Box 2: Yes -
User2 is a Network Contributor, with Select All Key, Secret & Certificate permissions, and Key Vault Reader.
The Network Contributor role lets you manage networks, but not access to them.

Box 3: Yes -
User3 is a Key Vault Contributor and a User Access Administrator for Vault.
The Key Vault Contributor role allows you to manage key vaults, but does not allow you to assign roles in Azure RBAC, and does not allow you to access secrets, keys, or certificates.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles#network-contributor https://charbelnemnom.com/enable-purge-protection-key-vault-azure-policy/
answer_summary: Everything here hinges on the management plane: changing purge protection or a vault's network rules requires Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write, which neither Security administrator nor Key Vault Reader provides — while Key Vault Contributor does let User3 edit access policies.

verification.note: Row 2 changed from Yes to No. Editing a key vault's 'Firewalls and virtual networks' settings writes to the vault object (Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write), which Key Vault Reader does not have; Network Contributor covers Microsoft.Network resources such as subnets, not Key Vault. Also worth noting purge protection is one-way — once enabled it cannot be disabled.

answer_summary: Application security groups are regional and, once populated, confined to one virtual network. ASG1 already holds a VNET1 interface so only VM2 can join it; ASG2 is empty, so any West US interface could be added first — but VM3 is in Central US and can never be added.

slot_rationales.ASG1: VM2 only — the first member (VM1) is in VNET1, and every other interface in the ASG must be in that same virtual network. VM3 and VM4 are in other virtual networks.
slot_rationales.ASG2: VM1, VM2 and VM4 — all three are in the West US region where ASG2 was created, so any of them could be the first interface added (after which the ASG is pinned to that VM's virtual network). VM3 is in Central US, so it is ineligible regardless.

verification.note: ASG2 changed from all four VMs to VM1, VM2 and VM4. An application security group is a regional resource and a network interface can only be added to an ASG in its own region, so a Central US interface cannot join a West US ASG — VNet peering does not change that.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure key vault.

You need to configure the maximum number of days for which new keys are valid. The solution must minimize administrative effort.

What should you use?
answer_summary: Azure Policy has built-in definitions that cap how long new keys may be valid (maximum validity in days) and evaluate them automatically across the vault, which is far less effort than checking each key by hand.

option_rationales.A: Purview catalogues and governs data, not Key Vault key lifetimes.
option_rationales.B: Vault properties control soft delete, purge protection, network access and the permission model — there is no maximum-key-validity property.
option_rationales.C: Blueprints deploys governance artifacts (and is deprecated); it would only wrap the same policy.
option_rationales.D: Azure Policy's built-in Key Vault definitions include a maximum validity period for keys/certificates, applied and monitored automatically.

verification.note: Community 100% D. The relevant built-ins are Key Vault policies such as 'Keys should have more than the specified number of days before expiration' and the certificate/key maximum-validity definitions, which support Audit or Deny.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 account named storage1.

You deploy an Azure Synapse Analytics workspace named synapsews1 to a managed virtual network.

You need to enable access from synapsews1 to storage1.

What should you configure?
answer_summary: A Synapse workspace in a managed virtual network reaches other Azure PaaS resources through a managed private endpoint, which gives it a private IP in the managed network — peering and gateways are not available there.

option_rationales.A: You cannot peer the Microsoft-managed virtual network that hosts the workspace.
option_rationales.B: A managed private endpoint to storage1 is the supported way for a managed-VNet workspace to reach the Data Lake account privately.
option_rationales.C: An NSG filters traffic; it establishes no connectivity to a PaaS endpoint.
option_rationales.D: A virtual network gateway provides VPN/ExpressRoute connectivity, which is not how a workspace reaches a storage account.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Also remember the storage account must approve the private endpoint connection, and 'Allow trusted Azure services' or the workspace's managed identity may still be needed for some operations.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.

| Name | Type | Resource group |
|------|------|----------------|
| RG1 | Resource group | Not applicable |
| RG2 | Resource group | Not applicable |
| RG3 | Resource group | Not applicable |
| SQL1 | Azure SQL Database | RG3 |

Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) is disabled on SQL1.
You assign policies to the resource groups as shown in the following table.

| Name | Condition | Effect if condition is false | Assignment |
|------|-----------|------------------------------|------------|
| Policy1 | TDE enabled | Deny | RG1, RG2 |
| Policy2 | TDE enabled | DeployIfNotExists | RG2, RG3 |
| Policy3 | TDE enabled | Audit | RG1 |

You plan to deploy Azure SQL databases by using an Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template. The databases will be configured as shown in the following table.

| Name | Resource group | TDE |
|------|----------------|-----|
| SQL2 | RG2 | Disabled |
| SQL3 | RG1 | Disabled |

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: SQL1 will have TDE enabled automatically.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Policy2's DeployIfNotExists applies to RG3, but such effects only run on create/update — existing non-compliant resources are simply marked non-compliant until an explicit remediation task is triggered, so SQL1's TDE stays off.

hotspot_rows.statement: The deployment of SQL2 will fail.
hotspot_rows.rationale: SQL2 is deployed into RG2, which carries Policy1 with a Deny effect for TDE-disabled databases, so the deployment is blocked.

hotspot_rows.statement: SQL3 will be deployed and marked as noncompliant.
hotspot_rows.rationale: SQL3 is deployed into RG1, and Policy1 (Deny) is assigned to RG1 as well as RG2 — so SQL3 is blocked too. Policy3's Audit effect on RG1 would only have flagged it as non-compliant if the deployment had been allowed.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/policy/concepts/effects
answer_summary: Deny is evaluated at deployment time and beats the other effects: both new databases have TDE disabled and both land in resource groups carrying Policy1, so both deployments fail. And DeployIfNotExists does not touch the pre-existing SQL1 until you run a remediation task.

verification.note: Row 3 changed from Yes to No. Policy1's assignment list includes RG1, and a Deny effect prevents the resource from being created at all, so SQL3 cannot be 'deployed and marked as noncompliant' — Deny takes precedence over Audit when both apply.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1. Sub1 has an Azure Storage account named storage1 that contains the resources shown in the following table.

| Name | Type |
|------|------|
| Container1 | Blob container |
| Share1 | File share |

You generate a shared access signature (SAS) to connect to the blob service and the file service.
Which tool can you use to access the contents in Container1 and Share1 by using the SAS? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
answer_summary: Azure Storage Explorer can attach to both a blob container and a file share using nothing but a SAS URI, which is why it is the tool for each resource.

slot_rationales.Tools for Container1: Azure Storage Explorer — 'Attach to a resource' accepts a blob container SAS URL directly, with no account key or sign-in required.
slot_rationales.Tools for Share1: Azure Storage Explorer — the same attach flow works for a file share SAS URL (mounting the share with net use/SMB would need the account key instead).

verification.note: Still true. AzCopy also supports SAS for both services, and the portal's Storage browser can use a SAS, so read the offered choices carefully on the real exam.

question_stem:
You have an Azure Storage account named storage1 that has a container named container1.
You need to prevent the blobs in container1 from being modified.
What should you do?

options.A: From container1, change the access level.
options.B: From container1, add an access policy.
options.C: From container1, modify the Access Control (IAM) settings.
options.D: From storage1, enable soft delete for blobs.

explanation:
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/storage-blob-immutable-storage?tabs=azure-portal
answer_summary: Preventing modification of blobs is immutability, configured as an access policy on the container — a time-based retention policy or a legal hold, both under the container's Access policy blade.

option_rationales.A: The access level (private/blob/container) controls anonymous read access, not whether blobs can be changed.
option_rationales.B: Adding an immutability access policy (time-based retention or legal hold) makes the blobs write-once, read-many so they cannot be modified or deleted.
option_rationales.C: IAM settings control who has permissions; an authorized user could still overwrite the blobs.
option_rationales.D: Soft delete helps you recover after a change or deletion — it does not prevent one.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Immutability policies can now also be set at account scope and, for time-based retention, locked to become unbreakable — version-level immutability is the newer variant.

question_stem:
Your company has an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com.
You plan to create several security alerts by using Azure Monitor.
You need to prepare the Azure subscription for the alerts.
What should you create first?
answer_summary: Log-based alerts need somewhere to hold and query the data, so the Log Analytics workspace is the first thing to create — diagnostic settings then send the logs there and alert rules query it.

option_rationales.A: A storage account is for archiving; you cannot run alert queries against it.
option_rationales.B: A Log Analytics workspace stores the log data and is the target that log search alert rules query.
option_rationales.C: An event hub streams logs to external systems, not for Azure Monitor alerting.
option_rationales.D: An Automation account runs runbooks — useful as an alert response, not as the prerequisite.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Entra ID sign-in and audit logs still require a diagnostic setting pointing at the workspace before they can be queried or alerted on.

question_stem:
You company has an Azure subscription named Sub1. Sub1 contains an Azure web app named WebApp1 that uses Azure Application Insights.
WebApp1 requires users to authenticate by using OAuth 2.0 client secrets.
Developers at the company plan to create a multi-step web test app that performs synthetic transactions emulating user traffic to Web App1.
You need to ensure that web tests can run unattended.
What should you do first?

options.A: In Microsoft Visual Studio, modify the .webtest file.
options.B: Upload the .webtest file to Application Insights.
options.C: Register the web test app in Azure AD.
options.D: Add a plug-in to the web test app.

answer_summary: The test has to authenticate with OAuth 2.0 client credentials, so the test application itself needs an identity: register it in Microsoft Entra ID first, then it can obtain tokens and run unattended.

option_rationales.A: Editing the .webtest file cannot create the client identity the OAuth flow needs.
option_rationales.B: Uploading the test is how you run it, but without a registered app it cannot acquire a token, so the unattended run would fail authentication.
option_rationales.C: Registering the web test app in Entra ID gives it the client ID and secret needed to request tokens for WebApp1, which is the prerequisite for unattended runs.
option_rationales.D: A plug-in might help handle the token in the test, but the registration must exist first.

verification.note: Answer changed from B to C (community 85% C). Currency: multi-step web tests based on .webtest files are retired in Application Insights — standard tests (single URL) or TrackAvailability-based custom tests are the current options, and the identity prerequisite is unchanged.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription named Subscription1.
You deploy a Linux virtual machine named VM1 to Subscription1.
You need to monitor the metrics and the logs of VM1.
What should you use?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/extensions/diagnostics-linux
answer_summary: The Linux Diagnostic Extension 3.0 is the agent that collects both performance metrics and logs (syslog) from a Linux VM and forwards them to Azure Monitor.

option_rationales.A: The Performance Diagnostics extension runs one-off troubleshooting collections, not ongoing monitoring.
option_rationales.B: HDInsight is a managed analytics cluster service.
option_rationales.C: LAD 3.0 gathers metrics and logs from the VM and sends them to a storage account, event hub or Azure Monitor.
option_rationales.D: Analysis Services is a BI modelling service.

verification.note: Community 90% C. Currency: the Linux Diagnostic Extension is legacy — the Azure Monitor Agent with data collection rules is the current way to gather Linux metrics and syslog.

question_stem:
You onboard Azure Sentinel. You connect Azure Sentinel to Azure Security Center.
You need to automate the mitigation of incidents in Azure Sentinel. The solution must minimize administrative effort.
What should you create?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/tutorial-respond-threats-playbook
answer_summary: Automated response in Sentinel is a playbook — a Logic App triggered by an incident or alert — which needs no code and can be attached with an automation rule.

option_rationales.A: An alert (analytics) rule detects and creates incidents; it does not mitigate them.
option_rationales.B: A playbook runs the response actions (isolate, disable a user, notify, open a ticket) and is designed for exactly this, with minimal effort.
option_rationales.C: A function app means writing and hosting code — more effort than a playbook.
option_rationales.D: A runbook lives in Azure Automation and is not natively wired into Sentinel incidents.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Azure Sentinel is now Microsoft Sentinel, and playbooks are attached to incidents through automation rules; Defender for Cloud alerts flow in through the Defender for Cloud connector or Defender XDR.

question_stem:
You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com.
You need to configure diagnostic settings for contoso.com. The solution must meet the following requirements:
=> Retain logs for two years.
=> Query logs by using the Kusto query language.
=> Minimize administrative effort.
Where should you store the logs?
answer_summary: Only a Log Analytics workspace gives both requirements at once: retention configurable up to two years and KQL querying — with no extra plumbing to build.

option_rationales.A: An event hub is a streaming pipeline with a short retention window and no query capability.
option_rationales.B: A workspace supports interactive retention up to 730 days and is queried with KQL directly.
option_rationales.C: A storage account can hold logs cheaply for years but cannot be queried with KQL without exporting the data elsewhere.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Interactive retention is still up to two years (730 days) per table, and long-term retention now extends to 12 years with archive tiers — searchable via search jobs or table restore rather than direct KQL.

question_stem:
You are troubleshooting a security issue for an Azure Storage account.
You enable the diagnostic logs for the storage account.
What should you use to retrieve the diagnostics logs?
explanation:
If you want to download the metrics for long-term storage or to analyze them locally, you must use a tool or write some code to read the tables. You must download the minute metrics for analysis. The tables do not appear if you list all the tables in your storage account, but you can access them directly by name.
Many storage-browsing tools are aware of these tables and enable you to view them directly (see Azure Storage Client Tools for a list of available tools).
Microsoft provides several graphical user interface (GUI) tools for working with the data in your Azure Storage account. All of the tools outlined in the following table are free.

| Azure Storage client tool | Supported platforms | Block Blob | Page Blob | Append Blob | Tables | Queues | Files |
|----------------------------|---------------------|------------|-----------|--------------|--------|--------|-------|
| Azure portal | Web | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Azure Storage Explorer | Windows, OSX | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Microsoft Visual Studio Cloud Explorer | Windows | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |

Note:
There are several versions of this question in the exam. The questions in the exam have two different correct answers:
1. Azure Storage Explorer
2. AZCopy
Other incorrect answer options you may see on the exam include the following:
1. SQL query editor in Azure
2. File Explorer in Windows
3. Azure Monitor
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-analytics-metrics?toc=%2fazure%2fstorage%2fblobs%2ftoc.json
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-explorers
answer_summary: Classic storage analytics writes its logs into the hidden $logs container in the same account, and you pull them down with a storage tool such as AzCopy — no security portal surfaces them.

option_rationales.A: The Security & Compliance admin center covers Microsoft 365 data, not Azure Storage logs.
option_rationales.B: Security Center shows security recommendations and alerts, not raw storage diagnostic logs.
option_rationales.C: Cosmos DB Explorer works with Cosmos databases.
option_rationales.D: AzCopy can download the log blobs from the $logs container (which does not appear in a normal container listing) for local analysis.

verification.note: Community 100% D. Currency: classic Storage Analytics logging is deprecated — current practice is a diagnostic setting sending StorageRead/Write/Delete logs to a Log Analytics workspace, where you query them with KQL instead of downloading files.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Operating system |
|------|------------------|
| VM1 | Windows Server 2016 |
| VM2 | Ubuntu Server 18.04 LTS |

From Azure Security Center, you turn on Auto Provisioning.
You deploy the virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Operating system |
|------|------------------|
| VM3 | Windows Server 2016 |
| VM4 | Ubuntu Server 18.04 LTS |

On which virtual machines is the Microsoft Monitoring Agent installed?
explanation:
When automatic provisioning is enabled, Security Center provisions the Microsoft Monitoring Agent on all supported Azure VMs and any new ones that are created.
Supported Operating systems include: Ubuntu 14.04 LTS (x86/x64), 16.04 LTS (x86/x64), and 18.04 LTS (x64) and Windows Server 2008 R2, 2012, 2012 R2,
2016, version 1709 and 1803.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security-center/security-center-faq
answer_summary: Auto provisioning installs the agent on every supported VM in the subscription — both the machines that already exist and any created afterwards — and all four operating systems here are supported.

option_rationales.A: Provisioning is not limited to newly created VMs.
option_rationales.B: Linux is supported too, so VM2 and VM4 are included.
option_rationales.C: Existing VMs (VM1 and VM2) are also provisioned when the setting is turned on.
option_rationales.D: All four VMs get the agent: Windows Server 2016 and Ubuntu 18.04 are both supported platforms.

verification.note: Community 100% D. Currency: the Microsoft Monitoring Agent/Log Analytics agent reached end of support in August 2024. Defender for Cloud now auto-provisions the Azure Monitor Agent and the Defender for Endpoint sensor instead.

question_stem:
SIMULATION -
You need to email an alert to a user named admin1@contoso.com if the average CPU usage of a virtual machine named VM1 is greater than 70 percent for a period of 15 minutes.
To complete this task, sign in to the Azure portal.
explanation:
Create an alert rule on a metric with the Azure portal

2. Select Alerts (Classic) under the MONITORING section. The text and icon may vary slightly for different resources.
