question_stem:
SIMULATION -
You need to collect all the audit failure data from the security log of a virtual machine named VM1 to an Azure Storage account.
To complete this task, sign in to the Azure portal.
This task might take several minutes to complete You can perform other tasks while the task completes.
explanation:
Step 1: Create a workspace -
Azure Monitor can collect data directly from your Azure virtual machines into a Log Analytics workspace for detailed analysis and correlation.
1. In the Azure portal, select All services. In the list of resources, type Log Analytics. As you begin typing, the list filters based on your input. Select Log Analytics workspaces.

2. Select Create, and then select choices for the following items:

While the information is verified and the workspace is created, you can track its progress under Notifications from the menu.
Step 2: Enable the Log Analytics VM Extension
Installing the Log Analytics VM extension for Windows and Linux allows Azure Monitor to collect data from your Azure VMs.
1. In the Azure portal, select All services found in the upper left-hand corner. In the list of resources, type Log Analytics. As you begin typing, the list filters based on your input. Select Log Analytics workspaces.
2. In your list of Log Analytics workspaces, select DefaultWorkspace (the name you created in step 1).
3. On the left-hand menu, under Workspace Data Sources, select Virtual machines.
4. In the list of Virtual machines, select a virtual machine you want to install the agent on. Notice that the Log Analytics connection status for the VM indicates that it is Not connected.
5. In the details for your virtual machine, select Connect. The agent is automatically installed and configured for your Log Analytics workspace. This process takes a few minutes, during which time the Status shows Connecting.
After you install and connect the agent, the Log Analytics connection status will be updated with This workspace.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/learn/quick-collect-azurevm

diagrams.diagram_description: Screenshot of Azure portal showing the Log Analytics workspace creation dialog with fields for Log Analytics Workspace (DefaultLAWorkspace), Subscription (Microsoft Azure), Resource group (Prod), Location (East US), and Pricing tier (Per GB (2018)).

answer_summary: Turn on guest-level diagnostics for VM1 and point it at the storage account, then in the Windows event logs settings select the Security log at the Audit failure level so those events are written to the account.

verification.note: The Azure Diagnostics extension route (VM → Diagnostic settings → Logs → Security log, Audit failure → storage account) is what satisfies 'to a storage account'. With the modern Azure Monitor Agent you would instead create a data collection rule with a security-event XPath filter and a storage or workspace destination.

question_stem:
You have 10 virtual machines on a single subnet that has a single network security group (NSG).
You need to log the network traffic to an Azure Storage account.
What should you do?

options.A: Install the Network Performance Monitor solution.
options.B: Create an Azure Log Analytics workspace.
options.C: Enable diagnostic logging for the NSG.

explanation:
A network security group (NSG) enables you to filter inbound traffic to, and outbound traffic from, a virtual machine (VM). You can log network traffic that flows through an NSG with Network Watcher's NSG flow log capability. Steps include:
=> Create a VM with a network security group
=> Enable Network Watcher and register the Microsoft.Insights provider
=> Enable a traffic flow log for an NSG, using Network Watcher's NSG flow log capability
=> Download logged data

View logged data -

Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/network-watcher-nsg-flow-logging-portal
answer_summary: NSG flow logs are the Network Watcher feature that records the traffic flowing through an NSG and writes it to a storage account — diagnostic logs for an NSG only capture rule counters and events.

option_rationales.A: Network Performance Monitor measures connectivity and latency, not per-flow traffic records.
option_rationales.B: A workspace is a destination for analytics (Traffic Analytics), but it is not what captures the traffic.
option_rationales.C: NSG diagnostic logs cover rule counters and events, not the individual network flows.
option_rationales.D: NSG flow logs write 5-tuple flow records (with allow/deny decisions) into a storage account.

verification.note: Community 100% D. Currency: NSG flow logs are being retired (announced end of support 30 September 2027) in favour of VNet flow logs, which capture at virtual network scope and feed the same Traffic Analytics.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You plan to use Azure Log Analytics to collect logs from 200 servers that run Windows Server 2016.

explanation:
Reference:
https://blogs.technet.microsoft.com/manageabilityguys/2015/11/19/enabling-the-microsoft-monitoring-agent-in-windows-json-templates/

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription that contains the alerts shown in the following exhibit.

Use the drop-down menus to select the answer choice that completes each statement based on the information presented in the graphic.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

dragdrop_slots.The state of Alert1 that was fired at 11: can be changed to Closed only
dragdrop_slots.The state of Alert2 that was fired at 11: can be changed to New or Acknowledged

explanation:
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/platform/alerts-overview

diagrams.diagram_description: Screenshot of Azure portal All Alerts blade showing a table with four alerts (Alert1 twice and Alert2 twice) with columns for SEVERITY (all Sev4), MONITOR CONDITION (all Fired), ALERT STATE (New, Acknowledged, Acknowledged, Closed), MONITOR SERVICE (all ActivityLog Admin), SIGNAL TYPE (all Log), and FIRED TIME (6/6/2019 11:23:53, 11:23:52, 11:23:25, 11:23:24).

answer_summary: Alert state moves forward through the lifecycle in this question's model: an Acknowledged alert can only be moved on to Closed, while a Closed alert can be reopened as New or set to Acknowledged.

slot_rationales.The state of Alert1 that was fired at 11: That instance is already Acknowledged, so the remaining transition is to Closed.
slot_rationales.The state of Alert2 that was fired at 11: That instance is Closed, so it can be brought back as New or moved to Acknowledged.

verification.note: Kept as graded, but note the practical behaviour: alert state in Azure Monitor is a simple user-set field with three values (New, Acknowledged, Closed) and the portal does not actually enforce a one-way path, so a real Acknowledged alert can also be set back to New. Alert state is separate from monitor condition (Fired/Resolved), which only the service sets.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that is associated to an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com.
You are assigned the Global administrator role for the tenant. You are responsible for managing Azure Security Center settings.
You need to create a custom sensitivity label.
What should you do?

options.A: Create a custom sensitive information type.
options.B: Elevate access for global administrators in Azure AD.
options.C: Upgrade the pricing tier of the Security Center to Standard.
options.D: Enable integration with Microsoft Cloud App Security.

explanation:
First, you need to create a new sensitive information type because you can't directly modify the default rules.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/office365/securitycompliance/customize-a-built-in-sensitive-information-type
answer_summary: A custom sensitivity label needs a detection pattern behind it, and because the built-in rules cannot be edited you first create a custom sensitive information type.

option_rationales.A: Creating a custom sensitive information type gives the label something to match on, and is the documented first step.
option_rationales.B: Elevating access lets a Global Administrator manage all Azure subscriptions — nothing to do with labels.
option_rationales.C: The Security Center pricing tier enables workload protection features, not labelling.
option_rationales.D: The Defender for Cloud Apps integration shares alerts and app discovery data.

verification.note: Community 100% A. Labels and sensitive information types now live in Microsoft Purview Information Protection.

answer_summary: Where a blueprint is saved determines who can see it, but assignment scope is always a subscription — so both blueprints can only be assigned to Subscription1.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the Azure Log Analytics workspaces shown in the following table.

| Name | Location | Description |
|------|----------|-------------|
| Workspace1 | East US | Used by Azure Sentinel |
| Workspace2 | West US | Not applicable |

You create the virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Location | Operating system | Connected to |
|------|----------|------------------|-------------|
| VM1 | East US | Windows Server 2019 | None |
| VM2 | East US | Windows Server 2019 | Workspace2 |
| VM3 | West US | Windows Server 2019 | None |
| VM4 | West US | Windows Server 2019 | Workspace2 |

You plan to use Azure Sentinel to monitor Windows Defender Firewall on the virtual machines.
Which virtual machines you can connect to Azure Sentinel?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/connect-windows-firewall
answer_summary: Sentinel collects from any machine whose agent reports to its workspace, regardless of region — and a Windows agent can report to several workspaces at once, so the VMs already attached to Workspace2 can be added too.

option_rationales.A: There is no restriction limiting you to unconnected VMs.
option_rationales.B: VM2 and VM4 can also be connected: the Windows agent supports multi-homing to several workspaces.
option_rationales.C: All four VMs can be connected to Workspace1 and monitored by Sentinel; workspace region does not have to match the VM region.
option_rationales.D: VM3 and VM4 in West US are equally eligible.

verification.note: Community 100% C. Multi-homing was a Windows-agent capability of the legacy MMA; with the Azure Monitor Agent a machine can be associated with multiple data collection rules and workspaces, so the conclusion still holds.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription that contains a user named Admin1 and a resource group named RG1.
In Azure Monitor, you create the alert rules shown in the following table.

| Name | Resource | Condition |
|------|----------|----------|
| Rule1 | RG1 | All security operations |
| Rule2 | RG1 | All administrative operations |
| Rule3 | Azure subscription | All security operations by Admin1 |
| Rule4 | Azure subscription | All administrative operations by Admin1 |

Admin1 performs the following actions on RG1:
=> Adds a virtual network named VNET1
=> Adds a Delete lock named Lock1

Which rules will trigger an alert as a result of the actions of Admin1? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
answer_summary: Both actions are administrative operations in the activity log (creating a virtual network and creating a lock), and neither is a security operation — so the two administrative rules fire in each case, one scoped to RG1 and one to the subscription filtered by Admin1.

slot_rationales.Adding VNET1: Rule2 and Rule4 only. Creating a virtual network is logged as an administrative operation; Rule2 covers administrative operations on RG1 and Rule4 covers Admin1's administrative operations across the subscription. The security-operation rules (Rule1, Rule3) do not match.
slot_rationales.Adding Lock1: Rule2 and Rule4 only. Creating a management lock is also an administrative operation (Microsoft.Authorization/locks/write), not a security operation, so the same two rules fire.

verification.note: Still accurate: 'Security' in activity log alerts refers to Microsoft.Security operations (Defender for Cloud alerts and settings), which is why neither action triggers Rule1 or Rule3.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains 100 virtual machines and has Azure Defender enabled.
You plan to perform a vulnerability scan of each virtual machine.
You need to deploy the vulnerability scanner extension to the virtual machines by using an Azure Resource Manager template.
Which two values should you specify in the code to automate the deployment of the extension to the virtual machines? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.C: the Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) ID
options.D: the Key Vault managed storage account key

answer_summary: The stored key pairs the identity the extension runs as with the tenant/Entra identifier it authenticates against — the two values the template must carry so the scanner can enrol each VM automatically.

option_rationales.A: The stored answer takes the user-assigned managed identity as the identity to attach for the scanner's enrolment.
option_rationales.B: A workspace ID is what agent extensions that report to Log Analytics need; several sources argue this pairing (with a system-assigned identity) instead — see the note.
option_rationales.C: The Entra (Azure AD) tenant ID is the second stored value, identifying the directory the identity belongs to.
option_rationales.D: A Key Vault managed storage account key is unrelated to vulnerability scanning.
option_rationales.E: A system-assigned managed identity is the alternative identity choice in the competing answer.
option_rationales.F: The primary shared key belongs to storage accounts and workspaces, not to the scanner extension.

verification.note: Community is split exactly 50/50 between AC and BE, and this bank supplies no explanation, so the stored key has been left as AC rather than guessed at. It is also the most obsolete item in this section: the Qualys-based integrated vulnerability scanner was retired in 2024, and Defender for Servers now uses Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management, which needs no extension deployment at all.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains a user named Admin1 and a virtual machine named VM1. VM1 runs Windows Server 2019 and was deployed by using an Azure Resource Manager template. VM1 is the member of a backend pool of a public Azure Basic Load Balancer.
Admin1 reports that VM1 is listed as Unsupported on the Just in time VM access blade of Azure Security Center.
You need to ensure that Admin1 can enable just in time (JIT) VM access for VM1.
What should you do?

options.A: Create and configure a network security group (NSG).
options.B: Create and configure an additional public IP address for VM1.
options.C: Replace the Basic Load Balancer with an Azure Standard Load Balancer.
options.D: Assign an Azure Active Directory Premium Plan 1 license to Admin1.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security-center/security-center-just-in-time?tabs=jit-config-asc%2Cjit-request-asc
answer_summary: JIT works by editing NSG (or Azure Firewall) rules, so a VM with neither shows as Unsupported. Creating and associating an NSG with VM5's NIC or subnet is what makes JIT available.

option_rationales.A: Adding an NSG (at NIC or subnet level) gives JIT the rules it needs to manipulate, which clears the Unsupported state.
option_rationales.B: An additional public IP address does not change JIT support.
option_rationales.C: The load balancer SKU is a red herring here — the missing NSG is what makes the VM unsupported.
option_rationales.D: JIT is licensed through Defender for Servers, not through an Entra ID user licence.

verification.note: Community 100% A, and current documentation still lists 'VMs without an NSG or a supported Azure Firewall configuration' (and classic VMs) as the unsupported cases. JIT itself requires Defender for Servers Plan 2.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure Sentinel workspace that contains an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) connector, an Azure Log Analytics query named Query1, and a playbook named Playbook1.
Query1 returns a subset of security events generated by Azure AD.
You plan to create an Azure Sentinel analytic rule based on Query1 that will trigger Playbook1.
You need to ensure that you can add Playbook1 to the new rule.
What should you do? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/tutorial-detect-threats-custom https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/tutorial-respond-threats-playbook
answer_summary: Only a Scheduled analytics rule can be built from a saved KQL query, and the playbook has to be reachable by Sentinel — configured with a managed identity so the Logic App can be triggered and can act with granted permissions.

slot_rationales.Create the rule and set the type to: Scheduled — this is the rule type that runs a KQL query on a schedule; Microsoft security / Fusion / anomaly rule types cannot use your own query.
slot_rationales.Configure the playbook to include: A system-assigned managed identity, so the playbook has an identity Sentinel can authorize (the Logic App must also use the Microsoft Sentinel alert/incident trigger to appear in the rule's automated response list).

verification.note: Rule type is unambiguous. On the second box, the practical requirement is that the Logic App starts with a Microsoft Sentinel trigger and that the connection is authorized — managed identity is now Microsoft's recommended way to do that, replacing a shared API connection.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.

| Name | Type | Attached to | NSG |
|------|------|-------------|-----|
| NSG1 | Network security group (NSG) | VM5 | Not applicable |
| NSG2 | Network security group (NSG) | Subnet1 | Not applicable |
| Subnet1 | Subnet | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| VM5 | Virtual machine | Subnet1 | NSG1 |

An IP address of 10.1.0.4 is assigned to VM5. VM5 does not have a public IP address.
VM5 has just in time (JIT) VM access configured as shown in the following exhibit.

JIT VM access configuration
VM5
+ Add | Save | X Discard

Configure the ports for which the just-in-time VM access will be applicable

| Port | Protocol | Allowed source IPs | IP range | Time range (hours) |
|------|----------|-------------------|----------|--------------------|
| 3389 | Any | Per request | N/A | 3 hours | ... |

You enable JIT VM access for VM5.
NSG1 has the inbound rules shown in the following exhibit.

| Priority | Name | Port | Protocol | Source | Destination | Action |
|----------|------|------|----------|--------|-------------|--------|
| 100 | ⚠ SecurityCenter-JITRule-... | 3389 | Any | Any | 10.1.0.4 | ⊙ Allow |
| 1000 | SecurityCenter-JITRule_341... | 3389 | Any | Any | 10.1.0.4 | ⊗ Deny |
| 1001 | RDP | 3389 | TCP | Any | Any | ⊙ Allow |
| 65000 | AllowVnetInBound | Any | Any | VirtualNetwork | VirtualNetwork | ⊙ Allow |
| 65001 | AllowAzureLoadBalancerIn... | Any | Any | AzureLoadBalancer | Any | ⊙ Allow |
| 65500 | DenyAllInBound | Any | Any | Any | Any | ⊗ Deny |

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: Deleting the security rule that has a priority of 100 will revoke the approved JIT access request.
hotspot_rows.rationale: The priority-100 SecurityCenter-JITRule entry is the rule Defender for Cloud created when the request was approved; removing it takes the approved access away immediately.

hotspot_rows.statement: Remote Desktop access to VM5 is blocked.
hotspot_rows.rationale: VM5 has only the private address 10.1.0.4 and no public IP, so Remote Desktop from outside the virtual network cannot reach it whatever the NSG rules say.

hotspot_rows.statement: An Azure Bastion host will enable Remote Desktop access to VM5 from the internet.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Marked No by the exam key — see the note, because a Bastion host is precisely the service designed to reach private-only VMs.

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure Portal screenshot showing JIT VM access configuration interface with port settings and NSG1 inbound security rules table.

answer_summary: The JIT allow rule at priority 100 is the approved request itself, so deleting it withdraws the access. VM5 has no public IP address, so there is no path for Remote Desktop from the internet in the first place.

verification.note: Rows 1 and 2 are sound. Row 3 is questionable: Azure Bastion exists to give RDP/SSH access to VMs that have no public IP, and with the priority-100 allow rule in place it would work (the requirements being a Bastion host in the VNet, an AzureBastionSubnet, and NSG rules permitting 3389 from that subnet). The key only holds if you assume the JIT deny rule at priority 1000 is in effect because no request is approved.

question_stem:
You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant and a root management group.
You create 10 Azure subscriptions and add the subscriptions to the root management group.
You need to create an Azure Blueprints definition that will be stored in the root management group.
What should you do first?

options.A: Modify the role-based access control (RBAC) role assignments for the root management group.
options.B: Add an Azure Policy definition to the root management group.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/elevate-access-global-admin
answer_summary: A Global Administrator has no Azure resource permissions by default, so before a blueprint can be saved at the root management group you must give yourself rights there — elevate access and take a role assignment on the root group.

option_rationales.A: Creating a blueprint definition at the root management group needs Microsoft.Blueprint write permission at that scope, so the role assignments (via elevate access, then Owner/Contributor on the root group) must be fixed first.
option_rationales.B: Adding a policy definition does not grant you the permission the blueprint needs.
option_rationales.C: A user-assigned identity is unrelated to authoring a blueprint (blueprint assignments can use one, but that comes later).
option_rationales.D: A service principal is not required to create a definition.

verification.note: Community 100% A. The elevate-access mechanism for Global Administrators is unchanged; Azure Blueprints itself is deprecated in favour of Template Specs and deployment stacks.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com that contains the users shown in the following table.

| Name | Role |
|------|------|
| Admin1 | Global administrator |
| Admin2 | Group administrator |
| Admin3 | User administrator |

Contoso.com contains a group naming policy. The policy has a custom blocked word list rule that includes the word Contoso.
Which users can create a group named Contoso Sales in contoso.com? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/enterprise-users/groups-naming-policy

The naming policy (prefix/suffix and blocked words) governs Microsoft 365 groups only, so a security group named Contoso Sales is unaffected — and Global administrator, Group administrator and User administrator can all create groups.
slot_rationales.Users who can create a Microsoft 365 gro: Admin1 and Admin3 only. The blocked-word rule applies here, and the exempt roles are Global Administrator, User Administrator, Partner Tier 1/2 Support and Directory Writers — Group administrator is not on that list.

You have five Azure subscriptions linked to a single Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant.
You create an Azure Policy initiative named SecurityPolicyInitiative1.
You identify which standard role assignments must be configured on all new resource groups.
You need to enforce SecurityPolicyInitiative1 and the role assignments when a new resource group is created.
Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
Select and Place:
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/blueprints/create-blueprint-portal https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-australia/azure-policy

diagrams.diagram_description: Drag-drop answer area showing available actions (Publish an Azure Blueprints version, Assign an Azure blueprint, Create a policy assignment, Create a custom role-based access control (RBAC) role, Create a dedicated management subscription, Create an Azure Blueprints definition, Create an initiative assignment) on the left and three target slots on the right.

question_stem:
You have three on-premises servers named Server1, Server2, and Server3 that run Windows Server 2019. Server1 and Server2 are located on the internal network. Server3 is located on the perimeter network. All servers have access to Azure.
From Azure Sentinel, you install a Windows firewall data connector.
You need to collect Microsoft Defender Firewall data from the servers for Azure Sentinel.
What should you do?

options.A: Create an event subscription from Server1, Server2, and Server3.
options.B: Install the On-premises data gateway on each server.
options.C: Install the Microsoft Monitoring Agent on each server.
options.D: Install the Microsoft Monitoring Agent on Server1 and Server2. Install the On-premises data gateway on Server3.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/connect-windows-firewall
answer_summary: Sentinel's Windows firewall connector reads the firewall event log through the Log Analytics agent, so the agent must be installed on each server — including the one in the perimeter network, which only needs outbound access.

option_rationales.A: Event subscriptions (WEF) forward to a Windows collector, which is not how this connector ingests data.
option_rationales.B: The on-premises data gateway proxies data for services such as Power BI and Logic Apps; it does not collect firewall logs.
option_rationales.C: Installing the agent on all three servers connects them to the workspace so the firewall data connector can collect their logs.
option_rationales.D: There is no need to treat Server3 differently — the agent works from a perimeter network as long as outbound HTTPS to Azure is allowed.

verification.note: Community 100% C. Currency: the Log Analytics agent is retired — on-premises servers are now onboarded with Azure Arc and the Azure Monitor Agent, and the connector is configured through a data collection rule.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains several Azure SQL databases and an Azure Sentinel workspace.
You need to create a saved query in the workspace to find events reported by Azure Defender for SQL.
What should you do?

options.A: From Azure CLI, run the Get-AzOperationalInsightsWorkspace cmdlet.
options.B: From the Azure SQL Database query editor, create a Transact-SQL query.
options.C: From the Azure Sentinel workspace, create a Kusto query language query.
options.D: From Microsoft SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS), create a Transact-SQL query.

answer_summary: Defender for SQL alerts are ingested into the Sentinel workspace, so you write a KQL query there and save it — SQL query tools cannot see workspace data.

option_rationales.A: That cmdlet returns workspace metadata, and it is PowerShell rather than a saved query.
option_rationales.B: T-SQL runs against the database itself and cannot query security alerts in Log Analytics.
option_rationales.C: A KQL query in the Sentinel workspace (saved as a query or hunting query) is what finds the Defender for SQL events.
option_rationales.D: SSMS is again a SQL client, not a log analytics tool.

verification.note: Community 100% C. Defender for SQL alerts land in the SecurityAlert table, and saved searches/hunting queries are still authored in KQL.

question_stem:

Which components are required for the rule? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

explanation:

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/tutorial-detect-threats-custom https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/tutorial-respond-threats-playbook
answer_summary: An analytics rule detects with a KQL query and responds with a playbook — the query defines the threat logic, and the playbook (a Logic App) performs the automation.

slot_rationales.Detect suspicious threats: A KQL query — a scheduled analytics rule runs the query on a cadence and raises alerts/incidents from its results.
slot_rationales.Automate responses: A playbook — the Logic App triggered by the alert or incident that carries out the response actions.

question_stem:
You are collecting events from Azure virtual machines to an Azure Log Analytics workspace.
You plan to create alerts based on the collected events.
You need to identify which Azure services can be used to create the alerts.
Which two services should you identify? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
answer_summary: Both Azure Monitor (log search alert rules) and Microsoft Sentinel (analytics rules) can raise alerts from data in a Log Analytics workspace; the other services do not alert on workspace queries.

option_rationales.A: Azure Monitor creates log search alert rules directly against the workspace data.
option_rationales.B: Defender for Cloud generates its own security alerts and recommendations but is not a general tool for alerting on your collected events.
option_rationales.C: Analysis Services is a BI modelling engine.
option_rationales.D: Microsoft Sentinel's scheduled analytics rules run KQL over the same workspace and raise alerts and incidents.
option_rationales.E: Advisor issues best-practice recommendations, not alerts on log data.

verification.note: Community 100% AD. Unchanged, though Sentinel is now Microsoft Sentinel and can also run on a Defender XDR-integrated workspace.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You suspect that users are attempting to sign in to resources to which they have no access.
You need to create an Azure Log Analytics query to identify failed user sign-in attempts from the last three days. The results must only show users who had more than five failed sign-in attempts.
How should you configure the query? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

```
let timeframe = 3d;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(3d)
| where AcccountType == 'User' and [dropdown: ActivityID, DataType, EventID, QuantityUnit] == 4625
| summarize failed_login_attempts= [dropdown: Count(), Countif(), Makeset(), Split()]
latest_failed_login=arg_max(TimeGenerated, Account) by Account
| where failed_login_attempts > 5
```
explanation:
The following example identifies user accounts that failed to log in more than five times in the last day, and when they last attempted to log in.
let timeframe = 1d;

SecurityEvent -
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where AccountType == 'User' and EventID == 4625 // 4625 - failed log in
| summarize failed_login_attempts=count(), latest_failed_login=arg_max(TimeGenerated, Account) by Account
| where failed_login_attempts > 5
answer_summary: Windows failed logons are event 4625, so the filter is on EventID, and the threshold test needs a plain count() in the summarize that a later where clause compares against five.

slot_rationales.| where AcccountType == 'User' and [drop: EventID — 4625 is the Windows security event for a failed logon; ActivityID and DataType are not fields that carry it.
slot_rationales.| summarize failed_login_attempts= [drop: Count() — aggregate the failures per account, then filter with 'where failed_login_attempts > 5'. countif() takes a predicate and is not what the threshold needs here.

verification.note: Matches Microsoft's sample query. Note that events must be collected into the SecurityEvent table (via a data collection rule with the Azure Monitor Agent today) for the query to return anything.

question_stem:

options.D: Create an Azure Log Analytics workspace.

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security-center/security-center-custom-alert
answer_summary: Custom alert rules were a paid-tier feature stored against a workspace, so two things are needed: a Log Analytics workspace to hold the rule and its data, and the Security Center pricing tier upgraded from Free to Standard.

option_rationales.A: Identity Protection is unrelated to Security Center alert rules.
option_rationales.B: No storage account is required for custom alert rules.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that contains an Azure Log Analytics workspace named LAW1.
You have 100 on-premises servers that run Windows Server 2012 R2 and Windows Server 2016. The servers connect to LAW1. LAW1 is configured to collect security-related performance counters from the connected servers.
You need to configure alerts based on the data collected by LAW1. The solution must meet the following requirements:
⇒ Alert rules must support dimensions.
⇒ The time it takes to generate an alert must be minimized.
⇒ Alert notifications must be generated only once when the alert is generated and once when the alert is resolved.
Which signal type should you use when you create the alert rules?
explanation:
Metric alerts in Azure Monitor provide a way to get notified when one of your metrics cross a threshold. Metric alerts work on a range of multi-dimensional platform metrics, custom metrics, Application Insights standard and custom metrics.
Note: Signals are emitted by the target resource and can be of several types. Metric, Activity log, Application Insights, and Log.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/platform/alerts-metric
answer_summary: Metric alerts are the only signal type that supports dimensions, evaluates in near real time, and is stateful — firing one notification when the condition is met and one when it resolves.

option_rationales.A: Log alerts run a query on a schedule, so detection is slower and (at the time) they did not resolve automatically.
option_rationales.B: Log (Saved Query) has the same latency characteristics and is just a saved search variant.
option_rationales.C: Metric alerts support multi-dimensional metrics, minute-level evaluation and automatic resolution notifications.
option_rationales.D: Activity log alerts watch control-plane operations, not collected performance counters.

verification.note: Community 100% C. Log search alerts have since gained dimensions and auto-mitigation, but metric alerts remain the fastest and are still the intended answer here.

dragdrop_slots.Assignment remediation task: A managed identity that has the Contributor role

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/policy/how-to/remediate-resources
answer_summary: Installing something that is missing means the DeployIfNotExists effect, and the remediation task runs as the assignment's managed identity — which must hold a role strong enough to deploy the extension (Contributor here).

Hot Area:

dragdrop_slots.Prevent the modification of permissions: A role-based access control (RBAC) role assignment at the resource group level

answer_summary: Applying the same Owner assignment to RG1 in twenty subscriptions consistently is a Blueprints job (a role-assignment artifact), and stopping anyone from changing those permissions afterwards needs blueprint resource locking, which is enforced through a deny assignment.

slot_rationales.Configure role-based access control (RBA: Azure Blueprints — a role-assignment artifact in a blueprint assigned to each subscription creates the Owner assignment for Group1 on RG1 identically everywhere, and re-applies it if it is removed.
slot_rationales.Prevent the modification of permissions: Stored as an RBAC role assignment at the resource group level — but see the note: an assignment grants access, it cannot prevent changes. Blueprint resource locking (a deny assignment) is what blocks modification.

verification.note: First box corrected from 'Azure Security Center', which has no ability to create role assignments at all. The second box is left as stored because the original option list is not preserved in this bank, but treat it with suspicion: preventing modification of permissions requires a deny assignment — created by blueprint resource locking, or today by a deployment stack with deny settings. Azure Blueprints itself is deprecated.

question_stem:

You have an Azure subscription that contains 100 virtual machines. Azure Diagnostics is enabled on all the virtual machines.

=> Query the security events of a virtual machine that runs Windows Server 2016.
What should you use in Azure Monitor? To answer, drag the appropriate configuration settings to the correct details. Each configuration setting may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Select and Place:
explanation:
Box1: Activity log -
Azure activity logs provide insight into the operations that were performed on resources in your subscription. Activity logs were previously known as »Audit logs« or »Operational logs,« because they report control-plane events for your subscriptions.
Activity logs help you determine the »what, who, and when« for write operations (that is, PUT, POST, or DELETE).

Box 2: Logs -
Log Integration collects Azure diagnostics from your Windows virtual machines, Azure activity logs, Azure Security Center alerts, and Azure resource provider logs. This integration provides a unified dashboard for all your assets, whether they're on-premises or in the cloud, so that you can aggregate, correlate, analyze, and alert for security events.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/azure-log-audit

slot_rationales.Query the security events of a virtual m: Logs — the collected SecurityEvent/Event records live in a Log Analytics workspace and are queried there with KQL.

question_stem:

|------|------|----------------|
| RG1 | Resource group | Not applicable |
| VM1 | Virtual machine | RG1 |
| VM2 | Virtual machine | RG1 |
| ActionGroup1 | Action group | RG1 |

VM1 and VM2 are stopped.
You create an alert rule that has the following settings:
=> Resource: RG1
=> Condition: All Administrative operations
=> Actions: Action groups configured for this alert rule: ActionGroup1
=> Alert rule name: Alert1
You create an action rule that has the following settings:
=> Scope: VM1
=> Filter criteria: Resource Type = "Virtual Machines"
=> Define on this scope: Suppression
=> Suppression config: From now (always)
=> Name: ActionRule1
For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
Note: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: If you start VM1, an alert is triggered.
hotspot_rows.rationale: The action rule's scope is VM1 with suppression configured indefinitely, so the administrative operation of starting VM1 generates no notification.

hotspot_rows.statement: If you start VM2, an alert is triggered.
hotspot_rows.rationale: VM2 is outside the suppression rule's scope, so starting it is an administrative operation that triggers Alert1 and notifies ActionGroup1.

hotspot_rows.statement: If you add a tag to RG1, an alert is triggered.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Adding a tag is a write to the resource (Microsoft.Resources/tags/write), which the activity log categorises as Administrative — and RG1 is the alert rule's scope, so the alert fires.

explanation:
Box 1:
The scope for the action rule is set to VM1 and is set to suppress alerts indefinitely.
Box 2:
The scope for the action rule is not set to VM2.
Box 3:
Adding a tag is not an administrative operation.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/platform/alerts-activity-log https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/platform/alerts-action-rules
answer_summary: The action (alert processing) rule suppresses alerts only in its own scope — VM1 — so VM1's alerts are silenced while VM2's still fire. And tagging a resource group is an ARM write, which the activity log records under Administrative.

verification.note: Row 3 changed from No to Yes. The bank's explanation claims tagging is not an administrative operation, but every create/update/delete performed through Azure Resource Manager — including tag writes — is logged in the Administrative category of the activity log. Naming has also moved on: action rules are now called alert processing rules.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that contains the virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Resource group |
|------|----------------|
| VM1 | RG1 |
| VM2 | RG2 |
| VM3 | RG1 |
| VM4 | RG2 |

You need to ensure that the virtual machines in RG1 have the Remote Desktop port closed until an authorized user requests access.
What should you configure?

options.A: Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
options.C: Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) conditional access

explanation:
Just-in-time (JIT) virtual machine (VM) access can be used to lock down inbound traffic to your Azure VMs, reducing exposure to attacks while providing easy access to connect to VMs when needed.
Note: When just-in-time is enabled, Security Center locks down inbound traffic to your Azure VMs by creating an NSG rule. You select the ports on the VM to which inbound traffic will be locked down. These ports are controlled by the just-in-time solution.
When a user requests access to a VM, Security Center checks that the user has Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) permissions that permit them to successfully request access to a VM. If the request is approved, Security Center automatically configures the Network Security Groups (NSGs) and Azure Firewall to allow inbound traffic to the selected ports and requested source IP addresses or ranges, for the amount of time that was specified. After the time has expired, Security
Center restores the NSGs to their previous states. Those connections that are already established are not being interrupted, however.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security-center/security-center-just-in-time
answer_summary: Just-in-time VM access keeps the RDP port closed with an NSG deny rule and opens it only for an approved request, for a limited time and source — exactly the described requirement.

option_rationales.A: PIM makes directory/Azure role assignments time-bound; it does not open or close network ports.
option_rationales.B: An application security group is a grouping used inside NSG rules — it grants no request-and-approve workflow.
option_rationales.C: Conditional Access governs authentication to cloud apps, not RDP reachability.
option_rationales.D: JIT VM access blocks inbound RDP by default and adds a temporary allow rule when an authorized user requests access.

verification.note: Community 100% D. JIT still requires an NSG (or supported Azure Firewall) and Defender for Servers Plan 2, and the request can be approved per port, source IP and duration.

question_stem:
SIMULATION -
You need to ensure that the events in the NetworkSecurityGroupRuleCounter log of the VNET01-Subnet0-NSG network security group (NSG) are stored in the logs1234578 Azure Storage account for 30 days.
To complete this task, sign in to the Azure portal.
explanation:
You need to configure the diagnostic logging for the NetworkSecurityGroupRuleCounter log.
1. In the Azure portal, type Network Security Groups in the search box, select Network Security Groups from the search results then select VNET01-Subnet0-NSG. Alternatively, browse to Network Security Groups in the left navigation pane.
2. In the properties of the Network Security Group, click on Diagnostic Settings.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains a resource group named RG1 and a security group named ServerAdmins. RG1 contains 10 virtual machines, a virtual network named VNET1, and a network security group (NSG) named NSG1. ServerAdmins can access the virtual machines by using RDP.

What should you configure?

options.A: an Azure policy assigned to RG1
options.B: a just in time (JIT) VM access policy in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
options.C: an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Privileged Identity Management (PIM) role assignment
options.D: an Azure Bastion host on VNET1

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security-center/just-in-time-explained
answer_summary: Just-in-time VM access is the feature that keeps RDP denied in the NSG and opens it — for a requested duration such as 60 minutes, from a requested source — only when an authorized member asks.

option_rationales.A: Azure Policy governs configuration; it has no request-and-approve access workflow.
option_rationales.B: A JIT policy on the VMs sets the maximum request duration (for example one hour) and modifies NSG1's rules automatically for that window.
option_rationales.C: PIM makes role assignments time-bound but never touches the network path.
option_rationales.D: Bastion provides browser-based RDP without a public IP, but it does not time-box or gate access by request.

verification.note: Community 100% B. The maximum request window is configured per port in the JIT policy, and JIT needs Defender for Servers Plan 2.

question_stem:

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You are configuring just in time (JIT) VM access to a Windows Server 2019 Azure virtual machine.
You need to grant users PowerShell access to the virtual machine by using JIT VM access.
What should you configure? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
answer_summary: Requesting JIT access is a write operation on the VM, so users need Write permission on it, and PowerShell remoting over HTTPS uses WinRM on TCP 5986 — that is the port the JIT policy must expose.

slot_rationales.Permission that must be granted to users: Write — a JIT request modifies the NSG/firewall rules for that VM, so the requester needs write permission on the machine (plus the Microsoft.Security jitNetworkAccessPolicies initiate action).
slot_rationales.TCP port that must be allowed: 5986 — WinRM over HTTPS, the secure PowerShell remoting port. 5985 is the cleartext HTTP variant, 3389 is RDP and 22 is SSH.

verification.note: Unchanged. JIT's default policy covers 22, 3389, 5985 and 5986, and PowerShell remoting to Azure VMs would normally be done over 5986 or via Bastion/Arc.

question_stem:
You are troubleshooting a security issue for an Azure Storage account.
You enable the diagnostic logs for the storage account.
What should you use to retrieve the diagnostics logs?
explanation:
If you want to download the metrics for long-term storage or to analyze them locally, you must use a tool or write some code to read the tables. You must download the minute metrics for analysis. The tables do not appear if you list all the tables in your storage account, but you can access them directly by name.
Many storage-browsing tools are aware of these tables and enable you to view them directly (see Azure Storage Client Tools for a list of available tools).
Microsoft provides several graphical user interface (GUI) tools for working with the data in your Azure Storage account. All of the tools outlined in the following table are free.

| Azure Storage client tool | Supported platforms | Block Blob | Page Blob | Append Blob | Tables | Queues | Files |
|---------------------------|---------------------|------------|-----------|--------------|--------|--------|-------|
| Azure portal | Web | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Azure Storage Explorer | Windows, OSX | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Microsoft Visual Studio Cloud Explorer | Windows | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |

Note:
There are several versions of this question in the exam. The questions in the exam have two different correct answers:
1. Azure Storage Explorer
2. AZCopy
Other incorrect answer options you may see on the exam include the following:
1. Azure Monitor
2. The Security & Compliance admin center
3. Azure Cosmos DB explorer
4. Azure Monitor
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-analytics-metrics?toc=%2fazure%2fstorage%2fblobs%2ftoc.json
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-explorers

diagrams.diagram_description: Table showing Azure Storage client tools and their support for different blob types, tables, queues, and files across various platforms.

answer_summary: Classic diagnostic logs are blobs in the account's hidden $logs container, so a storage client is needed — Azure Storage Explorer can open that container and download them.

option_rationales.A: Storage Explorer can attach to the account and browse $logs, which is not visible in a normal container listing.
option_rationales.B: The SQL query editor works against SQL databases.
option_rationales.C: Windows File Explorer cannot browse blob containers (only mounted file shares).
option_rationales.D: Defender for Cloud surfaces security recommendations and alerts, not raw storage logs.

verification.note: Community 100% A. Currency: classic Storage Analytics logging is deprecated in favour of diagnostic settings to a workspace, where the data is queried with KQL.

question_stem:
You have an Azure Sentinel workspace.
You need to create a playbook.
Which two triggers will start the playbook? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.A: An Azure Sentinel scheduled query rule is executed.
options.B: An Azure Sentinel data connector is added.
options.C: An Azure Sentinel alert is generated.
options.D: An Azure Sentinel hunting query result is returned.
options.E: An Azure Sentinel incident is created.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/tutorial-respond-threats-playbook
answer_summary: A playbook is a Logic App started by a Sentinel trigger, and the two available at the time were the alert trigger and the incident trigger — data connectors, hunting queries and rule executions are not triggers.

option_rationales.A: A scheduled rule running is not itself a trigger; the alert or incident it produces is.
option_rationales.B: Adding a data connector is a configuration change, not an event a playbook can subscribe to.
option_rationales.C: The 'When a response to an Azure Sentinel alert is triggered' action starts a playbook from an alert.
option_rationales.D: Hunting query results are explored interactively or bookmarked; they do not start playbooks.
option_rationales.E: The incident trigger starts a playbook when an incident is created (or updated).

verification.note: Community 88% CE. Microsoft Sentinel has since added an entity trigger (run a playbook on a specific entity during investigation), so a current exam item could list three.

question_stem:
You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant that contains a user named User1.
You plan to enable passwordless authentication for the tenant.
You need to ensure that User1 can enable the combined registration experience. The solution must use the principle of least privilege.
Which role should you assign to User1?
explanation:
Authentication Administrator.
Users with this role can set or reset any authentication method (including passwords) for non-administrators and some roles. Authentication Administrators can require users who are non-administrators or assigned to some roles to re-register against existing non-password credentials (for example, MFA or FIDO), and can also revoke remember MFA on the device, which prompts for MFA on the next sign-in.
Note: Before combined registration, users registered authentication methods for Azure AD Multi-Factor Authentication and self-service password reset (SSPR) separately. People were confused that similar methods were used for Azure AD Multi-Factor Authentication and SSPR but they had to register for both features.
Now, with combined registration, users can register once and get the benefits of both Azure AD Multi-Factor Authentication and SSPR.
Azure Active Directory role enable the combined registration experience
Incorrect:
Privileged Role Administrator.
Users with this role can manage role assignments in Azure Active Directory, as well as within Azure AD Privileged Identity Management. They can create and manage groups that can be assigned to Azure AD roles. In addition, this role allows management of all aspects of Privileged Identity Management and administrative units.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/authentication/howto-registration-mfa-sspr-combined https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/roles/permissions-reference#privileged-role-administrator
answer_summary: Enabling the combined security-information registration experience is a tenant-wide setting, and turning tenant features on requires Global Administrator — Authentication administrator only manages individual users' methods.

option_rationales.A: Security administrator manages security features and policies but not this tenant user-feature setting.
option_rationales.B: Privileged role administrator manages role assignments and PIM.
option_rationales.C: Authentication administrator can reset or configure authentication methods for individual non-admin users, which is not the same as enabling the tenant feature.
option_rationales.D: Global Administrator can enable the combined registration experience for the tenant.

verification.note: Answer changed from C to D (community 100% D). Currency: combined registration has been generally available and enabled for all tenants for years, so the toggle this question refers to no longer exists; the modern equivalents are the Authentication methods policy and registration campaigns, managed by an Authentication Policy Administrator.

question_stem:
You are troubleshooting a security issue for an Azure Storage account.
You enable Azure Storage Analytics logs and archive it to a storage account.
What should you use to retrieve the diagnostics logs?
explanation:
One of the simplest ways to set/get an Azure Storage Blob's metadata is by using the cross-platform Microsoft Azure Storage Explorer, which is a standalone app from Microsoft that allows you to easily work with Azure Storage data on Windows, macOS and Linux.
Note: All logs are stored in block blobs in a container named $logs, which is automatically created when Storage Analytics is enabled for a storage account.
If you use your storage-browsing tool to navigate to the container directly, you will see all the blobs that contain your logging data. Most storage browsing tools enable you to view the metadata of blobs; you can also read this information using PowerShell or programmatically.
Reference:
https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/features/storage-explorer/
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-analytics-logging
answer_summary: Archived analytics logs are blobs in a storage account, so Azure Storage Explorer is the tool that can browse and download them.

option_rationales.A: Cosmos DB Explorer is for Cosmos data.
option_rationales.B: Azure Monitor reads data sent to a workspace, not blobs written by classic analytics logging.
option_rationales.C: Defender for Cloud shows alerts and recommendations.
option_rationales.D: Storage Explorer works cross-platform against the account, including the $logs container.

verification.note: Community 100% D.

question_stem:
You have the Azure resources shown in the following table.

| Name | Type | Parent |
|------|------|--------|
| Management1 | Management group | Tenant Root Group |
| Subscription1 | Subscription | Management1 |
| RG1 | Resource group | Subscription1 |
| RG2 | Resource group | Subscription1 |
| VM1 | Virtual machine | RG1 |
| VM2 | Virtual machine | RG2 |

You need to meet the following requirements:
=> Internet-facing virtual machines must be protected by using network security groups (NSGs).
=> All the virtual machines must have disk encryption enabled.
What is the minimum number of security policies that you should create in Microsoft Defender for Cloud?
explanation:
Azure Policy definition Internet-facing virtual machines should be protected with network security groups. We need a security for each of the VMs for Internet- facing protection.
Note: A network security group contains security rules that allow or deny inbound network traffic to, or outbound network traffic from, several types of Azure resources. For each rule, you can specify source and destination, port, and protocol.
We only need one security policy for disk encryption to apply on both for VM1 and VM2 (on all VMs).
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/qolilcy-reference https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/network-security-groups-overview

diagrams.diagram_description: Table showing Azure resource hierarchy with Management1 containing Subscription1, which contains RG1 and RG2, and VM1 and VM2 in their respective resource groups.

answer_summary: One policy per requirement is enough, because a single assignment at subscription (or management group) scope is inherited by both resource groups and both VMs — so two policies, not one per resource group.

option_rationales.A: One policy cannot express two unrelated requirements (NSG protection and disk encryption).
option_rationales.B: Two: 'Internet-facing virtual machines should be protected with network security groups' and a disk-encryption policy, each assigned once at a scope that covers both VMs.
option_rationales.C: Three assumes you need a separate assignment per resource group, which inheritance makes unnecessary.
option_rationales.D: Four is one per VM per requirement — far more than needed.

verification.note: Answer changed from C to B (community 100% B). Policy assignments are inherited down the hierarchy, so a single assignment at Subscription1 or Management1 covers RG1, RG2 and both VMs.

explanation:
Box 1: 4 -
A container can have up to 5 stored access policies.
Maximum number of stored access policies per blob container: 5
Box 2: 1 -
Blob version supports one version-level immutability policy and one legal hold. A policy on a blob version can override a default policy specified on the account or container.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/scalability-targets https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/immutable-storage-overview

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure Portal screenshot showing stored access policies and immutable blob storage configuration for a blob container.

answer_summary: A container supports five stored access policies (one exists, so four more) and one time-based retention policy — the only additional immutability policy you can add alongside it is a legal hold.

You create the Azure policy shown in the following exhibit.

**Assign policy**

**Basics Parameters Remediation Non-compliance messages Review + create**

**Basics**

|-------|-------|
| Scope | Azure Pass - Sponsorship/RG1 |
| Exclusions | Azure Pass - Sponsorship/RG1/NSG1 |
| Policy definition | Flow logs should be enabled for every network security group |
| Assignment name | Flow logs should be enabled for every network security group |
| Description | Description1 |
| Policy enforcement | Enabled |
| Assigned by | Admin1 |

**Parameters**

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| effect | Audit |

**Remediation**

| Field | Value |

| Managed identity location | westeurope |
| Create a remediation task | No |

**Non-compliance messages**

| Field | Value |

You assign the policy to RG1.

What will occur if you assign the policy to NSG1 and NSG2?

options.A: Flow logs will be enabled for NSG2 only.
options.B: Flow logs will be disabled for NSG1 and NSG2.
options.C: Flow logs will be enabled for NSG1 and NSG2.
options.D: Flow logs will be enabled for NSG1 only.

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure Portal screenshot showing Azure Policy assignment configuration with scope, exclusions, policy definition, remediation settings, and parameters.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT
-

You have a management group named MG1 that contains an Azure subscription and a resource group named RG1. RG1 contains a virtual machine named VM1.

You have the custom Azure roles shown in the following table.

| Name | Scoped to |
|------|----------|
| Role1 | MG1 |
| Role2 | RG1 |

The permissions for Role1 are shown in the following role definition file.

```json
"permissions": [
  {
    "Actions": [
      ...
    ],
    "notActions": [
      "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete"
    ],
    "dataActions": [],
    "notDataActions": []
  }
]
```

The permissions for Role2 are shown in the following role definition file.

```json
"permissions": [
  {
    "actions": [
      "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/*"
    ],
    "notActions": [],
    "dataActions": [],
    "notDataActions": []
  }
]
```

You assign the roles to the users shown in the following table.

| Name | Role |
|------|------|
| User1 | Role1 |
| User2 | Role1, Role2 |
| User3 | Role2 |

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

hotspot_rows.statement: User1 can delete VM1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: User1 has only Role1, whose notActions removes Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete, so the delete is not permitted anywhere in MG1.

hotspot_rows.statement: User2 can delete VM1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: User2 holds Role1 and Role2. Effective permissions are the union of assignments, and Role2 grants Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/* at RG1 with no notActions — so User2 can delete VM1.

hotspot_rows.statement: User3 can delete VM1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: User3 holds Role2 at RG1, which includes the delete action, so VM1 can be deleted.

answer_summary: NotActions subtracts only within its own role, and it is not a deny rule — so a user who also holds Role2 (which allows every virtual machine action at RG1) can delete VM1 even though Role1 withholds delete.

verification.note: Row 2 changed from No to Yes. Microsoft's RBAC documentation states plainly that NotActions is not a deny rule: if another role assignment grants the action, the user can perform it. Only deny assignments (as created by blueprint locks or deployment stacks) actually block.

question_stem:
You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant.

You need to prevent nonprivileged Azure AD users from creating service principles in Azure AD.

What should you do in the Azure Active Directory admin center of the tenant?

options.A: From the User settings blade, set Users can register applications to No.
options.B: From the Properties blade, set Access management for Azure resources to No.
options.C: From the User settings blade, set Restrict access to Azure AD administration portal to Yes.
options.D: From the Properties blade, set Enable Security defaults to Yes.

answer_summary: Registering an application is what creates a service principal, so setting 'Users can register applications' to No in User settings stops non-privileged users from creating them.

option_rationales.A: Turning off 'Users can register applications' removes the default ability for any member user to create app registrations (and their service principals).
option_rationales.B: 'Access management for Azure resources' governs a Global Administrator's elevate-access capability.
option_rationales.C: Restricting the administration portal only hides the portal — it does not block API or PowerShell-based app creation.
option_rationales.D: Security defaults enforce MFA baselines; they do not affect app registration.

verification.note: Community 100% A. The setting still exists (Microsoft Entra ID → Users → User settings), and the granular way to allow exceptions is the Application Developer role or a custom role with app-registration permissions.

| Vnet3 | West US | 10.3.0.0/16 | Vnet2 |

The subscription contains the subnets shown in the following table.

| Name | Virtual network | IP address range |
|------|----------------|------------------|
| Subnet1-1 | Vnet1 | 10.1.1.0/24 |
| Subnet1-2 | Vnet1 | 10.1.2.0/24 |
| AzureFirewallSubnet | Vnet1 | 10.1.3.0/24 |
| Subnet2-1 | Vnet2 | 10.2.1.0/24 |
| Subnet3-1 | Vnet3 | 10.3.1.0/24 |

The subscription contains the routes shown in the following table.

| Name | Subnet | IP address prefix | Next hop type | Next hop IP address |
|------|--------|-------------------|---------------|---------------------|
| Rt1 | Subnet1-1 | 0.0.0.0/0 | Virtual appliance | 10.1.3.4 |
| Rt2 | Subnet1-2 | 10.1.1.0/24 | Virtual appliance | 10.1.3.4 |
| Rt3 | Subnet2-1 | 10.1.1.0/24 | Virtual appliance | 10.1.3.4 |
| Rt4 | Subnet3-1 | 10.2.1.0/24 | Virtual appliance | 10.1.3.4 |

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

hotspot_rows.statement: Traffic from Subnet1-1 to Subnet 1-2 is routed through Fw1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Destination 10.1.2.0/24 is inside Vnet1's own address space, so the system route for 10.1.0.0/16 is a longer prefix match than Rt1's 0.0.0.0/0 — intra-VNet traffic bypasses the firewall (Rt2 only affects the return path from Subnet1-2, which makes the flow asymmetric).

hotspot_rows.statement: Traffic from Subnet2-1 to Subnet 1-1 is routed through Fw1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Rt3 sends 10.1.1.0/24 to 10.1.3.4, and that /24 is more specific than the 10.1.0.0/16 route learned from the Vnet1–Vnet2 peering, so traffic from Subnet2-1 is directed to Fw1.

hotspot_rows.statement: Traffic from Subnet3-1 to the internet is routed through Fw1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Rt4 only covers 10.2.1.0/24. Internet-bound traffic from Subnet3-1 matches the default system route (next hop Internet), so it never reaches the firewall — a 0.0.0.0/0 UDR would be needed.

diagrams.diagram_description: Tables showing Azure virtual networks, subnets, and route configurations with network address spaces, peering relationships, and next-hop virtual appliance settings.

answer_summary: Azure picks routes by longest prefix match, and a user-defined route only wins over a system route for the same prefix. So the /24 UDR on Subnet2-1 does divert traffic to the firewall, while the 0.0.0.0/0 UDR on Subnet1-1 loses to the VNet's own 10.1.0.0/16 system route, and Subnet3-1 has no default route to the firewall at all.

verification.note: All three rows changed after working through Azure's route-selection rules: routes are chosen by longest prefix match, and a UDR only takes precedence over a system or BGP route when the prefixes are identical. One caveat on row 2: Vnet2 is in East US while Fw1 is in UK West, so this crosses a global peering — the route still points at the firewall, but Azure Firewall is intended to serve spokes reachable in its own region and cross-region hairpinning of this kind is not a supported design.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains a managed identity named Identity1 and the Azure key vaults shown in the following table.

| Name | Permission model |
|------|------------------|
| KeyVault1 | Vault access policy |
| KeyVault2 | Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC) |

KeyVault1 contains an access policy that grants Identity1 the following key permissions:

• Get
• List
• Wrap
• Unwrap

You need to provide Identity1 with the same permissions for KeyVault2. The solution must use the principle of least privilege.

Which role should you assign to Identity1?

options.A: Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User

answer_summary: The access policy grants only Get, List, Wrap and Unwrap, and the RBAC role that matches exactly that set is Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User — Crypto Officer would add create, delete, backup, restore and purge.

option_rationales.A: Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User grants read on keys plus wrap and unwrap — precisely the four permissions, and nothing more.
option_rationales.B: Key Vault Crypto User also allows encrypt, decrypt, sign and verify, which the identity does not need.
option_rationales.C: Key Vault Reader can see key metadata but cannot wrap or unwrap.
option_rationales.D: Key Vault Crypto Officer allows any key operation including create, delete and purge — far beyond least privilege.

verification.note: Answer changed from D to A (community 73% A). Crypto Service Encryption User is the role Microsoft documents for service-side encryption with a customer-managed key, which is exactly the get/list/wrap/unwrap pattern the vault access policy expressed.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure SQL database named SQL1 and an Azure key vault named KeyVault1. KeyVault1 stores the keys shown in the following table.

| Name | Type | RSA key size | Elliptic curve name |
|------|------|--------------|---------------------|
| Key1 | RSA | 2048 | Not applicable |
| Key2 | RSA | 3072 | Not applicable |
| Key3 | RSA | 4096 | Not applicable |
| Key4 | EC | Not applicable | P-512 |

You need to configure Transparent Data Encryption (TDE). TDE will use a customer-managed key for SQL1.
Which keys can you use?
explanation:
The key must be an asymmetric, RSA or RSA HSM key. The supported key lengths are 2048-bit and 3072-bit.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/transparent-data-encryption-byok-overview
answer_summary: TDE with a customer-managed key requires an asymmetric RSA (or RSA-HSM) key of 2048 or 3072 bits — so Key1 and Key2 qualify, while the 4096-bit key and the elliptic-curve key do not.

option_rationales.A: Key1 (RSA 2048) is also supported, so limiting to Key2 is wrong.
option_rationales.B: Key2 (RSA 3072) is equally valid.
option_rationales.C: Key3 is 4096-bit, which was outside the supported sizes for this feature.
option_rationales.D: Key4 is an elliptic-curve key; TDE protectors must be RSA.
option_rationales.E: Key1 (2048) and Key2 (3072) are the supported RSA sizes.

verification.note: Community 100% E, and EC keys are still unsupported. Currency caveat: Microsoft's supported RSA key sizes for the TDE protector now include 4096-bit as well as 2048 and 3072, so on today's platform Key3 would also be usable — check the current docs before relying on the 2048/3072-only answer.

Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: You can recover Policy1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Access policies are configuration on the vault, not vault objects, so soft delete does not retain them — Policy1 cannot be recovered and must be recreated.

hotspot_rows.statement: You can add a new key named Item1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Item1 still exists in a soft-deleted state and its name stays reserved for the retention period, so a new key called Item1 cannot be created until the old one is recovered or purged.

hotspot_rows.statement: You can recover Item2.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Item2 is a secret protected by soft delete, so it can be recovered within the retention period (7–90 days).

explanation:
Box1: No -
Policies cannot be recovered.
Box2: Soft delete is enabled by default on all key vaults. You cannot add a new key named Item1 because an object named Item1 exists in a soft-deleted state.
Box3: Soft delete is now enabled by default on all key vaults so you can recover Item2.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/soft-delete-overview https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/soft-delete-change
answer_summary: Soft delete protects vault objects — keys, secrets and certificates — but not access policies, and a soft-deleted object keeps its name reserved until it is recovered or purged.

verification.note: Soft delete is now mandatory on all key vaults, which makes the name-reservation behaviour in row 2 a permanent characteristic; purge protection additionally prevents early purging.

question_stem:
You have an Azure SQL Database server named SQL1.
For SQL1, you turn on Azure Defender for SQL to detect all threat detection types.
Which action will Azure Defender for SQL detect as a threat?

options.A: A user updates more than 50 percent of the records in a table.
options.B: A user attempts to sign in as SELECT * FROM table1.
options.C: A user is added to the db_owner database role.
options.D: A user deletes more than 100 records from the same table.

explanation:
Advanced Threat Protection can detect potential SQL injections: This alert is triggered when an active exploit happens against an identified application vulnerability to SQL injection. This means the attacker is trying to inject malicious SQL statements using the vulnerable application code or stored procedures.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/azure-defender-for-sql
answer_summary: Defender for SQL looks for attack patterns, and a login name containing SQL syntax is a textbook injection attempt — bulk updates or deletes by a legitimate user are normal data operations, and role changes are audited rather than alerted.

option_rationales.A: Updating many rows is ordinary application behaviour, not a threat pattern.
option_rationales.B: Submitting 'SELECT * FROM table1' as a username is an injection attempt, which triggers a SQL injection alert.
option_rationales.C: Adding a user to db_owner is a privilege change you would find through auditing, not a Defender for SQL threat alert.
option_rationales.D: Deleting many records is again a data operation, not an attack signature.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Advanced Threat Protection is now Microsoft Defender for SQL, and the injection alerts (potential injection and vulnerability to injection) work the same way; unusual data-exfiltration volumes are covered by separate anomaly alerts.

2. The most sensitive label is applied.

Automatic classification applies to Word, Excel, and PowerPoint when documents are saved, and apply to Outlook when emails are sent.
Automatic classification does not apply to Microsoft Notepad.

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/information-protection/configure-policy-classification
answer_summary: When several automatic labels match, the label positioned last in the policy order wins, so a Word document matching both patterns gets Label2 — and a plain-text file gets nothing, because automatic classification only runs in the Office applications.

slot_rationales.If User1 creates a Microsoft Word file t: Label2 only — 'White' matches Label1's case-sensitive pattern and 'Black' matches Label2's case-insensitive pattern, and when multiple conditions apply the last label in the evaluation order is applied.

options.B: Add an app setting to the WebApp1 configuration.

options.D: Configure the TLS/SSL binding for WebApp1.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/configure-ssl-certificate-in-code
answer_summary: An uploaded certificate is only loaded into the app's certificate store when you tell App Service to do it — historically by adding the WEBSITE_LOAD_CERTIFICATES app setting with the certificate thumbprint (or *).
