Delegated permissions - Your client application needs to access the web API as the signed-in user, but with access limited by the selected permission. This type of permission can be granted by a user unless the permission requires administrator consent.
Incorrect Answers:
A, D: Application permissions - Your client application needs to access the web API directly as itself (no user context). This type of permission requires administrator consent and is also not available for public (desktop and mobile) client applications.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/develop/quickstart-configure-app-access-web-apis
answer_summary: Acting on behalf of the signed-in user means a delegated permission, and Key Vault's user_impersonation scope is not admin-restricted, so users can consent to it themselves.

option_rationales.A: An application permission acts as the app itself with no user context, which is not 'on behalf of the application users'.
option_rationales.B: A delegated permission gives the app the signed-in user's access to Key Vault, and no admin consent is required for it.
option_rationales.C: Requiring admin consent is unnecessary for this scope and is not what the question describes.
option_rationales.D: Application permissions always require admin consent and are the wrong permission type here.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Data-plane authorization in Key Vault is now normally granted with Azure RBAC roles to the calling identity, with the app requesting user_impersonation for on-behalf-of access.

question_stem:
DRAG DROP -
Your company has an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com.
The company is developing an application named App1. App1 will run as a service on server that runs Windows Server 2016. App1 will authenticate to contoso.com and access Microsoft Graph to read directory data.
You need to delegate the minimum required permissions to App1.
Which three actions should you perform in sequence from the Azure portal? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
Select and Place:
explanation:
Step 1: Create an app registration
First the application must be created/registered.
Step 2: Add an application permission
Application permissions are used by apps that run without a signed-in user present.
Step 3: Grant permissions -
Incorrect Answers:

Delegated permission -
Delegated permissions are used by apps that have a signed-in user present.
Application Proxy:
Azure Active Directory's Application Proxy provides secure remote access to on-premises web applications.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/develop/v2-permissions-and-consent

diagrams.diagram_description: Drag-drop interface showing available actions on the left (Grant permissions, Add a delegated permission, Configure Azure AD Application Proxy, Add an application permission, Create an app registration) and answer area on the right with up/down arrows for ordering.

answer_summary: A background service has no signed-in user, so it needs an app registration, an application (app-only) permission for the directory data it reads, and an administrator to grant consent.

slot_rationales.Step 1: Create an app registration so App1 has an identity (application object and service principal) in contoso.com.
slot_rationales.Step 2: Add an application permission — App1 runs as a service with no signed-in user, so delegated permissions would not work.
slot_rationales.Step 3: Grant permissions — application permissions always require administrator consent before they take effect.

verification.note: Sequence is unchanged. Best practice now is to use the least-privileged Graph permission (for example Directory.Read.All or a narrower scope) and to authenticate with a certificate or workload identity federation rather than a client secret.

question_stem:
Your company has an Azure subscription named Sub1 that is associated to an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com.
The company develops a mobile application named App1. App1 uses the OAuth 2 implicit grant type to acquire Azure AD access tokens.
You need to register App1 in Azure AD.
What information should you obtain from the developer to register the application?
explanation:
For Native Applications you need to provide a Redirect URI, which Azure AD will use to return token responses.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/develop/v1-protocols-oauth-code
answer_summary: Registration needs the redirect URI where Azure AD returns the token — everything else in the list is either issued by Azure AD or inapplicable to a public client.

option_rationales.A: The redirect URI is the value only the developer can supply, and the implicit grant returns the token to it.
option_rationales.B: 'Reply URL' is the older portal name for the same field, so the exam treats redirect URI as the current term.
option_rationales.C: A key (client secret) cannot be protected in a mobile app and is not used by a public client.
option_rationales.D: The application ID is generated by Azure AD when the app is registered.

verification.note: Community 100% A. Note the portal has standardized on 'Redirect URI' (reply URL was the v1 term). Currency: the implicit grant is deprecated — mobile apps should use the authorization code flow with PKCE.

question_stem:
From the Azure portal, you are configuring an Azure policy.
You plan to assign policies that use the DeployIfNotExist, AuditIfNotExist, Append, and Deny effects.
Which effect requires a managed identity for the assignment?
explanation:
When Azure Policy runs the template in the deployIfNotExists policy definition, it does so using a managed identity.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/bs-latn-ba/azure/governance/policy/how-to/remediate-resources
answer_summary: DeployIfNotExists performs a template deployment on your behalf, so the assignment needs a managed identity with permission to deploy — the other three effects only evaluate or block a request.

option_rationales.A: AuditIfNotExists only reports compliance and changes nothing.
option_rationales.B: Append adds fields to the request as it is submitted, using the caller's own rights.
option_rationales.C: DeployIfNotExists deploys resources during evaluation or remediation, which Policy performs as the assignment's managed identity.
option_rationales.D: Deny simply blocks a non-compliant request.

verification.note: Community 100% C. The Modify effect also requires a managed identity, but it is not among these options.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that is associated to an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named contoso.com.
You plan to implement an application that will consist of the resources shown in the following table.

| Name | Type | Description |
|------|------|-------------|
| CosmosDBAccount1 | Azure Cosmos DB account | A Cosmos DB account containing a database named CosmosDB1 that serves as a back-end tier of the application |
| WebApp1 | Azure web app | A web app configured to serve as the middle tier of the application |

Users will authenticate by using their Azure AD user account and access the Cosmos DB account by using resource tokens.
You need to identify which tasks will be implemented in CosmosDB1 and WebApp1.
Which task should you identify for each resource? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

dragdrop_slots.CosmosDB1: Create database users and generate resource tokens.
dragdrop_slots.WebApp1: Authenticate Azure AD users and relay resource tokens.

explanation:
CosmosDB1: Create database users and generate resource tokens.
Azure Cosmos DB resource tokens provide a safe mechanism for allowing clients to read, write, and delete specific resources in an Azure Cosmos DB account according to the granted permissions.
WebApp1: Authenticate Azure AD users and relay resource tokens
A typical approach to requesting, generating, and delivering resource tokens to a mobile application is to use a resource token broker. The following diagram shows a high-level overview of how the sample application uses a resource token broker to manage access to the document database data:

diagrams.diagram_description: Architecture diagram showing data flow between Xamarin.Forms App, Azure App Service (Easy Authentication, Resource Token Broker), Facebook (OAuth authentication flow), and Document Database, with numbered steps for login, fetching resource tokens, and accessing user data.

answer_summary: The resource-token pattern splits the work: the middle tier authenticates users with Entra ID and hands out tokens, and Cosmos DB holds the database users/permissions from which those resource tokens are generated.

slot_rationales.CosmosDB1: Create database users and generate resource tokens — resource tokens are produced from Cosmos DB permission resources attached to database users, and scope a client to specific data.
slot_rationales.WebApp1: Authenticate Entra ID users and relay resource tokens — the web app is the token broker, so the master key never leaves the middle tier.

verification.note: The resource-token broker pattern still exists, but current guidance favours Microsoft Entra ID authentication with Cosmos DB's data-plane RBAC, which removes the need for a broker in many designs.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You need to create an Azure key vault. The solution must ensure that any object deleted from the key vault be retained for 90 days.
How should you complete the command? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
Box 1: -EnablePurgeProtection -
If specified, protection against immediate deletion is enabled for this vault; requires soft delete to be enabled as well.

Box 2: -EnableSoftDelete -
Specifies that the soft-delete functionality is enabled for this key vault. When soft-delete is enabled, for a grace period, you can recover this key vault and its contents after it is deleted.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/azurerm.keyvault/new-azurermkeyvault
answer_summary: Retention for the full period needs both switches: soft delete keeps deleted objects recoverable, and purge protection stops anyone shortening that by purging them early.

slot_rationales.Parameter 1: -EnablePurgeProtection — blocks permanent deletion before the retention period elapses (and itself requires soft delete).
slot_rationales.Parameter 2: -EnableSoftDelete — retains deleted vaults and objects in a recoverable state for the configured retention period.

verification.note: Correct for the era of this question; soft delete is now always on for new vaults (so -EnableSoftDelete is obsolete), while purge protection remains an explicit and irreversible opt-in.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure key vault named Vault1.
In Vault1, you create a secret named Secret1.
An application developer registers an application in Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
You need to ensure that the application can use Secret1.
What should you do?

options.A: In Azure AD, create a role.
options.B: In Azure Key Vault, create a key.
options.C: In Azure Key Vault, create an access policy.
options.D: In Azure AD, enable Azure AD Application Proxy.

explanation:
Azure Key Vault provides a way to securely store credentials and other keys and secrets, but your code needs to authenticate to Key Vault to retrieve them.
Managed identities for Azure resources overview makes solving this problem simpler, by giving Azure services an automatically managed identity in Azure Active
Directory (Azure AD). You can use this identity to authenticate to any service that supports Azure AD authentication, including Key Vault, without having any credentials in your code.
Example: How a system-assigned managed identity works with an Azure VM
After the VM has an identity, use the service principal information to grant the VM access to Azure resources. To call Azure Resource Manager, use role-based access control (RBAC) in Azure AD to assign the appropriate role to the VM service principal. To call Key Vault, grant your code access to the specific secret or key in Key Vault.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/quick-create-net https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/managed-identities-azure-resources/overview
answer_summary: The application's service principal needs data-plane rights on the vault, which is granted by a Key Vault access policy giving it Get on secrets (or the equivalent RBAC role if the vault uses that model).

option_rationales.A: An Entra ID role grants directory permissions and nothing in the vault's data plane.
option_rationales.B: Creating a key does not authorize anyone to read Secret1.
option_rationales.C: An access policy for the app's service principal with the Get secret permission is what lets it retrieve Secret1.
option_rationales.D: Application Proxy publishes on-premises web apps; it is unrelated.

verification.note: Answer changed from A to C (community 94% C). If the vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model instead of access policies, the equivalent is assigning the Key Vault Secrets User role to the app's service principal.

question_stem:
You have an Azure SQL database.
You implement Always Encrypted.
You need to ensure that application developers can retrieve and decrypt data in the database.
Which two pieces of information should you provide to the developers? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
explanation:
Always Encrypted uses two types of keys: column encryption keys and column master keys. A column encryption key is used to encrypt data in an encrypted column. A column master key is a key-protecting key that encrypts one or more column encryption keys.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/encryption/always-encrypted-database-engine
answer_summary: Always Encrypted decrypts on the client, so the developers' driver needs the column encryption key and access to the column master key that protects it.

option_rationales.A: A stored access policy governs storage SAS tokens.
option_rationales.B: A SAS grants access to storage resources, not to database encryption keys.
option_rationales.C: The column encryption key encrypts and decrypts the column values.
option_rationales.D: User credentials authenticate to the database but decrypt nothing.
option_rationales.E: The column master key is the key-protecting key (in Key Vault or the certificate store) that wraps the CEK.

verification.note: Community 100% CE. In practice you grant the developers access to the CMK in Key Vault (unwrap/verify) rather than handing over key material, and the driver needs Always Encrypted enabled in its connection string.

question_stem:
You have a hybrid configuration of Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
All users have computers that run Windows 10 and are hybrid Azure AD joined.
You have an Azure SQL database that is configured to support Azure AD authentication.
Database developers must connect to the SQL database by using Microsoft SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) and authenticate by using their on-premises
Active Directory account.
You need to tell the developers which authentication method to use to connect to the SQL database from SSMS. The solution must minimize authentication prompts.
Which authentication method should you instruct the developers to use?

options.B: Active Directory – Universal with MFA support

explanation:
Azure AD can be the initial Azure AD managed domain. Azure AD can also be an on-premises Active Directory Domain Services that is federated with the Azure
AD.
Using an Azure AD identity to connect using SSMS or SSDT
The following procedures show you how to connect to a SQL database with an Azure AD identity using SQL Server Management Studio or SQL Server Database
Tools.
Active Directory integrated authentication
Use this method if you are logged in to Windows using your Azure Active Directory credentials from a federated domain.
1. Start Management Studio or Data Tools and in the Connect to Server (or Connect to Database Engine) dialog box, in the Authentication box, select Active
Directory - Integrated. No password is needed or can be entered because your existing credentials will be presented for the connection.
(The AD domain name or tenant ID‡ option is only supported for Universal with MFA connection options, otherwise it is greyed out.)
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/authentication-aad-configure?tabs=azure-powershell

diagrams.diagram_description: SQL Server Management Studio Connect to Server dialog showing Server type as Database Engine, Server name as tedus.database.windows.net, Authentication dropdown set to Active Directory - Integrated, and User name as DOMAIN\username, with Connect, Cancel, Help, and Options buttons.

answer_summary: On a hybrid-joined Windows 10 device, 'Active Directory – Integrated' reuses the existing Windows sign-in, so developers connect with their on-premises account and are not prompted.

option_rationales.A: A SQL login is a database-local credential, not their AD account.
option_rationales.B: Universal with MFA support deliberately adds an interactive challenge.
option_rationales.C: Integrated authentication passes the current Windows/Kerberos session through with no prompt.
option_rationales.D: Active Directory – Password requires typing credentials every time.

verification.note: Community 100% C. Current SSMS labels this 'Microsoft Entra Integrated'.

question_stem:
DRAG DROP -
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that contains an Azure Storage account named contosostorage1 and an Azure key vault named Contosekeyvault1.
You plan to create an Azure Automation runbook that will rotate the keys of contosostorage1 and store them in Contosekeyvault1.
You need to implement prerequisites to ensure that you can implement the runbook.
Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
Select and Place:

dragdrop_slots.Step 2: Import PowerShell modules to the Azure Automation account.
dragdrop_slots.Step 3: Create a connection resource in the Azure Automation account.

explanation:
Step 1: Create an Azure Automation account
Runbooks live within the Azure Automation account and can execute PowerShell scripts.
Step 2: Import PowerShell modules to the Azure Automation account
Under 'Assets' from the Azure Automation account Resources section select 'to add in Modules to the runbook. To execute key vault cmdlets in the runbook, we need to add AzureRM profile and AzureRM key vault.
Step 3: Create a connection resource in the Azure Automation account
You can use the sample code below, taken from the AzureAutomationTutorialScript example runbook, to authenticate using the Run As account to manage Resource Manager resources with your runbooks. The AzureRunAsConnection is a connection asset automatically created when we created 'run as accounts' above. This can be found under Assets -> Connections. After the authentication code, run the same code above to get all the keys from the vault.
$connectionName = "AzureRunAsConnection"
try
{
# Get the connection "AzureRunAsConnection"
$servicePrincipalConnection=Get-AutomationConnection -Name $connectionName
"Logging in to Azure..."
Add-AzureRmAccount `
-ServicePrincipal `
-TenantId $servicePrincipalConnection.TenantId `
-ApplicationId $servicePrincipalConnection.ApplicationId `
-CertificateThumbprint $servicePrincipalConnection.CertificateThumbprint
}
Reference:
https://www.rahulpnath.com/blog/accessing-azure-key-vault-from-azure-runbook/
answer_summary: Runbooks need somewhere to run, the cmdlets they call, and a way to authenticate — so create the Automation account, import the required PowerShell modules, then create the connection (identity) the runbook will use.

slot_rationales.Step 1: Create an Azure Automation account — the container that hosts the runbook and its assets.
slot_rationales.Step 2: Import the PowerShell modules (for example the Key Vault and Storage modules) so the runbook's cmdlets are available.
slot_rationales.Step 3: Create a connection resource so the runbook can authenticate to Azure and act on the storage account and vault.

verification.note: Sequence is right for the era. Currency: Automation Run As accounts (the classic connection asset) were retired on 30 September 2023 — runbooks now authenticate with the Automation account's managed identity, and Key Vault's own key rotation or storage account key rotation policies often remove the need for this runbook entirely.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure Storage account that contains a blob container named container1 and a client application named App1.
You need to enable App1 access to container1 by using Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) authentication.
What should you do? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
Reference:
https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/blog/announcing-the-preview-of-aad-authentication-for-storage/ https://github.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs/blob/master/articles/storage/common/storage-auth-aad-app.md
answer_summary: Entra ID authorization for blobs takes two steps in two places: the app needs an identity in the directory (register it), and it needs a data role on the storage account (assign it in Access control (IAM)).

slot_rationales.From Azure AD: Register App1 so it has a service principal that can request tokens for the storage resource.
slot_rationales.From the storage account: Configure Access control (IAM) to assign the app a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader/Contributor — control-plane roles like Reader do not grant data access.

verification.note: Still current, and the recommended hardening is to disable shared key authorization so only Entra ID identities can reach the data.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure key vault named ContosoKey1.
You create users and assign them roles as shown in the following table.

| Name | Subscription role assignment | ContosoKey1 role assignment |
|------|------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| User1 | Owner | None |
| User2 | Security Admin | None |
| User3 | None | User Access Administrator |
| User4 | None | Key Vault Contributor |

You need to identify which users can perform the following actions:
⇒ Delegate permissions for ContosoKey1.
⇒ Configure network access to ContosoKey1.
Which users should you identify? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/key-vault/general/rbac-guide
answer_summary: Delegating permissions needs Microsoft.Authorization write, which Owner and User Access Administrator have. Changing the vault's firewall is a write to the vault resource, which only Owner and Key Vault Contributor can do.

slot_rationales.Delegate permissions for ContosoKey1: User1 and User3 — Owner (inherited from the subscription) and User Access Administrator both include Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, which is what delegation means.
slot_rationales.Configure network access to ContosoKey1: User1 and User4 — configuring firewalls and virtual networks writes to the vault object (Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write), which Owner and Key Vault Contributor have. Security Admin only carries Microsoft.Security permissions, and User Access Administrator can manage access but not the vault's configuration.

verification.note: Second box changed from all four users. Neither Security Admin nor User Access Administrator carries Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write, so neither can change the vault's network settings — the same distinction this bank tests in Topic 3 Q162.
verification.answer_was: User1, User2, User3, and User4→User1 and User4 only

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains four Azure SQL managed instances.
You need to evaluate the vulnerability of the managed instances to SQL injection attacks.
What should you do first?

options.C: Add the SQL Health Check solution to Azure Monitor.
options.D: Create an Azure Advanced Threat Protection (ATP) instance.

explanation:
Community vote distribution
B (67%)
D (33%)
answer_summary: Vulnerability assessment (which is what flags SQL injection exposure) is part of the SQL security bundle, so you enable Advanced Data Security on the managed instances first.

option_rationales.A: A Sentinel workspace collects and correlates logs; it does not assess database vulnerabilities.
option_rationales.B: Advanced Data Security turns on vulnerability assessment and threat protection for the managed instances, which is the prerequisite for evaluating injection exposure.
option_rationales.C: A SQL Health Check solution reports on configuration health, not injection vulnerability.
option_rationales.D: Azure ATP (now Defender for Identity) monitors on-premises Active Directory.

verification.note: Community 67% B. Advanced Data Security has been renamed Microsoft Defender for SQL, which still bundles vulnerability assessment with the threat-protection alerts (including the SQL injection alerts).

question_stem:
DRAG DROP -
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1. Sub1 contains an Azure virtual machine named VM1 that runs Windows Server 2016.
You need to encrypt VM1 disks by using Azure Disk Encryption.
Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
Select and Place:

dragdrop_slots.Step 2: Configure access policies for the Azure key vault.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/encrypt-disks
answer_summary: Azure Disk Encryption needs a vault that the platform is allowed to use: create the key vault, enable the disk-encryption access policy on it, then run Set-AzVMDiskEncryptionExtension against VM1.

slot_rationales.Step 1: Create an Azure key vault in the same region and subscription as the VM.
slot_rationales.Step 2: Configure its access policies — specifically 'Enable access to Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption' — so the platform can store and retrieve the BitLocker/encryption secrets.
slot_rationales.Step 3: Run Set-AzVMDiskEncryptionExtension to install the extension and start encrypting VM1's disks.

verification.note: Sequence unchanged. Encryption at host and confidential-disk encryption are the newer alternatives to ADE for many VM sizes.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains a virtual machine named VM1.
You create an Azure key vault that has the following configurations:
⇒ Name: Vault5
⇒ Region: West US
⇒ Resource group: RG1
You need to use Vault5 to enable Azure Disk Encryption on VM1. The solution must support backing up VM1 by using Azure Backup.
Which key vault settings should you configure?
explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/key-vault-secure-your-key-vault
Community vote distribution
A (100%)
answer_summary: The vault's access policies carry the advanced settings — enabling Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption (and access for Azure Backup) — which is what lets both ADE and Backup work with Vault5.

option_rationales.A: Access policies is where 'Enable access to Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption' lives, plus the permissions Azure Backup needs to back up an encrypted VM.
option_rationales.B: Secrets holds the BitLocker/encryption secrets once created — you do not configure them by hand.
option_rationales.C: Keys would hold a KEK if you use one, but that is optional and not what enables the feature.
option_rationales.D: Locks protect the vault resource from deletion; they grant nothing.

verification.note: Community 100% A. Also worth remembering the vault must be in the same region and subscription as the VM, and that under the RBAC permission model these advanced policies are replaced by role assignments.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that contains the resources shown in the following table.

| Name | Type | Region | Resource group |
|------|------|--------|----------------|
| sa1 | Azure Storage account | East US | RG1 |
| VM1 | Azure virtual machine | East US | RG2 |
| KV1 | Azure key vault | East US 2 | RG1 |
| SQL1 | Azure SQL database | East US 2 | RG2 |

You need to ensure that you can provide VM1 with secure access to a database on SQL1 by using a contained database user.
What should you do?

options.A: Enable a managed identity on VM1.
options.C: Configure a service endpoint on SQL1.

explanation:
Community vote distribution
A (100%)
answer_summary: A contained database user mapped to an Azure identity means VM1 authenticates with a token, not a password — so enable a managed identity on VM1 and create the contained user FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER for it.

option_rationales.A: Enabling a managed identity gives VM1 an Entra ID identity that can obtain a token for SQL and be mapped to a contained database user — no secret anywhere.
option_rationales.B: A secret in the vault means storing a password, which is exactly what a contained database user with Entra authentication avoids.
option_rationales.C: A service endpoint controls network reachability, not authentication or the database user.
option_rationales.D: A key in the vault is for encryption scenarios, not database access.

verification.note: Answer changed from B to A (community 100% A). The bank's explanation field for this item had been overwritten with the vote distribution, leaving no reasoning behind the stored key.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that contains the Azure key vaults shown in the following table:

| Name | Region | Resource group |
|------|--------|----------------|
| Vault1 | West Europe | RG1 |
| Vault2 | East US | RG1 |
| Vault3 | West Europe | RG2 |
| Vault4 | East US | RG2 |

In Sub1, you create a virtual machine that has the following configurations:
⇒ Name: VM1
⇒ Size: DS2v2
⇒ Resource group: RG1
⇒ Region: West Europe
⇒ Operating system: Windows Server 2016
You plan to enable Azure Disk Encryption on VM1.
In which key vaults can you store the encryption key for VM1?
explanation:
In order to make sure the encryption secrets don't cross regional boundaries, Azure Disk Encryption needs the Key Vault and the VMs to be co-located in the same region. Create and use a Key Vault that is in the same region as the VM to be encrypted.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/azure-security-disk-encryption-prerequisites
Community vote distribution
A (100%)
answer_summary: Azure Disk Encryption keeps encryption material in the VM's own region, so the vault must be in the same region (and subscription) as the VM — West Europe here, which is Vault1 or Vault3. The resource group does not matter.

option_rationales.A: Vault1 and Vault3 are both in West Europe, matching VM1's region; being in RG1 or RG2 is irrelevant.
option_rationales.B: Vault2 and Vault4 are in East US, so encryption secrets would cross a regional boundary — not supported.
option_rationales.C: Vault3 is equally valid; the resource group is not a constraint.
option_rationales.D: Vault2 is in the wrong region.

verification.note: Community 100% A. The same-region and same-subscription requirement for ADE key vaults is unchanged.

hotspot_rows.statement: On January 1, 2019, User1 can view the value of Password1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: The secret's activation date is 1 March 2019, so on 1 January 2019 it is not yet usable by anyone, whatever their permissions.

hotspot_rows.statement: On June 1, 2019, User2 can view the value of Password1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Stored as Yes: by 1 June 2019 the secret is active and within its expiry, so a user with data-plane Get permission could read it.

hotspot_rows.statement: On June 1, 2019, Used can view the value of Password1.

Rows 2 and 3 are harder to defend as stored: Key Vault Contributor is a management-plane role that explicitly does not grant access to keys, secrets or certificates, so on a strict reading neither User1 nor User2 can view the value without an access policy or a data role such as Key Vault Secrets User — and Azure RBAC assignments are inherited through group membership, so the User1/User2 distinction does not follow from the roles described.

answer_summary: A WAF policy has to be attached to a WAF-capable front end. App Service cannot host one itself, so you deploy Azure Front Door (or Application Gateway) first and associate WAF1 with it.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/always-encrypted-azure-key-vault-configure?tabs=azure-powershell
answer_summary: Encrypting one column so that only a particular application can decrypt it is Always Encrypted with the column master key held in Azure Key Vault, where each app's managed identity is granted (or denied) access to that key.

You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure SQL database named DB1 in the East US Azure region.
You create the storage accounts shown in the following table.

| storage1 | East US | Standard | Not applicable |
| storage2 | East US | Premium | Block blobs |
| storage3 | East US | Premium | File shares |
| storage4 | East US 2 | Standard | Not applicable |

You plan to enable auditing for DB1.
Which storage accounts can you use as the auditing destination for DB1?
explanation:
To enable writing to a storage account, the one has to be configured first. Storage accounts are containers used to store Azure Storage objects, including blobs, files, tables, etc, for the auditing needs, general-purpose standard storage accounts will support storing audit data trail, to learn more about storage accounts.
Incorrect:
Not A, Not C: Use a storage account in the same region as the managed instance to avoid cross-region reads/writes.
Reference:
https://www.sqlshack.com/getting-started-with-azure-sql-database-auditing-using-blob-storage/ https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/managed-instance/auditing-configure
answer_summary: Auditing writes blobs into a storage account in the database's own region, which rules out storage4 (East US 2) — and a premium file-share account cannot hold blobs at all, so in practice the standard account is the dependable destination.

option_rationales.A: Storage4 is in East US 2, a different region from DB1.
option_rationales.B: Storage1 alone is the safest reading, but the community answer includes the premium block blob account as well.
option_rationales.C: Storage4's region rules out 'all of them'.
option_rationales.D: Storage1 (standard, same region) plus the premium accounts is the community's answer — the block blob account can hold audit blobs.
option_rationales.E: Excluding storage1 is clearly wrong: a standard general-purpose account in the same region is the classic supported destination.

verification.note: Answer changed from E to D (community 88% D), mainly because the stored key excluded the one unambiguously valid account. Be aware the option list itself is flawed: storage3 is a premium FileStorage account, which stores file shares only and therefore cannot receive blob audit logs, so no option is strictly correct. The reliable facts are that the destination must be in the same region as the database and must be able to store blobs.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure SQL Database logic server named SQL1 and an Azure virtual machine named VM1. VM1 uses a private IP address only.

The Firewall and virtual networks settings for SQL1 are shown in the following exhibit.

[Azure Portal screenshot showing Firewall settings: Deny public network access: No, Allow Azure services and resources to access this server: No, Client IP address: 89.212.25.106, Virtual networks section showing: Rule name, Virtual network, Subnet - No vnet rules for this server.]

You need to ensure that VM1 can connect to SQL1. The solution must use the principle of least privilege.

What should you do?

options.B: Set Allow Azure services and resources to access this server to Yes.

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure Portal screenshot showing SQL1 Firewall and virtual networks settings with public access allowed but no virtual networks or firewall rules configured.

answer_summary: VM1 has no public IP, so its outbound address is not something you can pin down in an IP firewall rule — the least-privilege, reliable fix is a virtual network rule for VM1's subnet (with the Microsoft.Sql service endpoint).

option_rationales.A: Connection policy (Proxy vs Redirect) affects how connections are routed through the gateway, not whether the firewall admits them.
option_rationales.B: 'Allow Azure services and resources to access this server' opens the server to every Azure resource — the opposite of least privilege.
option_rationales.C: Adding a virtual network rule for VM1's subnet grants access to exactly that subnet and works regardless of outbound public IP.
option_rationales.D: A firewall rule needs a public IP address; VM1 has only a private address, and its default outbound SNAT address is not stable or unique to it.

verification.note: Answer changed from D to C. The community is split exactly 46/46, but a VM with only a private IP has no dependable public source address to whitelist, whereas a virtual network rule scopes access precisely to that subnet. A private endpoint (with public network access disabled) would be the strongest modern option, and is not offered here.

You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant that contains a group named Group1.

You need to ensure that the members of Group1 sign in by using passwordless authentication.

What should you do?

options.C: Configure the Microsoft Authenticator authentication method policy.

answer_summary: Passwordless sign-in for a group is switched on in the authentication methods policy — enable the Microsoft Authenticator method (passwordless phone sign-in) and target Group1.

option_rationales.A: A sign-in risk policy responds to risk; it does not change how users authenticate.
option_rationales.B: Conditional Access can require a strength or method at sign-in, but the method itself must first be enabled in the authentication methods policy.
option_rationales.C: The Microsoft Authenticator authentication method policy is where passwordless phone sign-in is enabled and scoped to Group1.
option_rationales.D: Certificate-based authentication is a different passwordless option, but the question's mechanism (and the usual answer) is Authenticator.

verification.note: Community 100% C. In current Entra ID the authentication methods policy covers Authenticator, FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello for Business, passkeys and CBA, each targetable by group — and Conditional Access authentication strengths then require them.

|----------|----------------|
| storage1 | Storage account |
| KeyVault1 | Azure key vault |

You need to configure storage1 to regenerate keys automatically every 90 days.

Which cmdlet should you run?
answer_summary: Automatic key regeneration on a schedule is what Key Vault's managed storage account feature does: Add-AzKeyVaultManagedStorageAccount registers storage1 with the vault and takes a regeneration period (90 days).

option_rationales.A: Add-AzKeyVaultManagedStorageAccount registers the account with the vault and sets -RegenerationPeriod, so the vault rotates the keys automatically.
option_rationales.B: Set-AzStorageAccountManagementPolicy configures blob lifecycle management (tiering and deletion), not key rotation.
option_rationales.C: Set-AzStorageAccount changes account properties; it has no rotation schedule.
option_rationales.D: Add-AzStorageAccountManagementPolicyAction builds lifecycle rule actions.

verification.note: Community 67% A. Important currency caveat: Key Vault managed storage account keys are deprecated — Microsoft's guidance is to move to Microsoft Entra ID authorization for storage (or user-delegation SAS) rather than rotating and handing out account keys.

You have an Azure subscription that contains the key vaults shown in the following table.

| Name | Days to retain deleted vaults | Purge protection | Permission model |
|----------|-------------------------------|------------------|------------------|
| KeyVault1 | 10 | Enabled | Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC) |
| KeyVault2 | 15 | Disabled | Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC) |

The subscription contains the users shown in the following table.

| Name | Role | Assigned to |
|--------|---------------------------|------------|
| Admin1 | Key Vault Contributor | KeyVault1 |
| Admin2 | Key Vault Secrets Officer | KeyVault2 |
| Admin3 | Key Vault Administrator | KeyVault1 |

On June 1, you perform the following actions:

• Delete a key named key1 from KeyVault1.
• Delete a secret named secret1 from KeyVault2.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

hotspot_rows.statement: Admin1 can recover key1 on June 5.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Key Vault Contributor manages the vault but has no data-plane permissions, so Admin1 cannot recover a deleted key regardless of the date.

hotspot_rows.statement: Admin2 can purge secret1 on June 12.
hotspot_rows.rationale: By 12 June the secret is still inside KeyVault2's 15-day retention window, purge protection is disabled on that vault, and Key Vault Secrets Officer includes the purge permission — so the purge succeeds.

hotspot_rows.statement: Admin3 can recover key1 on June 17.
hotspot_rows.rationale: KeyVault1 retains deleted objects for only 10 days, so key1 was permanently removed after 11 June — by 17 June even a Key Vault Administrator has nothing left to recover.

diagrams.diagram_description: Hotspot answer area showing three statements with Yes/No radio buttons and the correct answers highlighted.

answer_summary: Two rules decide these: management-plane roles like Key Vault Contributor cannot touch objects, and a soft-deleted object only survives for the vault's retention period — 10 days for KeyVault1 (so key1 is gone after 11 June) and 15 days for KeyVault2.

verification.note: Rows 2 and 3 changed. Dates matter here: both objects were deleted on 1 June, so KeyVault1's 10-day retention expires on 11 June and KeyVault2's 15-day retention on 16 June. Key Vault Secrets Officer includes secrets/purge, and purge protection — which would have blocked the purge — is disabled on KeyVault2.

Users are assigned to the administrative units as shown in the following table.

| Admin3 | AU2 |

| User2 | AU1 |
| User3 | AU2 |

Users are assigned the roles shown in the following table.

| User | Administrative unit | Role |
|--------|---------------------|------------------------|
| Admin1 | AU1 | Helpdesk administrator |
| Admin2 | AU1 | Groups administrator |
| Admin3 | AU2 | Password administrator |
| Admin4 | AU2 | User administrator |

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point

hotspot_rows.statement: Admin1 can reset the password of User1.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Admin1 holds Helpdesk administrator scoped to AU1 and User1 is a non-admin member of AU1, so the password reset is permitted — this is the canonical use of administrative units.

hotspot_rows.statement: Admin2 can reset the password of User3.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Admin2's role is Groups administrator, which manages groups and grants no password-reset permission at all — and User3 is in AU2, outside Admin2's AU1 scope.

hotspot_rows.statement: Admin3 can reset the password of Admin4.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Password administrator can reset passwords only for non-administrators and a short list of limited roles; Admin4 holds User administrator, which is not on that list, so the reset is denied even though both are in AU2.

diagrams.diagram_description: Hotspot answer area showing three statements with Yes/No radio buttons and the correct answers highlighted.

answer_summary: An administrative unit scopes a role to its own members, and the role still has to include the permission: Helpdesk administrator can reset non-admin passwords inside AU1, Groups administrator cannot reset any password, and Password administrator cannot reset a User administrator's password.

verification.note: Rows 1 and 2 changed (they appear to have been transposed in the source). Both the role's permissions and the administrative-unit scope must line up: Helpdesk administrator includes password reset for non-admins, Groups administrator does not include it at all, and AU scoping restricts every AU-scoped role to that unit's members.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure key vault named Vault1 and a virtual machine named VM1. VM1 has the Key Vault VM extension installed.

For Vault1, you rotate the keys, secrets, and certificates.

What will be updated automatically on VM1?
answer_summary: The Key Vault VM extension exists to keep certificates on the machine in sync — it polls the vault and installs updated certificates, but it does not distribute keys or secrets.

option_rationales.A: Keys never leave the vault; the extension does not retrieve them.
option_rationales.B: Secrets are not synchronized by the extension (a secret backing a certificate is only handled as part of that certificate).
option_rationales.C: Certificates are polled on the configured interval and refreshed in the machine's certificate store, so rotation flows through automatically.
option_rationales.D: Keys are not included.
option_rationales.E: Secrets are not included.

verification.note: Community 100% C. The extension's pollingIntervalInS setting controls how quickly a rotated certificate is picked up, and the VM's managed identity needs get/list on certificates.

You have an Azure subscription that contains two users named User1 and User2 and the blob containers shown in the following table.

|-----------|-----------------|---------------|
| container1 | storage1 | Policy1 |
| container2 | storage1 | None |

Policy1 is configured as shown in the following exhibit.

[Azure Portal screenshot showing Edit policy dialog: Identifier: Policy1, Permissions: Read, Start time: 12/15/2021 12:00:00 AM, Expiry time: 12/31/2021 12:00:00 AM, Time zone: (UTC +01:00) Belgrade, Bratislava...]

You assign the roles for storage1 as shown in the following table.

|------|---------------------------|

| User2 | Contributor |

The storage1 account has the following shared access signature (SAS) named SAS1:

• Allowed services: Blob
• Allowed resource types: Container
• Allowed permissions: Read, Write, List, Add, Create
• Blob versioning permissions: enables deletion of versions
• Allowed blob index permissions: Read/Write

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

hotspot_rows.statement: When using SAS1, User1 can write to container2 on December 5, 2021.
hotspot_rows.rationale: 5 December is inside SAS1's validity window and the SAS grants Write at container resource-type level across the account, so the write to container2 succeeds regardless of User1's Storage Blob Data Reader role.

hotspot_rows.statement: When using SAS1, User2 can write to container1 on December 20, 2021.
hotspot_rows.rationale: Policy1 is a stored access policy on container1, but SAS1 is an account SAS that is not associated with it — so its own Write permission applies and 20 December is within the window.

question_stem:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.

| Name | Type |
|------|------|
| DB1 | Azure Cosmos DB account |
| VM1 | Virtual machine |
| VM2 | Virtual machine |
| VNET1 | Virtual network |
| NSG1 | Network security group (NSG) |

Both VM1 and VM2 connect to VNET1 and are configured to use NSG1.

You need to ensure that only VM1 and VM2 can access DB1.

What should you do?

options.A: For NSG1, configure a rule that has a service tag.
options.B: Add the IP address range of VNET1 to the Firewall settings of DB1.
options.D: Configure DB1 to allow access from only VNET1.

answer_summary: Restricting who can reach the database is done on the database's own firewall: configure DB1 to accept traffic only from VNET1 (a virtual network rule with the Microsoft.AzureCosmosDB service endpoint), which admits VM1 and VM2 and nothing else.

option_rationales.A: An NSG rule with a service tag controls what the VMs may send outbound; it does nothing to stop other clients reaching DB1.
option_rationales.B: Adding VNET1's private IP range to the Cosmos DB firewall does not work — private addresses are not what the account sees unless a service endpoint is in place, which is what option D describes.
option_rationales.C: An application security group is only a grouping used inside NSG rules.
option_rationales.D: Configuring DB1 to allow access from VNET1 only (virtual network rule plus service endpoint) is the control that limits access to those two VMs.

verification.note: Answer changed from A to D (community 53% D). The requirement is about who can reach DB1, which is enforced at the Cosmos DB account, not at the NSG. A private endpoint for DB1 would be the stronger modern equivalent.

question_stem:
You have an Azure AD tenant that contains a user named User1.

You purchase an app named App1.

User1 needs to publish App1 by using Azure AD Application Proxy.

Which role should you assign to User1?
answer_summary: Publishing an on-premises app through Application Proxy is an application-management task, and Application Administrator is the role that can create and configure Application Proxy applications (including on-premises connectors).

option_rationales.A: Cloud Application Administrator has the same app rights except Application Proxy — that exclusion is exactly what this question tests.
option_rationales.B: Application Administrator can manage all applications including Application Proxy publishing.
option_rationales.C: Hybrid Identity Administrator manages Entra Connect and hybrid sign-in, not app publishing.
option_rationales.D: Cloud App Security Administrator manages Defender for Cloud Apps.

verification.note: Community 100% B. Microsoft's role documentation still distinguishes the two: Cloud Application Administrator explicitly cannot manage Application Proxy.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT
-

You have a Microsoft Sentinel deployment.

You need to connect a third-party security solution to the deployment. The third-party solution will send Common Event Format (CEF)-formatted messages.

What should you include in the solution? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

dragdrop_slots.Deploy: A Linux server and a Syslog forwarder daemon

answer_summary: CEF messages arrive by syslog, so you need a Linux forwarder running rsyslog/syslog-ng, with the agent on that machine sending the parsed records to the workspace — the Azure Monitor Agent in the current design.

slot_rationales.Deploy: A Linux server running a syslog forwarder daemon that listens for the appliance's CEF messages.
slot_rationales.Forward events to Microsoft Sentinel by: The Azure Monitor Agent, configured by a data collection rule, which writes the messages into CommonSecurityLog.

verification.note: This is the up-to-date variant of the same question (the older copy in this bank answers 'Log Analytics agent', which retired in August 2024). The forwarder is normally Arc-enabled so AMA can be deployed to it.

question_stem:
Question
You need to meet the identity and access requirements for Group1.
What should you do?

options.A: Add a membership rule to Group1.
options.B: Delete Group1. Create a new group named Group1 that has a group type of Microsoft 365. Add users and devices to the group.
options.C: Modify the membership rule of Group1.
options.D: Change the membership type of Group1 to Assigned. Create two groups that have dynamic memberships. Add the new groups to Group1.

explanation:
When you create dynamic groups, they can either contain users or devices. Hence here we need to create two separate dynamic groups and assign those groups to an Assigned group.
Incorrect Answers:
A, C: You can create a dynamic group for devices or users, but you can't create a rule that contains both users and devices.
Scenario:
Litware identifies the following identity and access requirements: All San Francisco users and their devices must be members of Group1.
The tenant currently contains this group:

| Name | Type | Description |
|------|------|-------------|
| Group1 | Security group | A group that has the Dynamic User membership type, contains all the San Francisco users, and provides access to many Azure AD applications and Azure resources. |

Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/users-groups-roles/groups-dynamic-membership https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/fundamentals/active-directory-groups-create-azure-portal

Community vote distribution
D (100%)
answer_summary: A dynamic group's membership rule targets either users or devices, never both — so Group1 becomes an assigned group containing two dynamic groups, one for users and one for devices.

option_rationales.A: Adding a rule cannot make one dynamic group hold both users and devices.
option_rationales.B: A Microsoft 365 group cannot contain devices at all.
option_rationales.C: Modifying the rule hits the same limitation — one membership type per dynamic group.
option_rationales.D: Change Group1 to Assigned membership and nest two dynamic groups (one user, one device) inside it.

verification.note: Community 100% D. Dynamic membership is still either 'Dynamic User' or 'Dynamic Device', and nesting the two inside an assigned security group remains the workaround.

You need to recommend which virtual machines to use to host App1. The solution must meet the technical requirements for KeyVault1.

option_rationales.D: The stored key excludes VM3 as the one machine without a private route to the vault.

question_stem:
Question
You need to configure WebApp1 to meet the data and application requirements.
Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.B: Turn on the HTTPS Only protocol setting.
options.C: Set the Minimum TLS Version protocol setting to 1.2.
options.D: Change the pricing tier of the App Service plan.
options.E: Turn on the Incoming client certificates protocol setting.

explanation:
A: To configure Certificates for use in Azure Websites Applications you need to upload a public Certificate.
C: Over time, multiple versions of TLS have been released to mitigate different vulnerabilities. TLS 1.2 is the most current version available for apps running on
Azure App Service.
Incorrect Answers:
B: We need support the http url as well.
Note:
WebApp1 is an Azure web app that is accessible by using https://www.litwareinc.com and http://www.litwareinc.com.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/app-service-web-configure-tls-mutual-auth https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/updates/app-service-and-functions-hosted-apps-can-now-update-tls-versions/

Community vote distribution
BE (56%)                    AB (23%)                    11%                    11%
answer_summary: 'WebApp1 must enforce mutual authentication' means client-certificate authentication: turn on Incoming client certificates, and turn on HTTPS Only, because client certificates are only negotiated over TLS.

option_rationales.A: Uploading a public certificate is about serving TLS for the custom domain, not about requiring one from the client.
option_rationales.B: HTTPS Only is required — mutual TLS cannot happen over plain HTTP, and the app is currently reachable on both.
option_rationales.C: Setting a minimum TLS version hardens the connection but does not implement mutual authentication.
option_rationales.D: The pricing tier does not gate client-certificate authentication.
option_rationales.E: Turning on Incoming client certificates (Require) is what makes App Service demand a client certificate — the mutual half of mutual authentication.

verification.note: Answer changed from AC to BE (community 56% BE). The case study requirement is 'WebApp1 must enforce mutual authentication', and App Service implements that with client certificates, which additionally requires HTTPS Only. The app code then validates the forwarded certificate.

dragdrop_slots.Action 1: From the Azure portal, create an Azure AD administrator for LitwareSQLServer1.

dragdrop_slots.Action 3: In SQLDB1, create contained database users.

explanation:
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/azure-sql/database/authentication-aad-overview
answer_summary: Contained database users for Entra identities can only be created by an Entra-authenticated administrator, so you set the Entra admin on the server, connect as that admin with SSMS, and then create the users in SQLDB1.

slot_rationales.Action 3: Create the contained database users in SQLDB1 and grant them the database roles they need.

verification.note: Sequence unchanged; the syntax is CREATE USER [name] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER, and the same applies to managed identities and groups.

explanation:

answer_summary: Creating a resource group needs write permission at subscription scope (Contributor is enough), while managing permissions needs Microsoft.Authorization write — which Contributor explicitly lacks and Owner has.

answer_summary: Azure Disk Encryption requires the key vault to be in the same region and subscription as the VM, and KeyVault1 is the only vault that sits in VM4's region.

option_rationales.A: KeyVault1 is in the same region (West US) and subscription as VM4, which is what ADE requires.

option_rationales.C: KeyVault3 is likewise outside VM4's region.

verification.note: Community 100% A. The same-region, same-subscription rule for ADE key vaults is unchanged.

HOTSPOT -
You implement the planned changes for ASG1 and ASG2.
In which NSGs can you use ASG1, and the network interfaces of which virtual machines can you assign to ASG2?
Hot Area:
answer_summary: An application security group is bound to one virtual network: it can only be referenced by NSGs that protect resources in that network, and only network interfaces from that same network (and region) can be added to it.

question_stem:
You plan to implement JIT VM access.
Which virtual machines will be supported?

diagrams.diagram_description: Azure resource hierarchy diagram showing Tenant Root Group, MG1, Subscription1, and RG1.

answer_summary: Just-in-time access can only manage machines it can protect: an Azure VM with an NSG (or supported Azure Firewall) in front of it. Classic-deployment VMs and machines with no NSG are listed as unsupported.

option_rationales.A: The three VMs that meet the requirements — an Azure Resource Manager VM protected by an NSG — are supported.
option_rationales.B: One of the machines fails the prerequisites, so not all four qualify.
option_rationales.C: The stored key; the community reads the resource tables as excluding VM1 rather than VM2 and VM4.
option_rationales.D: A single VM would be right only if the others all lacked an NSG.

verification.note: Answer changed from C to A on the strength of a 98% community vote — but note the resource tables this question depends on were not captured in this bank, so the reasoning cannot be fully reconstructed here. The durable rule is the one in the summary: JIT needs an ARM VM with an NSG or supported Azure Firewall, and Defender for Servers Plan 2.

question_stem:
DRAG DROP -
You need to deploy AKS1 to meet the platform protection requirements.
Which four actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
NOTE: More than one order of answer choices is correct. You will receive credit for any of the correct orders you select.
Select and Place:
explanation:
Scenario: Azure AD users must be able to authenticate to AKS1 by using their Azure AD credentials.
Litware plans to deploy AKS1, which is a managed AKS (Azure Kubernetes Services) cluster.
Step 1: Create a server application
To provide Azure AD authentication for an AKS cluster, two Azure AD applications are created. The first application is a server component that provides user authentication.
Step 2: Create a client application
The second application is a client component that's used when you're prompted by the CLI for authentication. This client application uses the server application for the actual authentication of the credentials provided by the client.
Step 3: Deploy an AKS cluster.
Use the az group create command to create a resource group for the AKS cluster.
Use the az aks create command to deploy the AKS cluster.
Step 4: Create an RBAC binding.
Before you use an Azure Active Directory account with an AKS cluster, you must create role-binding or cluster role-binding. Roles define the permissions to grant, and bindings apply them to desired users. These assignments can be applied to a given namespace, or across the entire cluster.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/aks/azure-ad-integration

diagrams.diagram_description: Drag-drop answer area showing available actions (Deploy an AKS cluster, Create a client application, Create a server application, Create an RBAC binding, Create a custom RBAC role) on the left and four numbered target slots on the right.

answer_summary: The legacy AKS Entra integration needs both halves of the OAuth pair before the cluster exists: create the server application, create the client application, deploy the cluster referencing them, then bind Kubernetes roles to directory identities.

slot_rationales.Step 1: Create the server application, which validates tokens and exposes the group claims Kubernetes needs.
slot_rationales.Step 2: Create the client application, used by kubectl to sign users in.
slot_rationales.Step 3: Deploy the AKS cluster, supplying those application IDs so the API server trusts them.
slot_rationales.Step 4: Create an RBAC binding mapping directory users or groups to Kubernetes roles — without it, authenticated users have no permissions.

verification.note: Correct for the deprecated legacy integration. Current AKS uses AKS-managed Microsoft Entra integration, where no manual app registrations are needed and Azure RBAC for Kubernetes authorization can replace hand-written role bindings.

question_stem:
You need to ensure that users can access VM0. The solution must meet the platform protection requirements.
What should you do?

options.B: On Firewall, configure a network traffic filtering rule.
options.D: On Firewall, configure a DNAT rule.

explanation:
Azure Firewall has the following known issue:
Conflict with Azure Security Center (ASC) Just-in-Time (JIT) feature.
If a virtual machine is accessed using JIT, and is in a subnet with a user-defined route that points to Azure Firewall as a default gateway, ASC JIT doesn't work.
This is a result of asymmetric routing â€" a packet comes in via the virtual machine public IP (JIT opened the access), but the return path is via the firewall, which drops the packet because there is no established session on the firewall.
Solution: To work around this issue, place the JIT virtual machines on a separate subnet that doesn't have a user-defined route to the firewall.
Scenario:

| Name | Type | Description |
|------|------|-------------|
| Firewall1 | Azure Firewall | An Azure firewall on VNet1. |
| RT1 | Route table | A route table that will contain a route pointing to Firewall1 as the default gateway and will be assigned to Subnet0. |

Following the implementation of the planned changes, the IT team must be able to connect to VM0 by using JIT VM access.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/overview
answer_summary: The blocker is a documented conflict: if a VM sits in a subnet whose user-defined route sends traffic to Azure Firewall, just-in-time access breaks because the response traffic is asymmetric. Moving VM0 to the subnet without that route restores access.

option_rationales.A: Moving VM0 to Subnet1 takes it out of the subnet whose UDR points at the firewall, which resolves the JIT conflict.
option_rationales.B: A network rule on the firewall does not fix the asymmetric routing that breaks JIT.
option_rationales.C: Assigning the route table to AzureFirewallSubnet would make matters worse — that subnet must keep its default routing.
option_rationales.D: A DNAT rule would publish the VM through the firewall, which is not what the platform protection requirements ask for.

verification.note: Community 100% A. The JIT/forced-tunnelling conflict is still documented; Bastion is the usual way to avoid the whole problem.

You are evaluating the security of the network communication between the virtual machines in Sub2.
For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: From VM1, you can successfully ping the public IP address of VM2.
hotspot_rows.rationale: The outbound rules allow all traffic to the Internet, so pinging VM2's public IP address from VM1 succeeds.

hotspot_rows.statement: From VM1, you can successfully ping the private IP address of VM3.
hotspot_rows.rationale: VM3 is reachable over the private address space with the NSG rules in force between those subnets, so the ping succeeds.

hotspot_rows.statement: From VM1, you can successfully ping the private IP address of VM5.
hotspot_rows.rationale: VM5 is not reachable from VM1 — no route or allow rule joins them, so the ping fails.

explanation:
Box 1: Yes. All traffic is allowed out to the Internet so you can ping the public IP.
NSG1, NSG2, NSG3, and NSG4 have the outbound security rules shown in the following table.

| Priority | Port | Protocol | Source | Destination | Action |
|----------|------|----------|--------|-------------|--------|
| 65000 | Any | Any | VirtualNetwork | VirtualNetwork | Allow |
| 65001 | Any | Any | Any | Internet | Allow |
| 65500 | Any | Any | Any | Any | Deny |

Box 2: Yes. VM3 is on Subnet12. There is no NSG attached to Subnet12 so the traffic will be allowed by default.

Box 3: No (because VM5 is in a separate VNet).
Note: Sub2 contains the virtual machines shown in the following table.

| Name | Network interface | Application security group | Connected to |
|------|-------------------|---------------------------|-------------|
| VM1 | NIC1 | ASG1 | Subnet11 |
| VM2 | NIC2 | ASG2 | Subnet11 |
| VM3 | NIC3 | None | Subnet12 |
| VM4 | NIC4 | ASG1 | Subnet13 |
| VM5 | NIC5 | None | Subnet21 |

| Name | Associated to |
|------|---------------|
| NSG1 | NIC2 |
| NSG2 | Subnet11 |
| NSG3 | Subnet13 |
| NSG4 | Subnet21 |

| Name | Subnet |
|------|--------|
| VNetwork1 | Subnet11, Subnet12, and Subnet13 |
| VNetwork2 | Subnet21 |
answer_summary: Outbound rules allow all Internet traffic, and the VMs in the peered/same virtual network can reach each other, but the machine in the isolated network cannot be reached — so the first two pings succeed and the third does not.

hotspot_rows.rationale: The web server is reached over TCP, and the rule for ASG1 allows TCP to VM4 — so the connection from VM1 works even though its ping does not.

explanation:
Box 1: No. VM4 is in Subnet13 which has NSG3 attached to it.
VM1 is in ASG1. NSG3 would only allow ICMP pings from ASG2 but not ASG1. Only TCP traffic is allowed from ASG1.
NSG3 has the inbound security rules shown in the following table.

| Priority | Port | Protocol | Source | Destination | Action |
|----------|------|----------|--------|-------------|--------|
| 100 | Any | TCP | ASG1 | ASG1 | Allow |
| 150 | Any | Any | ASG2 | VirtualNetwork | Allow |
| 200 | Any | Any | Any | Any | Deny |
| 65000 | Any | Any | VirtualNetwork | VirtualNetwork | Allow |
| 65001 | Any | Any | AzureLoadBalancer | Any | Allow |
| 65500 | Any | Any | Any | Any | Deny |

Box 2: Yes.
VM2 is in ASG2. Any protocol is allowed from ASG2 so ICMP ping would be allowed.

Box3. VM1 is in ASG1. TCP traffic is allowed from ASG1 so VM1 could connect to the web server as connections to the web server would be on ports TCP 80 or TCP 443.

option_rationales.D: DDoS protection is a separate feature and not a prerequisite.

verification.note: Community 100% A. The subnet name and minimum size requirements are unchanged.

question_stem:
HOTSPOT -
You are evaluating the security of VM1, VM2, and VM3 in Sub2.
For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:

hotspot_rows.statement: From the Internet, you can connect to the web server on VM1 by using HTTP.
hotspot_rows.rationale: The NSG covering VM1 has an inbound rule allowing TCP 80, so the web server is reachable from the Internet.

hotspot_rows.statement: From the Internet, you can connect to the web server on VM2 by using HTTP.
hotspot_rows.rationale: No inbound rule permits port 80 for VM2, so the default DenyAllInBound applies and the connection fails.

hotspot_rows.statement: From the Internet, you can connect to the web server on VM3 by using HTTP.
hotspot_rows.rationale: VM3's NSG allows inbound HTTP, so its web server is reachable.

explanation:
VM1: Yes. NSG2 applies to VM1 and this allows inbound traffic on port 80.
NSG2, NSG3, and NSG4 have the outbound security rules shown in the following table.

| Priority | Port | Protocol | Source | Destination | Action |
|----------|------|----------|--------|-------------|--------|
| 65000 | Any | Any | VirtualNetwork | VirtualNetwork | Allow |
| 65001 | Any | Any | Any | Internet | Allow |
| 65500 | Any | Any | Any | Any | Deny |

VM2: No. NSG2 and NSG1 apply to VM2. NSG2 allows the inbound traffic on port 80 but NSG1 does not allow it.
VM3: Yes. There are no NSGs applying to VM3 so all ports will be open.
answer_summary: Whether HTTP reaches each web server depends on the NSG applied to that VM's NIC or subnet: two of them have an inbound rule allowing port 80, the third does not.

verification.note: Answers kept as stored. Note that a VM also needs a public IP (or a load balancer/NAT in front) for Internet traffic to arrive at all, which is the other half of this style of question.

Question
HOTSPOT -
You assign User8 the Owner role for RG4, RG5, and RG6.
In which resource groups can User8 create virtual networks and NSGs by using the Azure portal? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
Box 1: RG6 only -
The policy does not allow the creation of virtual networks/subnets in RG5. Only NSGs can be created in RG4.
RG2 and RG3 both have Read-only locks.
Box 2: The policy does not allow the creation of NSGs in RG5.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/policy/overview
answer_summary: Owner rights alone are not enough — Azure Policy still blocks the resource types it denies, and locks block writes. Only the resource groups where policy permits that type allow creation.

slot_rationales.User8 can create virtual networks in: RG6 only — the policy assignment prevents virtual networks being created in the other resource groups, whatever role User8 holds.
slot_rationales.User8 can create NSGs in: RG4 and RG6 only — NSGs are permitted there, while the policy blocks them elsewhere.

verification.note: The principle is the durable point: a Deny policy effect overrides RBAC, and a ReadOnly or CanNotDelete lock overrides both.

question_stem:
Question
HOTSPOT -
Which virtual networks in Sub1 can User9 modify and delete in their current state? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
Hot Area:
explanation:
Box 1: VNET4 and VNET1 only -
RG1 has only Delete lock, while there are no locks on RG4.
RG2 and RG3 both have Read-only locks.

Box 2: VNET4 only -
There are no locks on RG4, while the other resource groups have either Delete or Read-only locks.
Note: As an administrator, you may need to lock a subscription, resource group, or resource to prevent other users in your organization from accidentally deleting or modifying critical resources. You can set the lock level to CanNotDelete or ReadOnly. In the portal, the locks are called Delete and Read-only respectively.
=> CanNotDelete means authorized users can still read and modify a resource, but they can't delete the resource.
=> ReadOnly means authorized users can read a resource, but they can't delete or update the resource. Applying this lock is similar to restricting all authorized users to the permissions granted by the Reader role.
Scenario:
Sub1 contains six resource groups named RG1, RG2, RG3, RG4, RG5, and RG6.
User9 creates the virtual networks shown in the following table.

| Name | Resource group |
|------|----------------|
| VNET1 | RG1 |
| VNET2 | RG2 |
| VNET3 | RG3 |
| VNET4 | RG4 |

Sub1 contains the locks shown in the following table.

| Name | Set on | Lock type |
|------|--------|----------|
| Lock1 | RG1 | Delete |
| Lock2 | RG2 | Read-only |
| Lock3 | RG3 | Delete |
| Lock4 | RG3 | Read-only |

Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/resource-group-lock-resources
answer_summary: Locks decide this, not roles: a resource group with a CanNotDelete lock still allows modification, while a ReadOnly lock blocks both — so more networks can be modified than deleted.

slot_rationales.Virtual networks that User9 can modify: VNET4 and VNET1 — VNET1's resource group carries only a Delete lock (writes still allowed) and VNET4's group has no lock at all.
slot_rationales.Virtual networks that User9 can delete: VNET4 only — the CanNotDelete lock stops VNET1 being removed, and the ReadOnly locks elsewhere stop everything.

verification.note: Lock semantics are unchanged: CanNotDelete allows read and write but not delete; ReadOnly allows read only, and both are inherited by child resources.

question_stem:
Question
You need to ensure that you can meet the security operations requirements.
What should you do first?

options.A: Turn on Auto Provisioning in Security Center.
options.B: Integrate Security Center and Microsoft Cloud App Security.
options.C: Upgrade the pricing tier of Security Center to Standard.
options.D: Modify the Security Center workspace configuration.

explanation:
The Standard tier extends the capabilities of the Free tier to workloads running in private and other public clouds, providing unified security management and threat protection across your hybrid cloud workloads. The Standard tier also adds advanced threat detection capabilities, which uses built-in behavioral analytics and machine learning to identify attacks and zero-days exploits, access and application controls to reduce exposure to network attacks and malware, and more.
Scenario: Security Operations Requirements
Litware must be able to customize the operating system security configurations in Azure Security Center.
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security-center/security-center-pricing
answer_summary: The security operations capabilities in this scenario belong to the paid tier, so the first step is upgrading Security Center from Free to Standard on the subscription.

option_rationales.A: Auto provisioning deploys the agent, but the features being asked for are gated by the pricing tier.
option_rationales.B: The Cloud App Security integration shares alerts and discovery data; it is not the prerequisite.
option_rationales.C: Upgrading to Standard unlocks the workload protection and security operations features the requirements describe.
option_rationales.D: Changing the workspace configuration decides where data is stored, not which features are licensed.

verification.note: Community 100% C. Currency: Security Center is now Microsoft Defender for Cloud and Free/Standard has been replaced by per-workload Defender plans, so the modern equivalent is enabling the relevant Defender plan(s) on the subscription.
